_what: Trail, highlight and route links per stop, with the evidence tier for each one.
_why: The trail boxes were built when direct listing URLs could not be found, so half the named trails render as a search magnifier (135 of 265 main-loop items, 129 of 233 extension items). They can be found now. This file is the source; build_links.py injects it into STOPS/EXT_DATA. Editing the consts by hand is silently overwritten by the next build.

_tiers.official: Fetched from the managing authority (state park, NPS, USFS) and confirmed 200 with the expected content type, from this machine.
_tiers.indexed: Returned by web search with a matching title and a review count. The page itself could NOT be loaded — alltrails.com answers 403 to every request from here, so a 403 proves nothing either way. Real, but one tier below official.
_tiers.unlisted: Confirmed to exist by the managing authority, but no AllTrails listing found. Deliberately carries no trail link rather than a search that goes nowhere.

_match.exact: The official trail and the AllTrails listing are the same object.
_match.contains: The AllTrails listing is a longer user-assembled route that includes this official trail. Both are shown; the official name and length stay primary.

_uses: From the managing authority, not inferred. hike | bike | horse.
_cruise: true only where reviews support riding it at cruising pace on gravel tyres: rail-grade or packed surface, no walk sections, no puncture-hazard reports. Bike-legal is not sufficient. Technical singletrack is bike-legal nearly everywhere and is not what this flags.
_dogs: Dog rules per stop, each fetched from the managing authority and quoted. NOT generalised across authorities: the same agency gives opposite answers at neighbouring stops — Mesa Verde allows dogs on Wetherill Mesa and bans them on Chapin Mesa; Point Lobos will not let a dog stay in a parked car while Fort Ord, the other half of the same stop, has marked off-leash segments. 17 main-loop stops are deliberately still empty: the authority publishes no rule and inferring one would be the same error as a constructed URL.

caprock-canyons.dogs: Leashed at all times. Free-roaming bison on trails and on park roads — TPWD publishes a number, not a judgement call: "Stay at least 50 yards away. Never surround, crowd, approach or follow bison or any other park wildlife."
caprock-canyons.note: TPWD: 'All trails are multiuse unless otherwise indicated.' Every named trail here permits hiking, biking and equestrian, so use is an attribute, not a section. The canyon trails are rocky singletrack — bike-legal but not cruising.

biking.name: Caprock Canyons Trailway
biking.official_length: 64 mi, former Fort Worth & Denver rail bed, through the 742-ft Clarity Tunnel
biking.cruise_reason: Ruled out on rider reports, not on paper. Surface is a sand-and-clay mix needing 700x35c minimum; rocky for the ~13 mi from South Plains to Clarity Tunnel; repeated goathead puncture reports; the tunnel itself is sandy and guano-covered and has to be walked. Described as remote and for prepared riders.
biking.reviews_note: No star rating surfaced for this listing in any search result — count only, not an omission in the data entry.

blurb_fix.problem: The activity card says the Trailway is 'a flat, packed-gravel former rail bed'. Riders describe sand and clay, rock, and goatheads. That description reads as an invitation to a casual ride.
blurb_fix.with: former rail bed — sand and clay, rocky in sections, gravel tyres and puncture kit

Bike or walk the Caprock Canyons Trailwa.entity: Caprock Canyons State Park and Trailway
Bike or walk the Caprock Canyons Trailwa.cruise_reason: Sand and clay needing 700x35c, rocky for 13 mi, goathead punctures, and the tunnel has to be walked.

caprock-canyons.dogs_source_quote: Do not approach bison. Bison are wild. Stay at least 50 yards away.
caprock-canyons.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — TPWD publishes a NUMBER where our card says "substantial distance". The page states "Stay at least 50 yards away. Never surround, crowd, approach or follow bison or any other park wildlife." The card should carry 50 yards; a vague phrase is not actionable at a trailhead. Two further points: the leash rule on this page is only "Keep pets on leashes" (the 6 ft maximum comes from TPWD's statewide park rules, not this page), and "in the campground" COULD NOT BE SOURCED — TPWD describes free-roaming bison on the prairie and park roads but no TPWD page states they range through the campground. Note also TPWD ties the 50-yard distance to people, not specifically to dogs.

offroad.name: Forest Road 604
offroad.distance: not published on the free listing
offroad.difficulty: not published — Trails Offroad paywalls its difficulty scale
offroad.season: No published gate date found. FR 604 runs through the Jemez National Recreation Area at roughly 8,000 ft; late March is mud and residual snow season on Jemez forest roads. Stop arrives 24 Mar 2027 — treat access as unverified, not assured.
offroad.note: Not a Santa Fe day trip in the usual sense — FR 604 is in the western Jemez, an hour and a half out via Los Alamos, not on the Santa Fe side of the forest. Ponderosa and aspen, gentle grade, spur roads off it. One of only two roads in that area signed for dispersed camping. Santa Fe NF has repeatedly issued prescribed-burn advisories asking people to stay off FR 604 and FR 607 during burn windows — spring is burn season, so check before driving out.

great-sand-dunes.dogs: Leashed, 6 ft max. Permitted on Mosca Pass Trail (Preserve), Dunes Overlook Trail, Medano Pass Primitive Road, main use areas and Pinon Flats Campground. NOT permitted off the Dunes Overlook Trail, in the dunefield beyond the first high ridge, north of Point of No Return, or on Sand Ramp Trail.
great-sand-dunes.note: All five existing trail entries already carry direct URLs. This stop needs the dog overlay, not links: two of the five are explicitly dog-permitted and the dunefield ones are limited.
great-sand-dunes.needs_check_why: The NPS pets page names Mosca Pass and Dunes Overlook as permitted and the dunefield beyond the first high ridge as prohibited. It does not name Montville or Wellington either way. Not inferring — to be confirmed with the park.
great-sand-dunes.trail_dogs_why: NPS names Mosca Pass and Dunes Overlook as permitted and the dunefield beyond the first high ridge as prohibited, which rules out High Dune. It says nothing either way about Montville or Wellington Ditch, so those stay null and show no icon rather than a guess.
great-sand-dunes.dogs_source_quote: Pets are permitted on leash on Montville Trail and Mosca Pass Trail. Please be sure to clean up after your pet.
great-sand-dunes._verdict: SAND RAMP TRAIL IS NOT DOG-LEGAL. No trail was added to this stop. NPS names it in the prohibition, not the permission: pets are not allowed "North of Point of No Return, including Sand Ramp Trail". The stop's existing `dogs` text in links_db already says this and is correct. The dog is well served here regardless — Mosca Pass Trail, Dunes Overlook Trail and Montville Nature Trail are all on the card already, all three dogs:true, and the 30 Mar-3 Apr 2027 dates block none of them.

not_a_trail.problem: IT IS A REAL TRAIL — it is not a dog trail, which is the opposite of what this pass went looking for. NPS Great Sand Dunes pets page, fetched, lists where pets are NOT allowed and includes verbatim "North of Point of No Return, including Sand Ramp Trail", alongside "North of Castle Creek Picnic Area, except along Medano Pass Primitive Road", "Off of the Dunes Overlook Trail", and "In the backcountry of the dunefield, beyond the first high ridge of dunes". The permitted list on the same page is "the Preserve (including Mosca Pass Trail) and main use areas of the Park (including Piñon Flats Campground, Dunes Overlook Trail, and along the Medano Pass Primitive Road)", leash 6 feet (2 m) or less. The trail itself is an 11-mile route (NPS) starting in Loop 2 of Piñon Flats Campground and running along the foothills to Sand Creek; NPS calls it "most commonly used as an access to various backpacking sites along the foothills, rather than as a destination trail for scenery" and says that after the first two miles "much of this trail is sandy soil or pure sand". Reaching the usual trailhead does NOT need 4x4 — NPS states "Point of No Return Trailhead provides standard 2WD access to the Sand Ramp Trail" — but that trailhead is precisely the point north of which the dog may not go. ON THE SOUTHERN SECTION: the first stretch out of Piñon Flats, before Castle Creek Picnic Area, is where the Dunes Overlook spur leaves, and NPS explicitly permits pets on the Dunes Overlook Trail, so the dog can plainly walk that far. But NPS never publishes it as "Sand Ramp Trail south of X is permitted" — it publishes a permitted list of named places and a prohibition naming this trail. That walk is already on the card as Dunes Overlook Trail (2.8 mi, Moderate, 4.6 (1,159), dogs:true), which is the honest way to carry it. Recorded here so a later pass does not add Sand Ramp Trail to the trails box on the strength of a pet rule that in fact bans it.

not_a_route.entry: Beginner off-road trails near the Arkansas Valley
not_a_route.problem: A trail system, not a route. The concrete thing behind it is the Fourmile Travel Management Area north of Buena Vista — ~100,000 acres of USFS and BLM land with roughly 200 miles of roads and trails open to OHV: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r02/psicc/recreation/fourmile-travel-management-area . Worth noting the best-known named route there, Chinaman Gulch / Carnage Canyon, is the opposite of beginner — it is rated challenging. If a beginner route is wanted here it needs to be picked by name from the Fourmile map, not from this phrase.

not_a_route.entry: Loaded camper: graded, dry roads only.
not_a_route.problem: A standing rig constraint filed as a list item, and one that no longer applies: every offroad route on this trip is driven in the towed 4x4, never the coach. Nothing to research and nothing to link.

scenicDrives_patch.name: US-50 through Bighorn Sheep Canyon
scenicDrives_patch.note: The Arkansas River canyon on US-50 between Salida and Parkdale (12 mi west of Canon City). Over 400 bighorn sheep use the cliffs; the pullouts along the river are the viewing. No designated-byway page exists for this stretch, so the Royal Gorge Region tourism board page is the best available source. Truck day-trip, as with every drive.
scenicDrives_patch.season: US-50 is a year-round primary route; no seasonal gate. Arrive 3 Apr 2027 — open, but early-April ice and rockfall are normal in the canyon.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: royalgorgeregion.com; visitcos.com directory

salida-buenavista.dogs: Only one of these has a published rule: Hecla Junction sits in the Arkansas Headwaters Recreation Area, where Colorado Parks and Wildlife lists leashed dogs as permitted — the Forest Service publishes nothing for Waterdog Lakes or Old Monarch Pass, and Salida's code is contradictory (7-5-250 allows a leashed dog in any public space, 7-5-220 calls a dog in an undesignated part of a park a nuisance), so the town and Tenderfoot trails stay unknown.

estes-rmnp.dogs: PROHIBITED on every trail. NPS: 'Pets are prohibited on ALL Rocky Mountain National Park trails, tundra, and meadows.' Leashed pets are confined to roads, parking areas, campgrounds and picnic areas. Violations are citable, with a mandatory court appearance in Denver.
estes-rmnp.dogs_impact: Five nights, 11-16 Apr 2027, and not one of the eight trails on this card can be walked with the dog. This is not a link problem and it is the most important thing on the stop.

estes-rmnp.activities_note: Every highlight here carries the red no-dogs pill. NPS bans pets from ALL RMNP trails, tundra and meadows, so four of these five are things the dog cannot come on — the exception being Trail Ridge Road, which is a drive.

offroad.name: Old Fall River Road
offroad.distance: 11 mi
offroad.difficulty: one-way uphill, primarily gravel
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP, WITHOUT AMBIGUITY. NPS's own opening/closing record for 1921-2009 shows the earliest opening ever recorded as 6 June (1935), with most years opening late June to 4 July. The stop is 11-16 Apr 2027 — the road has never in its recorded history been open that early. The dates table is at https://www.nps.gov/romo/learn/photosmultimedia/opening_closing_trr_ofr.htm
offroad.note: The first auto route into the park's high country, opened 1920, ending at the Alpine Visitor Center. NPS states 11 miles; recent news coverage of openings says 9.4 miles — the discrepancy is unresolved and the NPS figure is used here. Note also that pets are prohibited on all RMNP trails, tundra and meadows, so this is a drive-only outing even when it is open.

offroad.name: Pole Hill Road (FSR 122 / FSR 247)
offroad.difficulty: rated Easy 4 on the 4x4Explore scale; the Forest Service says only that the road is rough
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. The seasonal motorized period is 15 Jun to 30 Nov; the stop is 11-16 Apr 2027. The Forest Service page itself publishes no dates — the 15 Jun-30 Nov window comes from 4x4Explore's transcription of the Canyon Lakes Ranger District MVUM (https://www.4x4explore.com/rds/p_rds/pole_hl.html), which gives the same window for every 4x4 road in this district.
offroad.note: Loop road three miles east of Estes Park off Highway 36, including the Panorama Peak loop. Starts on private land; the National Forest boundary is 0.9 miles from the highway. USFS: "Dispersed camping with trailers along #122 is not recommended due to the roughness of the road" and "there is no access from Larimer County Road 18E to the east side of Pole Hill Road."
offroad.source: USFS Arapaho and Roosevelt NF (Canyon Lakes RD)

offroad.name: Johnny Park Road (FSR 118)
offroad.distance: 5.5 mi
offroad.difficulty: rated Easy 4 on the 4x4Explore scale; the Forest Service describes the road as rough
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. COTREX, the state's official trail register, records 15 Jun-30 Nov seasonal motorized access for 4.9 of the 5.5 miles, with 0.6 miles open year-round (https://trails.colorado.gov/roads/johnny-park-7505). The stop is 11-16 Apr 2027.
offroad.note: Reached 9.5 miles east of Estes Park on Highway 36 — a forest access sign directs you west on a gravel road toward the Big Elk Meadows subdivision, and Johnny Park Road is six miles along it. Also reachable from Big Owl or Cabin Creek Road north of Meeker Park. USFS: "Dispersed camping with a trailer is very limited on #118 due to the roughness of the road."
offroad.source: USFS Arapaho and Roosevelt NF (Canyon Lakes RD)

offroad.name: Pierson Park Road (FSR 119)
offroad.distance: 9.75 mi per COTREX; 13.61 mi including both segments per 4x4Explore
offroad.difficulty: rated Easy 4 on the 4x4Explore scale; the Forest Service publishes no grade
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. COTREX records 15 Jun-30 Nov seasonal access for 4WD vehicles, ATVs and motorcycles alike (https://trails.colorado.gov/roads/pierson-park-14192). The stop is 11-16 Apr 2027.
offroad.note: USFS: "High-clearance vehicles are recommended on this popular road south of Estes Park" and "Be aware of private property in the area." A Forest Service closure order has at times shut the southern portion of FSR 119 at its junction with County Road 82, so check the forest's alerts page before relying on a through route. The blunt summary for this stop: there is no driveable dirt near Estes Park in mid-April — every 4x4 road here sits behind a 15 June gate, and Old Fall River Road behind a June-at-the-earliest one.
offroad.source: USFS Arapaho and Roosevelt NF (Canyon Lakes RD)

flaming-gorge.dogs_source_quote: Dogs and other pets must be leashed or under direct control at all times.
flaming-gorge.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — the second half of our card is not the authority's. "Campgrounds are stricter — leashed at all times inside the campground" appears nowhere on the Ashley NF page, which states one forest-wide rule and no separate campground rule. wind-river.authority: USDA Forest Service — Bridger-Teton National Forest
wind-river.problem: All three entries in the trail box were TRAILHEADS, not trails — car parks with signboards. Replaced with the actual routes that leave them, per the rule that a trail entry must be a trail and must carry distance, time, difficulty and reviews.
wind-river.seasonal: The stop's own blurb, note and red weather flag already say the alpine trailheads are snowed in at this date. The trail box was the only part of the card that did not. Elkhart Park sits at 9,500 ft and winter road maintenance stops ~3 miles short of it, just past White Pine Ski Area; conditions reports put reliable access at mid-to-late June. Arrival is 24 Apr 2027, seven nights. Every trail below is out of reach on this visit and is tagged as such rather than removed — the stop is a deliberate lower-elevation scouting stop and the real Wind River visit is Pinedale, late May 2028, on the East trip.

trails.name: CCC Ponds Trail
trails.time: about 20 min on foot (8 min riding)
trails.difficulty: Easy — Trailforks grades it green; Pacer rates the walking route easy at about 6.6 ft of gain
trails.reviews: no AllTrails listing — official source only. Tripadvisor shows 4.5 from 17 for the CCC Ponds Recreation Area as a whole; no trail database publishes a review count
trails.dogs_note: BLM Pinedale Field Office land. BLM's own recreation guidance is that dogs are welcome on most BLM-managed trails and that leash policy is a local matter; the Pinedale office publishes no specific rule for CCC Ponds. Same sourcing standard used at Salida. NOT taken from AllTrails, which does not list this trail at all.
trails.season: The valley floor at about 7,430 ft, four miles from Pinedale, fed by Fremont Lake runoff. Part of the area is groomed for cross-country skiing in winter, which is the clearest signal that it is snow-covered rather than closed; by a 24 Apr arrival it is the first thing in the district to be walkable, and it may be wet. This is the answer to the stop's own recorded low-elevation gap.
trails.note: A short dirt singletrack loop around ponds the Civilian Conservation Corps built in the 1930s, at the foot of the Winds — riparian, birdy, and the one place at this stop you can walk the dog without waiting for June. Restrooms at the parking area.
trails.note_source: BLM Wyoming recreation page (authority); Trailforks for surface, length and green grade; Pacer for distance, gain and easy rating; Singletracks for the dirt-loop-versus-paved-path split; outdooractive/recreation.gov for elevation

offroad.name: Big Sandy Road (CR 118) to Big Sandy Trailhead
offroad.distance: roughly 60 miles from Pinedale — US-191 south ~12 mi, WY-353 ~15.5 mi, then Big Sandy–Elkhorn Road / CR 118 gravel to the trailhead
offroad.difficulty: graded gravel, not technical — the obstacle is snow and mud, not terrain
offroad.season: CONFLICTS WITH THE STOP DATES. Bridger-Teton opens Big Sandy Campground and trailhead access only once the snowpack lets the gravel road through — usually somewhere between June and July, closing early September. The stop arrives 24 Apr 2027, six to ten weeks before the road is normally driveable. Plan on the gate or the drifts stopping the truck well short of the trailhead.
offroad.note: Renamed from a verb phrase to the road it actually is. The Big Sandy Opening is the standard gateway to the Bridger Wilderness, which is why it is on the card, but late April is the wrong end of the year for it. Exact opening date varies every year with snow load — the Pinedale Ranger District is the only source that will know.

wind-river.dogs: Bridger-Teton's only dog order is somewhere else entirely — named Jackson Ranger District trails, 1 Dec to 1 May — and neither the Greater Yellowstone wilderness order (GYCC-7) nor any Pinedale Ranger District page says anything about dogs, so all four Wind River routes are unstated rather than confirmed.
wind-river.dogs_source_quote: Possessing a dog in or on the Described Areas and Described Trails unless it is tethered by a leash not longer than six feet.
wind-river._review: 7 nights, arrive 24 Apr 2027 at Boulder, WY. The card's four trails are all correct Wind River routes and every one of them is unreachable — Elkhart Park is at 9,500 ft with winter maintenance stopping three miles short, and AllTrails' entire Boulder index is 11-to-44-mile wilderness backpacks with June-to-October windows. The db already recorded the real gap: 'CCC Ponds and the New Fork River corridor... need a Wyoming Game & Fish / BLM source, not a trail-database one — outstanding.' That is what is closed here. Two additions rather than four, because a search of everything AllTrails indexes for Boulder and Pinedale turned up nothing else below the snow line — a short box that is true beats a full one that is not.

twin-falls.authority: City of Twin Falls / NPS (City of Rocks) / Idaho

trails.name: Snake River Canyon Rim Trail
trails.cruise_reason: Fully paved the whole way, mostly flat, and reviewers describe it as made for a family ride or pushing a stroller. Limited shade and wind are the only caveats. Passes right under Perrine Bridge.
trails.was: Snake River Canyon Rim Trail — had a review count but no star; 4.6 now sourced.

trails.name: Shoshone Falls Observation Deck Trail
trails.note_source: Paved path and boardwalk to several vantage points over the 900 ft-wide falls. Reviewers report the route can be poorly marked. Dog-friendly.
trails.was: Not in the trails box at all — Shoshone Falls was a highlight with no trail entry.

trails.name: Stripe Rock to North Fork Circle Creek Trail
trails.note_source: City of Rocks. Replaces a "South Fork Circle Creek and North Fork Circle Loop" entry whose url was constructed from the name and 404d — that loop is real and rated 4.8 from 375, but no search returned a direct link for it, so it is not linked here.
trails.was: Not in the trails box — City of Rocks was a highlight with no trails.

trails.name: Creekside Towers Trail
trails.note_source: City of Rocks — the reserve's most popular short loop, through the granite towers.

twin-falls.note: No star rating surfaced for this listing, only the review count.
twin-falls.dogs: Snake River Canyon Rim Trail and the Shoshone Falls observation trail are both reported dog-friendly. City of Rocks is an NPS-managed National Reserve co-managed with Idaho State Parks — leash rules apply; trail-by-trail policy not separately verified.
twin-falls.drop_note_why: It explained why the stop moved from mid-May to 1 May — reasoning that mattered while the date was being decided and is now history sitting above the things you act on. Its own conclusion is that you cannot know until about two weeks out anyway, since Shoshone Falls depends on federal releases from the Upper Snake reservoirs rather than the calendar. Removed from the card; the Idaho Power and USGS reasoning is preserved here and in git history if the date is ever revisited.

offroad.name: Devil's Corral / Snake River Rim Recreation Area
offroad.distance: 20 mi of routes across roughly 206 acres
offroad.difficulty: mostly beginner terrain with some intermediate and no expert; mostly hard-packed dirt with sandy patches and scattered rocks
offroad.season: OPEN ON THESE DATES. Published as year-round, daylight hours only (5am to 10pm). The stop is 1-3 May 2027 — no conflict.
offroad.note: On the Snake River canyon rim immediately north of Twin Falls; the hill Evel Knievel launched from in 1974 is visible from it. Managed by the BLM Twin Falls District and Jerome County, and registered 4x4 vehicles are permitted alongside motorcycles, ATVs and UTVs. Camping and overnight parking prohibited. Access: US-93 north about 5 miles, right onto Shoshone Falls Road just after the Perrine Bridge, parking about 100 yards on the right. No BLM page for this area could be found, so the mileage and difficulty are community-sourced and unverified against the land manager.
offroad.source: RiderPlanet USA (area managed by BLM Twin Falls District / Jerome County)

offroad.name: City of Rocks Back Country Byway
offroad.distance: 49 mi
offroad.difficulty: not published by NPS; the page describes only a "narrow, winding road" at Circle Creek Overlook
offroad.season: CONFLICTS — likely still impassable in places. NPS states "Many roads are not maintained during the winter and may become impassable from late November through May" (https://www.nps.gov/ciro/planyourvisit/basicinfo.htm). The stop is 1-3 May 2027, inside that window. The reserve is open 24/7 year-round but its roads are not maintained. Phone reserve headquarters before planning a day around it.
offroad.note: A 49-mile loop beginning in Albion, forming a half-circle around the Albion Mountain Range and passing through City of Rocks National Reserve. Roughly 65-75 miles from Twin Falls, so a full day out. NPS does not state which sections are gravel and which are paved — the surface breakdown could not be sourced.
offroad.source: NPS City of Rocks National Reserve

offroad.name: Milner Historic Recreation Area roads
offroad.season: UNKNOWN. No seasonal closure is published for this site, and an absence of dates is not confirmation that it is open — recorded as genuinely unknown.
offroad.note: BLM site on the south side of the Snake River about 9 miles west of Burley, roughly 2,050 acres with four miles of river shoreline — the largest accessible stretch of public land on the river in the Magic Valley. Oregon Trail ruts cross the loop road in a couple of places. The only vehicle guidance BLM publishes is that "RV's and large trailers are recommended to use the west entrance into the historic recreation area due to low clearance on the east end" — irrelevant for the truck, but it is the only road note there is. No road name, length, surface or difficulty is published; the Burley Field Office, 208-677-6600, would settle it.

twin-falls.dogs_source_quote: Dogs and other domestic animals are welcome in campsites and on trails.
twin-falls.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — our card hedges where the authority does not. It says City of Rocks' "trail-by-trail policy not separately verified"; the NPS page in fact states plainly that dogs are welcome on trails, leashed to 6 ft ("All pets must be restrained on a leash no longer than 6 feet."), with the Visitor Center the only exclusion. The hedge can be dropped. SEPARATELY UNSOURCED: the card's first sentence — Snake River Canyon Rim Trail and the Shoshone Falls observation trail "both reported dog-friendly" — is NOT covered by this page. Those are City of Twin Falls facilities, not NPS, and "reported" is not an authority. That half of the card remains unsourced. Also note the page does not mention Idaho State Parks co-management.

sawtooth-nra.authority: USDA Forest Service — Sawtooth National Recreation Area
sawtooth-nra.dogs: Allowed. Sawtooth Wilderness Regulations: "Dogs must be on leash while on trails from July 1 through Labor Day." The stay is 3–6 May 2027, OUTSIDE that window, so the leash requirement does not apply on these dates — voice control is the standard elsewhere on the forest and a leash is still the sensible choice around Redfish Lake's trailheads. One hard exclusion anywhere in the wilderness: "Dogs are not allowed in the Goat Creek drainage (tributary of the South Fork of the Payette River)." None of the trails on this card is in that drainage.

trails.name: Fishhook Creek Trail
trails.was: Fishhook Creek Trail / Redfish Lake trails — no url, two trails in one entry
trails.season: Best May-October — arrival is 3 May, the very start of it.

trails.name: Redfish Lake Loop

offroad.name: Yankee Fork Road (FR 070)
offroad.distance: 25 mi
offroad.difficulty: Easy; graded gravel with potholes after rain. "Standard high-clearance vehicle in dry conditions."
offroad.season: PARTIAL CONFLICT. "Snow closes the upper road from late November through April most years" — so the lower road may be driveable on 3-6 May 2027, but the upper section is marginal and everything worth stopping for is shut until Memorial Day weekend. No Forest Service opening date is published for this road.
offroad.note: Begins at Sunbeam on Highway 75 between Stanley and Challis and runs north up the Yankee Fork tributary of the Salmon River past the dredge tailings toward Bonanza and Custer. The lower few miles are the most likely thing to be driveable in early May of anything researched for this stop.
offroad.source: Ordealist (road managed by USFS Salmon-Challis National Forest)

offroad.name: Custer Motorway (FR 013 / FR 070)
offroad.distance: 46 mi
offroad.difficulty: Moderate; graded gravel for most of the route, deteriorating to rougher dirt on the climbs near the divide. "High-clearance vehicle. Not recommended for low-clearance vehicles or trailers."
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. "Snow closure. The route closes from approximately November through May." The destination is shut too: the Custer townsite opens Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day, and the Yankee Fork Gold Dredge runs tours from the Saturday before Memorial Day. The stop is 3-6 May 2027, three to four weeks before any of that opens.
offroad.note: The historic 1879 freight road from Challis to the Custer and Bonanza ghost towns, about 21 miles northeast of Stanley. FR 013 is the southern access, FR 070 the northern. The Salmon-Challis National Forest's own Custer Ghost Town page publishes no road number, mileage, surface or season, so the figures here are community-sourced and could not be verified against the Forest Service. One consolation for these dates: Bayhorse ghost town, in Land of the Yankee Fork State Park near Challis, opens for the season on 1 May, which does fall inside this stay.
offroad.source: Ordealist (route managed by USFS Salmon-Challis National Forest)

offroad.name: Fourth of July Creek Road (FSR 209)
offroad.season: UNKNOWN — no opening date is published. The Sawtooth National Forest trailhead page gives no road name, length, surface, vehicle recommendation or season, and the forest's current-conditions page carries no road status list for the Stanley area. The trailhead sits well above 7,000 ft in the White Clouds so early May is very unlikely, but that is inference, not a sourced date.
offroad.note: Recorded deliberately as an absence rather than dropped. The Forest Service confirms the trailhead exists and that it serves hikers, backpackers and pack animals, but publishes nothing about the access road. A call to the Sawtooth NF Supervisor's Office, 208-423-7500, would settle whether it is driveable in early May.

sawtooth-nra.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be on leash while on trails from July 1 through Labor Day.

trails.name: Inferno Cone Viewpoint

trails.note_source: Steep and short — 360-degree views over the Great Rift, the Snake River Plain and the Pioneers. Best-rated walking trail in the monument.

craters-of-the-moon.dogs: NPS: "Pets are not allowed on any trails or in the visitor center even if they are carried." Leashed pets "may walk on the road, in the campground, and in parking areas" (leash max six feet). Lava surfaces exceed 150F in summer.

offroad.name: BLM backcountry primitive road network (Arco-Minidoka Road, Laidlaw Road and connections)
offroad.difficulty: NPS: "Backcountry roads on the BLM portion of the monument are unpaved and can present challenging driving conditions any time of year", naming wash-outs, large sharp rocks, soft mud and no shoulder. BLM: "A network of primitive roads in the BLM backcountry offer driving and exploration opportunities for motorists with high-clearance, 4-wheel-drive vehicles" (https://www.blm.gov/visit/craters-moon-national-monument).
offroad.season: No seasonal gate is published for the BLM roads — NPS says conditions are challenging "any time of year", which is a warning rather than a closure. Early May is the mud end of that. The stop is 6-7 May 2027; treat as open but conditions-dependent, not as confirmed passable.
offroad.note: The park requires rather than recommends specific kit for these roads: "a high clearance, 4-wheel drive vehicle, a fire extinguisher, and a good map", and directs visitors to download the BLM travel map first (https://www.blm.gov/sites/blm.gov/files/Craters-of-the-moon_map.pdf). That map classifies roads only as improved or unimproved and names Arco-Minidoka Road, Laidlaw Road, North Laidlaw Road, Turnbull Road, Moran Road, Split Top Road, Wood Road, Wapi Road, Bear Trap Ice Caves Road, Arco-Caves Road, Kimama Road and Carey-Kimama Road, publishing no individual mileages. On the off-road prohibition, a BLM travel-tips PDF states that cross-country motorized travel is not allowed within the monument except immediately adjacent to roads — that wording came from a search snippet because the PDF itself returned 502 twice, so treat the exact phrasing as indexed rather than confirmed.
offroad.source: NPS Craters of the Moon NM & Preserve / BLM Idaho

offroad.name: Craters of the Moon Loop Road
offroad.distance: 7 mi
offroad.difficulty: paved — listed for its season, not its difficulty
offroad.season: PROBABLY OPEN, AND THIS IS THE DATE THAT MATTERS. NPS: "The Loop Road is typically open from mid April through late November as conditions allow." It is closed to motor vehicles "each year, generally from the late fall to late spring, when snow and ice accumulations create hazardous conditions". The stop is 6-7 May 2027, past the mid-April typical opening — but recent years have seen it reopen in stages, one segment at a time, so a partial opening is possible.
offroad.note: Paved, not an off-road route; included because it is the only maintained road in the NPS half of the monument and because its reopening is the one genuinely date-sensitive fact for this one-night stop. Reaches the cinder cones, the lava flow trails and Lava Flow Campground.
offroad.source: NPS Craters of the Moon NM & Preserve

offroad.name: Laidlaw Park Kipuka driving tour
offroad.season: No seasonal dates published. Same conditions caveat as the rest of the BLM backcountry network — unpaved, challenging any time of year, and early May is mud season.
offroad.note: BLM-Idaho's Shoshone Field Office publishes a georeferenced driving-tour map "to assist adventurous folks with 4WD vehicles interested in exploring the Laidlaw Park Kipuka of the Craters of the Moon Monument and Preserve." A companion brochure, 'Laidlaw Park: Sagebrush Oasis', is referenced. No route mileage or difficulty is published. Laidlaw Park is the large kipuka — an island of older ground surrounded by lava — in the southern, BLM-managed half of the monument.
offroad.source: BLM Idaho Shoshone Field Office (via AmeriGEOSS dataset listing)

yellowstone.dogs_source_quote: Pets are only allowed in developed areas and must stay within 100 feet (30.5 meters) of roads, parking areas, and campgrounds.

trails.time: about 45 min each way at walking pace; NPS publishes no time
trails.difficulty: Easy — NPS describes it as 'mostly level'. Asphalt.
trails.elevation_gain: NPS publishes none for this path; it is listed as 'mostly level'.
trails.needs: No trail-database listing was found for the Apgar-to-West-Glacier bike path under any name read, so it carries no rating and no review count. This is a recorded absence, not a failure to look — §3, 'no AllTrails listing, official source only'.

trails.dogs_source: NPS Glacier Pets page, verbatim: 'When the bike path between Apgar and West Glacier is free of snow dogs are allowed on leash.' This is the only place in Glacier National Park where NPS permits a dog off pavement-adjacent developed areas, and the only walk on this five-night stop the dog may legally take.

other_links.label: NPS — Hiking Lake McDonald (official mileage table)
other_links.note: 'Apgar Bike Path — 1.5 mi (2.4 km), mostly level. Trailhead: Asphalt path south of Apgar Backcountry Permit Office.'

trails.season: The dog permission is conditional on the path being FREE OF SNOW — that is NPS's own wording, not a paraphrase. At Apgar's 3,150 ft, 22-27 May is normally well clear, but it is the one thing to confirm on arrival at the visitor centre rather than assume.
trails.note: Entered as a trail because for this stop it is the single most consequential walk on the card: Glacier bans pets from every trail in the park and names this one exception. It runs along the Middle Fork side from West Glacier village to Apgar on Lake McDonald — flat, asphalt, and it ends at the lake shore with the classic view straight up the lake to the peaks. If the dog gets one outing a day for five days, this is it.

trails.name: Johns Lake Loop
trails.difficulty: Easy — 160 ft of gain over three miles. AllTrails: 84% of reviewers say this trail is easy.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed; the en-gb mirror read 3,201 the same day. No star rating was visible.
trails.dogs_source: NPS Glacier bans pets on all trails; no exception is named for this one.

other_links.label: NPS — Hiking Lake McDonald (official mileage table)
other_links.note: 'Johns Lake Loop — 3 mi (4.8 km), Elevation gain: 160 ft (49 m). Trailhead: Johns Lake Trailhead.'

trails.season: Low-elevation west-side forest just above Lake McDonald Lodge, on the section of Going-to-the-Sun Road that is plowed and open all year. It is walkable on these dates with no alpine question attached — which is precisely why it belongs on this card and not on a July one.
trails.note: The easy day this box was missing. Cedar and hemlock forest, Johns Lake itself, and — the real reason to go — Sacred Dancing Cascade and McDonald Falls on McDonald Creek, both running hard in late May on snowmelt. It is the best low-effort half-day available when the pass is shut, and it is at its absolute best on exactly these dates.

trails.name: Apgar Lookout Trail
trails.distance: 3.6 mi (5.8 km) one way — 7.2 mi (11.6 km) round trip
trails.time: 4-5 hours round trip; NPS publishes no time
trails.difficulty: Strenuous — a sustained climb of roughly 1,850-1,966 ft in 3.6 miles on switchbacks.
trails.elevation_gain: 1,850 ft (564 m) per NPS's Lake McDonald mileage table; 1,966 ft (599 m) per NPS's own Apgar Lookout Trailhead place page, with 107 ft of loss. Both are NPS figures and they disagree; both are recorded rather than one being picked.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible.
trails.dogs_source: NPS Glacier bans pets on all trails; no exception is named for this one.

other_links.label: NPS — Apgar Lookout Trailhead
other_links.note: 'Distance: 3.6 mi (5.8 km), one way. Elevation gain: 1,966 ft (599 m). Elevation loss: 107 ft (33 m).' Trailhead 0.5 mi north of the West Entrance then 2.4 mi down Quarter Circle Bridge Road. The view from the lookout is the one on the park's live webcam.

other_links.label: NPS — Hiking Lake McDonald (official mileage table)

trails.season: This is the reason it is on the card. The lookout sits at about 5,200 ft on a south-and-west-facing slope, and AllTrails' own description says the route 'is often free of snow in the late spring or early summer' — it is the recognised early-season Glacier hike, walkable weeks before anything at Logan Pass. It is graded Hard, which §3 normally pushes down the card, but on THESE dates it is the only real summit view in reach and it stays.
trails.note: The one proper climb available on 22-27 May, and it answers the exact problem this stop has: with the pass shut there is no high viewpoint on the card at all. A 1930s fire lookout above the west end of Lake McDonald, looking straight down the lake into the peaks and out over the Middle Fork. Steep and shadeless in its upper half after the 2003 Robert Fire; carry water and start early.

other_links.label: NPS — Logan Pass opening and closing dates, 1933 to present

trails.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. The trailhead is behind the Logan Pass Visitor Center and is reachable only when the alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road has been plowed open. NPS's own opening record shows Logan Pass has not opened before 19 June in the last fifteen years (24 Jun 2010, 13 Jul 2011, 19 Jun 2012, 21 Jun 2013, 13 Jul 2020, 25 Jun 2021, 13 Jul 2022), and only twice in ninety years has it opened as early as this stop's 22-27 May window. Even in the freak year that the gate is open, the boardwalk itself is normally under several feet of snow into July. Do not build a day around it.
trails.note: Listed deliberately as the thing these dates are costing, not as a plan. It is the most-walked trail in Glacier and the one everybody means by 'we went to Glacier' — boardwalk out from Logan Pass across the Hanging Gardens, mountain goats and bighorn at arm's length, and the Overlook onto Hidden Lake under Bearhat Mountain. Coming through on 22-27 May buys an empty west side, running waterfalls and no shuttle queue, and pays for it with this. Knowing that in advance is the point of the entry. The other big Logan Pass walks — the Highline Trail and Piegan Pass — are shut for the same reason and on the same evidence.

glacier.dogs_source_quote: Pets are not permitted on trails, along lake shores outside of developed locations, in the backcountry, or in any building.
glacier.dogs_source_note: Bike-path wording confirmed but conditional: the page says "When the bike path between Apgar and West Glacier is free of snow dogs are allowed on leash." Our card's "when snow-free" matches.
glacier.dates_checked: 22-27 May 2027, 5 nights, based at West Glacier. This date is the whole story of this stop and the previous selection did not reflect it.
glacier.trails_note: The card had Avalanche Lake, Trail of the Cedars, and a line of prose — 'Rocky Point and lower Lake McDonald walks.' — which §3 rejects as a box item; Rocky Point is a real NPS trail at 1.1 mi one way with 85 ft of gain from 0.2 mi north of Fish Creek Campground, and that is what the line means. The re-selection question for 22-27 May is not 'what are the best trails in Glacier', it is 'what is REACHABLE on 22-27 May', and the honest answer is: only the west side, only as far up Going-to-the-Sun Road as it has been plowed, which in late May is normally Avalanche Creek. Everything the park is famous for above that — Logan Pass, the Highline, Hidden Lake, Grinnell — is behind a closed gate. So this box gets three walkable additions chosen for that constraint, plus Hidden Lake Overlook entered as CLOSED so the card says out loud what the dates are costing.
glacier.gtsr_evidence: NPS's own record of Logan Pass opening dates (nps.gov/glac/learn/news/logan-pass-opening-and-closing-dates.htm) is unambiguous. Openings since 2010: 24 Jun 2010, 13 Jul 2011, 19 Jun 2012, 21 Jun 2013, 13 Jul 2020, 25 Jun 2021, 13 Jul 2022. The earliest opening in the whole 90-year record is 16 May 1987; the second earliest is 22 May 2005. In the last fifteen years the pass has never opened before 19 June. Arriving 22 May and leaving 27 May 2027, plan on the alpine section being shut and treat any opening as a windfall.
glacier.dogs_stop_level: NPS Glacier, Pets page, verbatim: 'Pets are not permitted on trails, along lake shores outside of developed locations, in the backcountry, or in any building.' There is exactly ONE named exception in the whole park and it is worth the dog's entire five nights: 'When the bike path between Apgar and West Glacier is free of snow dogs are allowed on leash.' It is entered below as a trail for that reason. NPS also warns that when a road is closed to vehicle traffic it counts as backcountry and dogs are NOT allowed — which matters here, because the closed upper Going-to-the-Sun Road is exactly the sort of walk that looks like a road and is legally a trail.

waterton.dogs: Allowed on trails, on a leash of 3 m or less — Parks Canada, and it is the law. Local bulletins close specific trails to dogs (groomed ski trails in winter, wildlife closures); check trailhead boards. This is the opposite of the US parks earlier on this leg.
waterton.dogs_impact: First stop on the trip where the dog can walk a national-park trail. Waterton follows five nights in Glacier where it could not leave the road.

trails.elevation_gain: Parks Canada publishes no elevation figure for this trail; it is effectively flat along the shore. Recorded as unpublished rather than guessed.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible.

trails.season: Walkable all year and not avalanche-exposed — Parks Canada's avalanche advisory covers the Moderate and Difficult Lake Louise trails, not this one. One caution specific to these dates: Lake Louise is a high, cold lake that commonly still carries ice into the first part of June, so on 30 May - 4 Jun the water may be white or grey rather than the turquoise the photographs promise. Parks Canada does not publish a thaw date, so this is flagged as a thing to check on the Lake Louise webcam the week before rather than stated as fact. It changes the pictures, not the walk.
trails.note: The omission that mattered on this card: five nights in Banff and nothing at all at Lake Louise. This is the walk everyone does and it earns it — straight out from the Chateau along the north shore under the Fairview cliffs to the head of the lake, where the Victoria Glacier fills the whole view and the quartzite climbing walls rise on the right. Flat, an hour, and the dog can come. Go at first light; by ten the lakeshore and its car park are full.

trails.name: Sundance Canyon Loop
trails.distance: 9.5 km (5.9 mi) round trip — a paved 3.7 km approach from Cave and Basin each way plus the canyon loop at the far end
trails.difficulty: Moderate — Parks Canada files it under the Banff area's Moderate hikes. The approach itself is paved and level; the canyon loop is where the climbing and the steps are.
trails.elevation_gain: Parks Canada publishes no elevation figure for this trail. Recorded as unpublished.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible. AllTrails reads the route as 5.6 mi out-and-back, close to Parks Canada's 9.5 km.
trails.uses_source: The 3.7 km approach from Cave and Basin is a paved multi-use path that Parks Canada permits bikes on; bikes must be left at the rack where the canyon loop begins. Recorded from the authority's own trail description, not inferred.
trails.cruise_note: The paved approach along the Bow is a strong `cruise` candidate — flat, paved, no walk-your-bike section on the approach itself — but the bike-legal boundary at the canyon rack needs confirming from Parks Canada before it is set true. Not asserted.
trails.dogs_source: Parks Canada Banff trail conditions: dogs allowed on all trails in summer, on leash, unless a specific restriction is posted. No restriction found for this trail.

trails.season: Low-elevation Bow valley floor, and Parks Canada's mid-October-to-mid-June avalanche advisory does not touch it. It is one of the few genuinely reliable half-days at Banff on 30 May - 4 Jun, when everything with altitude is still out of season.
trails.note: Added as the dependable day. It starts at Cave and Basin — the hot springs where Banff National Park was invented in 1885, worth the stop on its own — then runs the paved path along the Bow with Mount Rundle across the water, and finishes in a genuine slot of a canyon with waterfalls, bridges and a stepped loop. Dog-legal on leash the whole way, and the flat paved approach means the effort is all optional and all at the far end.

trails.name: Lake Agnes Trail (Lake Agnes Tea House)
trails.difficulty: Moderate — Parks Canada's classification. A steady climb from the Lake Louise shore past Mirror Lake to the hanging valley holding Lake Agnes.
trails.elevation_gain: Parks Canada publishes no elevation figure for this trail. Recorded as unpublished rather than taking a third-party number.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible. This is one of the most-reviewed trails in Canada, which is why it stays on the card despite the seasonal problem below.
trails.dogs_source: Parks Canada Banff trail conditions: dogs allowed on all trails in summer, on leash, unless a specific restriction is posted. No restriction found for this trail — but see the season note; the restriction that bites here is avalanche, not pets.

other_links.label: Parks Canada — Hiking in Banff (official trail table and avalanche advisory)
other_links.note: Lake Louise area, Moderate trails: 'Except for the Tramline Trail, these trails are exposed to avalanche hazard and travel is not recommended from mid-October through to mid-June.' Lake Agnes Trail is named in that list.

trails.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP — not by a gate, but by the managing authority's own advice, which is the reason it is flagged this hard. Parks Canada names the Lake Agnes Trail in the Lake Louise Moderate list and states: 'these trails are exposed to avalanche hazard and travel is not recommended from mid-October through to mid-June.' The stop runs 30 May to 4 Jun 2027, entirely inside that window and about two weeks short of its end. On top of that the tea house itself is a seasonal operation that does not normally open until the first part of June, so even a party willing to accept the hazard may find the reason for the walk shut. Do not plan a day on it; ring Lake Louise on 403-522-3833 for that week's conditions before considering it.
trails.note: Entered so the card says plainly what these dates cost at Lake Louise, and because it is the second most walked trail in the park — the climb past Mirror Lake to a hanging valley, a waterfall, a log tea house on the shore, and the Big Beehive above. If a warm spring has cleared it early and Parks Canada says so that week, it is the best half-day of the stop; on the published advice it is not. The Plain of Six Glaciers Trail sits in the same list under the same advisory for the same reason, and is out on the same dates.

banff.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be on a leash of 3 metres or less, and under control at all times – it is the law.
banff.dogs_source_note: Same national Parks Canada page as Waterton/Jasper/Kluane — no individual park page publishes the 3 m length. See the waterton note on the trail-closure clause.
banff.dates_checked: 30 May - 4 Jun 2027, 5 nights, based at Tunnel Mountain.
banff.trails_note: The card had Tunnel Mountain Summit, Johnston Canyon to Upper Falls and the Fenland Trail — three good picks, but all three are Banff-townsite trails, and the box contained NOTHING at Lake Louise. Five nights in Banff without the Lake Louise basin on the card is the gap. Two Lake Louise trails and one low-elevation Banff-area half-day are added. Note for the whole stop: Parks Canada states 'Moraine Lake Road is closed to personal vehicles year-round' — Moraine Lake, the Rockpile and Consolation Lakes are shuttle-only, and the shuttle season normally starts around the beginning of June, so 30 May - 4 Jun sits right on its opening edge. Book the Lake Louise / Moraine shuttle on Parks Canada's reservation system as soon as the window opens, or that whole valley is unreachable.
banff.dogs_stop_level: Parks Canada, Banff trail conditions page, verbatim: 'Dogs are allowed on all trails in the summer unless otherwise specified in trail restrictions and closures. Keep dogs on leash and under physical control at all times.' The dogs page adds the caveat that 'Dogs are not allowed on some trails' and points at the trail restrictions list, so `dogs: true` below means 'permitted under the park-wide summer rule, no restriction found for this trail' — check the Important Bulletins page on arrival, 403-762-1550. Banff is the first stop in weeks where the dog can actually come along, after Glacier banned it from everything.

jasper.dogs: Allowed on trails, on a leash of 3 m or less — Parks Canada, and it is the law. Local bulletins close specific trails to dogs (groomed ski trails in winter, wildlife closures); check trailhead boards. This is the opposite of the US parks earlier on this leg.

That is 2024 wildfire rehabilitation, not a seasonal gate. trails.season: Valley bottom at about 1,000 m, paved, and open long before anything with altitude. It is walkable on 4-9 Jun with no seasonal question at all, which is exactly why it belongs on a card for these dates.
trails.note: The easy one this box did not have — flat, paved, an hour, and the dog can come. Lake Annette sits with Lake Edith just across the Athabasca from town under the wall of Mount Tekarra, with a sand beach and interpretive panels round the shore. It is the obvious evening walk from Whistlers and the obvious wet-weather fallback, and with Maligne Canyon closed the stop needs one.

trails.season: Lakeshore at about 1,670 m. Maligne Lake itself is high and cold and thaws late — it is one of the last big lakes in the Rockies to clear — so on 4-9 Jun expect ice still on parts of it and check 511.alberta.ca for the state of the Maligne Lake Road before driving out. Parks Canada reports the loop itself in Good condition and does not flag it seasonally.
trails.note: Added because the Maligne valley was about to disappear from this stop entirely. Maligne Canyon is under a superintendent closure, and every other Maligne Lake trail on the card's level either bans dogs (Bald Hills, Opal Hills, Lorraine and Mona Lakes) or is a four-to-six-hour climb. This is the easy shoreline circuit at the north end of the lake, past Curly Phillips's 1928 boathouse to the viewpoint down the lake toward the Queen Elizabeth Ranges — and it is the trailhead for the Spirit Island boat, which is the reason most people drive out there. It carries no star rating because no trail database indexes it; that is a recorded absence, not a gap in the research.

trails.name: Wilcox Pass
trails.distance: 2.4 km (1.5 mi) return to the first viewpoint; 8 km (5.0 mi) return to the pass
trails.time: 1 hour return to the first viewpoint; 2-3 hours return to the pass (Parks Canada)
trails.difficulty: Parks Canada's two sources disagree and both are recorded: the day-hiking table classes trail 50 Moderate, while the trail conditions report grades both segments — 'Wilcox Viewpoint - Red Chairs (50)' and 'Upper Wilcox Pass (50)' — as Difficult. Treat the first viewpoint as moderate and the full pass as the harder grade.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed; the en-gb mirror read 268 the same day. No star rating was visible. The low count relative to how well known this hike is reflects that AllTrails also carries it under other route names, so treat it as a floor, not a verdict.
trails.uses_source: Parks Canada day-hiking table, trail 50: Biking No, Dogs Yes, Horses No.
trails.dogs_source: Parks Canada Jasper day-hiking table, Icefields Parkway section, Wilcox Pass (50): Dogs — Yes.

other_links.label: Parks Canada — Day hiking in Jasper National Park (official trail table)
other_links.note: 'Wilcox Pass — 2.4 km return to first viewpoint; 8 km return to pass — 1 hour return to first viewpoint, 2-3 hours return to Pass — 390 m — trail 50 — Moderate — Biking No — Dogs Yes — Horses No.'

trails.season: The one entry on this card with a real seasonal question. The pass tops out around 2,350 m and holds snow well into the summer; the commonly published usable season is late June to October, so 4-9 Jun is EARLY and the upper meadows are likely to be under snow with the trail hard to follow. This is not a closure — Parks Canada posts no closure and the trailhead off the Icefields Parkway at Wilcox Creek is reachable — so it is entered as walkable-with-a-caveat rather than flagged shut. The short 2.4 km leg to the first viewpoint and the red chairs is far more likely to go than the full 8 km to the pass, and on these dates that is the version to plan. Check the Jasper trail conditions report and 511.alberta.ca the day before.
trails.note: Added as the alpine day, because after the Cavell Road closure there was no longer one. It leaves the Icefields Parkway at the Columbia Icefield and climbs quickly out of the trees onto an open shoulder looking straight across at the Athabasca Glacier and Mount Athabasca — the single best view on the whole Parkway that does not involve paying to ride onto the ice. Bighorn sheep are close to guaranteed on the lower slopes. The dog is permitted, which on a trail of this quality is unusual. Do it as a day-trip out of Jasper in the truck; the Parkway is a fine coach road but this is not a coach errand.

scenicDrives_patch.name: Maligne Lake Road
scenicDrives_patch.note: 46–47 km from the Highway 16 turnoff (1.9 km east of Jasper) to the lake at road's end; about an hour each way without stops. Mostly paved. No fuel and no cell service on the road. Parks Canada discourages stopping for wildlife.
scenicDrives_patch.season: OPEN, with one thing shut. Maligne Lake Road reopened after the 2024 wildfire and Medicine Lake and the Maligne Lake area are accessible. Maligne Canyon — the marquee stop partway along the road — remained CLOSED through 2026 pending wildfire/geotechnical work, as did Edith Cavell Road. Arrive 4 Jun 2027: assume the drive works and check Maligne Canyon specifically.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: Parks Canada Jasper recovery page; CTV/CBC 2026 what's-open reporting

jasper.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be on a leash of 3 metres or less, and under control at all times – it is the law.
jasper.dogs_source_note: Same national Parks Canada page. Jasper has no park-level pets page, so the national rule is the only citable source for the 3 m figure at this stop.
jasper.trails_note: THE FINDING ON THIS STOP IS ABOUT A TRAIL ALREADY ON THE CARD. Parks Canada's Jasper trail conditions report lists 'Maligne Canyon (7, 7f) — Closed. Superintendent closure, no public access', and the day-hiking table carries the same trail as 'Maligne Canyon Closed until further notice'. The card's 'Sixth Bridge via Maligne Canyon Trail' is therefore not walkable as things stand, and that was not visible anywhere on the stop. It is not re-added here — it is already there — but it is the single most important thing to know about this box, and it should be re-checked against parks.canada.ca before the trip rather than assumed to have reopened. Second, the 2024 wildfire: Parks Canada states 'Edith Cavell Road closed until further notice due to 2024 wildfire damage. Astoria trailhead is not accessible.' That removes Path of the Glacier and Cavell Meadows — the two hikes a first-time visitor would otherwise be steered to — from the stop entirely, which is why neither appears below. With Maligne Canyon shut and Cavell unreachable, the card had effectively TWO working trails for five nights. Three are added: one easy walk by camp, one easy walk that restores Maligne Lake to the stop, and one alpine pass that is the best view-for-effort left on the Icefields Parkway.
jasper.dogs_stop_level: Parks Canada publishes a per-trail DOGS column in the Jasper day-hiking table, which makes this stop unusually well sourced. It also posts a standing notice: 'Dogs are prohibited from trails and areas in sensitive habitats to reduce the stress that dogs have on grizzly bears, caribou, ground-nesting birds, and/or other sensitive species.' In practice at Maligne Lake that bans the dog from Bald Hills, Opal Hills and Lorraine/Mona Lakes — all marked 'No dogs allowed' in the trail report — while Mary Schäffer and Moose Lake Loop are fine. Every `dogs` value below is taken from that column, not inferred.

trails.was: Lake Loop Trail — renamed to the listing's own title
trails.season: Best April-October; arrival 3 Jul is peak.
trails.note_source: Loons, foxes, moose, otters and beaver. Reviewers are consistent about heavy mosquitoes and muddy patches — bug cover matters more than boots here in July.
trails.stats_note: The card's original name, "Lake Loop Trail", is generic and Talkeetna Lakes Park holds several similarly-named loops (X Lake Loop, Z Lake Loop and the lake circuit itself), so it does not map one-to-one onto any listing. AllTrails' "Talkeetna Lake Trail" is the closest match, hence contains rather than exact. The managing authority is the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, which describes "a network of wide skate/classic trails throughout the woods surrounding the lake system", about eight miles in total.

offroad.name: Petersville Road
offroad.distance: first 9.4 miles paved; maintained gravel a further ~8.9 miles to the old Forks Roadhouse site at the Collinsville Road junction; primitive road for roughly 14.9 miles beyond that
offroad.difficulty: not published as a grade. 4WD recommended but not mandatory on the primitive section; the maintained portion is ordinary gravel
offroad.season: No formal closure, but conditions are only reliably good July through August — June and September are described as iffy, and snow lingers on the road beyond about mile 14 because of the Alaska Range. The stop arrives 3 Jul 2027, right at the front edge of the usable window. The paved and maintained gravel will be fine; the primitive section past the Forks may still be soft or snow-blocked.
offroad.note: Alaska DNR fact sheet used as the source because onX, which is the fullest listing, is paywalled. Collinsville Road, which branches at the Forks, is only maintained as far as the Peters Creek bridge and becomes a four-wheeler trail shortly after — that is an ATV route, not a truck route. This is Denali-view country on a clear day and mining-claim country the rest of the time; claims are active, so stay on the road.

dogs_unpublished.action: Phone the Matanuska-Susitna Borough on (907) 861-7801 and ask for Land & Resource Management (which matsu.gov/trails names as the trails contact) or Parks, Recreation, Trails & Library Services. Ask one question: is there an ADOPTED borough ordinance requiring dogs to be leashed in borough parks, or are dogs simply permitted at Talkeetna Lakes Park with no published rule. trails.name: Crescent Creek Trail #308 (to Crescent Lake)
trails.distance: 6.2 miles (10.0 km) one way to Crescent Lake — 12.4 mi out and back. AllTrails reads the out-and-back as 12.5 mi.
trails.difficulty: Easy to moderate — the USFS's own grading, with the note 'Trail is suitable for family outings and day hiking.' AllTrails grades the full 12.5 mi out-and-back 'challenging', which is a statement about the total distance rather than about the terrain; the climb is 940 ft spread over more than six miles.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed on duckduckgo.com; the en-gb mirror read 190 the same day. No star rating was visible.
trails.uses_source: USFS lists the recreation opportunities for trail 308 as Hiking, Fishing, Horse Riding and Camping, Biking, and Outdoor Science and Learning. Bike and horse use are the authority's own, not inferred. The USFS trail brochure adds one restriction worth knowing: the trail is closed to saddle and pack stock for part of the year — check the current dates with the district before planning a horse day.
trails.cruise_reason: Bike-legal is not the same as cruisable. This is 6.2 miles of narrow single-track climbing 940 ft up a creek valley and over a low ridge into a canyon — MTB terrain, not gravel-cruising terrain, and nothing like a rail grade. It stays on the card with a bike badge and is kept out of the biking view, per §4.
trails.needs: No published pet rule on the USFS trail page. Recorded as unknown. Chugach National Forest, 907-743-9500.

other_links.label: USFS — Crescent Creek Trail, Chugach National Forest
other_links.note: Source for every figure above. 'This 6.2-mile trail climbs gradually up the narrow valley of Crescent Creek through spruce/birch forest to Crescent Lake. Frequent openings afford views of nearby mountains.' Difficulty Easy to moderate; Trip Time (one way) 3-4 hours; Recommended Season June-October; Elevation Gain 940 feet. Trailhead: Mile 45 Sterling Highway, south onto Quartz Creek Road, past Quartz Creek and Crescent Creek campgrounds to Mile 3.5.

trails.season: Squarely in season. USFS gives the recommended season as June to October and notes that 'Snow can remain on the upper part of the trail until early June' — 10-14 July is a month clear of that, and it is also when the meadows along the middle section are in full wildflower.
trails.note: The addition that gets this stop out of the Russian River drainage. Everything already on the card leaves from the same corner of Cooper Landing; this leaves from Quartz Creek Road, three and a half miles up the other valley, and climbs gently through birch and spruce to Crescent Lake sitting just below tree line. Wildflower meadows alternating with forest the whole way, and grayling in the lake. Four nights does not need the full 12.4 miles — the canyon section a few miles in is the good part and makes a comfortable half-day turnaround. There is a Forest Service cabin at the lake on reservation for anyone who wants to make it two days.

offroad.name: Skilak Lake Road
offroad.distance: 19 miles, entrances at Sterling Highway mileposts 58 and 75.2
offroad.season: no seasonal closure published; the Kenai NWR Visitor Contact Station at Sterling MP 57.8 is open 10 June - 15 August, 10am-4pm daily
offroad.note: The best wildlife-viewing drive on the Kenai and the obvious first day out of this stop - the east entrance is a few miles west of Cooper Landing. ADF&G's advice is to "Drive the road slowly at 10 to 15 mph early in the day (before boaters start driving) or late in the evening". Access to Quartz/Crescent and the Lower and Upper Skilak Lake campgrounds. Surface is gravel; no vehicle restriction is published.

offroad.name: Snug Harbor Road / Cooper Lake Road
offroad.distance: 9 miles on Snug Harbor Road, then 2.5 miles more on Cooper Lake Road to the Rainbow Lake trailhead
offroad.season: Forest Service recommended season for the trail at the end: May-October
offroad.note: Forest Service: "At Mile 48 Sterling Highway in Cooper Landing turn south onto Snug Harbor Road. This turns into Cooper Lake Road after 9 miles. It is 2.5 miles further to the trailhead parking area." It starts in the middle of this stop, runs along the south shore of Kenai Lake and ends at Cooper Lake. Surface and vehicle requirements are not published by the Forest Service.

offroad.name: Palmer Creek Road, Hope
offroad.distance: Forest Service: "A 12 mile gravel road climbing from the Hope area to a high valley containing past and present mining activity"
offroad.difficulty: ADF&G: "Don't attempt to drive beyond the campground at milepost 6 without a high clearance vehicle and possibly four-wheel-drive"; beyond that it is "a much narrower and more rugged jeep trail" for another five miles
offroad.season: ADF&G: "This road is not maintained in winter; snow may be present on the road from mid-September to mid-May"
offroad.note: The real 4x4 day of the Kenai and the one that ends in alpine tundra. From Hope Highway MP 16.2, south on Resurrection Creek Road for half a mile, then left onto Palmer Creek Road six miles to Coeur d'Alene Campground; the road narrows there. "The roads are narrow and loose gravel may be present" and the campground "is not recommended for large RVs or trailers" - which is fine, the truck goes alone. Black bear, caribou, wolves, and all three ptarmigan species along it. Seward Ranger District 907-288-3178 for the state of the top five miles. Mid-July is dead centre of the window.

cooper-landing.trails_note: Three trails for four nights, and all three hang off the same road junction and the same drainage — Russian Lakes, Russian River Falls, and the Resurrection trail. One addition takes the box to four, which is the target for four nights, and it deliberately goes up the OTHER valley out of Cooper Landing. One thing to carry about the existing card that the dates make sharp: 10-14 July is the middle of the Russian River sockeye run, which means combat fishing at the confluence and the highest concentration of brown bears on the road system anywhere near Anchorage. Russian River Falls is already on the card and is exactly where the bears are. That is a reason to go early, carry spray and keep the dog leashed, not a reason to drop it — but it should not be a surprise on the day.
cooper-landing.dogs_stop_level: The USFS trail page for the addition below publishes no pet rule; its Restrictions section carries none. Dogs are generally permitted on Chugach National Forest trails but that is a generalisation, not a published rule for this trail, so `dogs` is recorded null. Chugach National Forest Supervisor's Office, 907-743-9500, or the Seward Ranger District would settle it.

seward.dogs_exception: Every Exit Glacier trail is closed to the dog. Tonsina, Two Lakes and Ptarmigan Lake are not on NPS land and no rule was found for them — unresearched, not a green light.

Tonsina Trail.quote: Yes, Pets are welcome at state parks and campgrounds if leashed and accompanied by the owner at all times; unleashed dogs are allowed in the backcountry but must be within voice command.
Tonsina Trail.why: Tonsina Point is on the Caines Head Trail, inside Caines Head State Recreation Area and reached from Lowell Point State Recreation Site — both Alaska State Parks units, per the official trail guide at https://dnr.alaska.gov/parks/maps/cainesheadtrail.pdf. The Caines Head unit page publishes no pet rule of its own, so the statewide state-parks rule governs.

seward.dogs_exception_add: Tonsina is the one Seward trail on this card the dog can walk: it is Alaska State Parks land, not Kenai Fjords, and state parks allow leashed pets. Two Lakes is a City of Seward park — the city's own Parks, Trails & Facilities page lists the trail and says nothing about dogs, and no Seward city code text could be reached (the code host answers a bot challenge), so it stays unknown. Ptarmigan Lake is Chugach National Forest and the forest publishes no pet rule for it. Every Exit Glacier trail remains closed to the dog.

Ptarmigan Lake — Chugach NF, Seward Ranger District, (907) 288-3178.

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Kachemak Bay State Park

trails.season: In season and at its best in late July. Access is the whole planning problem, not the season: the trailhead is MARINE ACCESS ONLY, by water taxi from the Homer Spit. The park advises a morning drop-off at Glacier Spit — a wind-exposed beach — and an afternoon or evening pick-up at the Saddle Trailhead in Halibut Cove, which is a protected anchorage. Book the taxi as a drop-at-one-end, collect-at-the-other, and the two trails below become one clean day.
trails.note: The best day of the whole Homer stop and it was not on the card. Flat walking through spruce and cottonwood and out across the Grewingk Glacier's dry outwash plain to a broad open beach on Grewingk Glacier Lake, with icebergs in the water and the glacier and the Kenai Mountains filling the far end. Two warnings from the park, both worth carrying: access to the glacier along the SOUTH end of the lake is 'difficult and hazardous — please do not attempt this route'; and landslides off the surrounding ridges into the lake can generate splash waves of fifty feet or more, so stay off the low lake flats if you linger.

trails.name: Saddle Trail
trails.difficulty: Moderate — the park's rating, qualified as 'short, steep climbs'. It switchbacks through steep forested terrain.
trails.needs: No standalone AllTrails listing for the Saddle Trail was found; it appears only inside the composite routes listed under Grewingk Glacier Lake Trail above. No review count, no star rating. Recorded as absent.

other_links.label: Friends of Kachemak Bay State Parks — Saddle Trail (state trail fact sheet)
other_links.note: 'Saddle Trail (1.0 mi/1.6 km). Rating: Moderate (short, steep climbs). Hiking Time: 25 minutes. Elevation Gain: 350 ft. Trailhead Access: Marine Access - Halibut cove (protected anchorage, mooring buoys), good afternoon pick-up.'

trails.season: Same season and same access as Glacier Lake Trail. The park notes there is no water at the trailhead and no camping there, and asks visitors to respect private property near the trailhead. It also states plainly that 'cliffs prohibit hiking the beach from the trailhead to the Right Beach Campsite, boat transport is necessary' — you cannot walk round the shore, so the boat has to be arranged properly.
trails.note: Not a separate day out: this is the OTHER END of the Grewingk walk, and it is entered on its own because it is what makes the day work. Drop at Glacier Spit in the morning, walk the flat Glacier Lake Trail to the lake, then climb this mile over the low ridge to Halibut Cove and be collected from a sheltered anchorage in the afternoon rather than off an exposed beach. Twenty-five minutes and 350 ft is the price of not backtracking. It also gives access to the Alpine Ridge and Lagoon trails for anyone with more day than sense.

trails.name: Bishop's Beach (and the Beluga Slough Trail)
trails.distance: The City of Homer publishes no measured length — it is a beach walk of 'miles of beautiful beach' below the bluffs, walked out and back as far as suits. The Beluga Slough Trail runs from the same car park to the Islands and Ocean Visitor Center.
trails.time: As long as you like; an hour out and back covers the good part
trails.difficulty: Easy — level gravel beach; the Beluga Slough Trail is a made trail with boardwalk sections.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. It is a small number and it means very little here: this is a city beach park, not a hiking destination, and it is on the card for what it is rather than for its rating.
trails.needs: The City of Homer's park page publishes no pet rule. Homer City Hall, 907-235-3170, parks@ci.homer.ak.us. Worth asking, because a beach two blocks from Old Town with 'miles of beautiful beach' would be the best dog walk of the stop if it is permitted.

other_links.label: City of Homer — Bishop's Beach Park
other_links.note: 'Two blocks from Old Town at the end of Beluga Place... Ample parking, restroom facilities, Beluga Slough trailhead, and beach combing.' Covered pavilion with fire pit and BBQ grill, reservable at $25 for four hours or $50 for a full day; free to use when not posted as reserved. No camping. The city asks visitors to respect that everything above the 17 ft Mean High Water line is private property.

trails.season: Year-round and tide-dependent rather than season-dependent. Go on a falling tide — Kachemak Bay has one of the largest tidal ranges in the world and the flats it uncovers are the whole point. Late July gives light until well past ten at night, which makes this the evening walk of the stop.
trails.note: The in-town walk the card did not have. Homer Spit Trail and Diamond Creek are both already on there, but neither is the beach under the bluffs at the end of Beluga Place, with the volcanoes — Iliamna, Redoubt, Augustine — across the water and Grewingk Glacier visible on a clear evening. Tide-pool life on the flats, beachcombing, and a covered pavilion with a fire pit if the weather turns. The Beluga Slough Trail from the same car park runs to the Islands and Ocean Visitor Center, which is the best wet-afternoon building in Homer and free.

offroad.note: "The road is 40.55km (25.2 miles) long, stretching from Sterling Highway (in Homer) to Fox River", and it is "fully paved except for the last few miles, which are unpaved" - so the offroad part is the final run out onto the Fox River flats at the head of the bay, past where the tour traffic turns round. homer.dates_checked: 23-29 Jul 2027, 6 nights. Late July is peak season in Homer — fireweed, the silver run starting on the Spit, and long light.
homer.trails_note: Every trail on the card was on the Homer side of the water: the Spit, Diamond Creek, the Homestead Trail. Six nights in Homer and nothing at all in KACHEMAK BAY STATE PARK, which is the reason people come and is the only Alaska state park you reach by boat. That is the gap. Two of its trails are added — they are two halves of one loop and one water-taxi day — plus the in-town beach walk. Alpine Ridge Trail was the other candidate across the bay and was deliberately left off: the park grades it Difficult with 'long climb, very very steep muddy sections', 2-4 hours ONE WAY and roughly 2,200 ft of gain, on 28 AllTrails reviews. §3 keeps a Hard trail only when the reviews are outstanding, and 28 is not outstanding; it is the wrong hike for this trip.
homer.dogs_stop_level: Neither Alaska State Parks nor the City of Homer publishes a pet rule on any of the pages read for this stop. All three entries below are therefore `dogs: null`. Homer City Hall, 907-235-3170 / parks@ci.homer.ak.us, would settle Bishop's Beach; Kachemak Bay State Park would settle the other two — and it matters, because a water taxi is involved and the operator's own dog policy is a second question on top of the park's.

trails.name: Roadside Trail
trails.note: ONE OF ONLY TWO TRAILS IN DENALI THE DOG MAY WALK. NPS pet page names the exceptions as the "Roadside Hiking Trail" and the "Roadside Bike Trail"; everywhere else — every park trail, all off-trail wilderness, and every park bus — is closed to pets. Leash 6 ft or shorter. READ THIS BEFORE THE TRAILHEAD: the AllTrails listing for this trail states dogs are NOT allowed. That is AllTrails applying Denali's blanket park rule to a listing; the authority names this trail as an exception and the authority is right. Runs from the Denali Visitor Center via the Taiga Trail up to Park Headquarters and the sled dog kennels — but the dog cannot come into the kennels demonstration, so this is a walk to the door, not a walk to the show.
trails.note_source: NPS Denali pets page (nps.gov/dena/planyourvisit/pets.htm), fetched: "Pets must be leashed (6' or shorter leash) at all times... Pets may be walked on the park road, in parking lots, or on campground roads", pets not permitted on park trails or off-trail, with the Roadside Hiking Trail and Roadside Bike Trail named as the two exceptions; "Pets are not permitted on any buses in Denali." NPS Roadside Trail page (nps.gov/dena/planyourvisit/roadside.htm), fetched: 1.8 miles (2.9 km), "moderately strenuous", ~400 ft total gain east to west, up to 15 percent grade, 36-inch compacted gravel surface. NPS's own trail page titles it "Roadside Trail"; the pets page calls the same trail the "Roadside Hiking Trail" to distinguish it from the bike trail. Time 2 h 07 min and difficulty 'Moderately challenging' are the AllTrails figures for the 4.4 mi round trip; NPS's own text has been published as both one hour and two hours one-way, so the round-trip figure is the safer one to plan on.
trails.stats_note: NPS 1.8 mi is one way. The AllTrails listing measures the same trail as a 4.4 mi out-and-back, which is the round trip plus the Taiga Trail connector at the visitor-center end.
