trails.name: Roadside Bike Trail
trails.cruise_reason: NPS: paved, 1.7 mi one way, losing 150 ft — a dedicated bike trail rather than a shared road, with a flat spur to the Riley Creek Day Use Area at the south end of Riley Creek Campground, which is where the coach is parked. No technical section and no puncture-hazard reports. NPS says to expect pedestrians, so it is a shared-use path, not a road ride.
trails.note: THE SECOND OF DENALI'S TWO PET-LEGAL TRAILS, and the one that starts at camp — its Riley Creek spur reaches the day-use area at the south end of Riley Creek Campground. Paved, running out to the Nenana River Canyon commercial strip. NPS names it in the pet rule alongside the Roadside Hiking Trail; leash 6 ft or shorter. No AllTrails listing exists for it — that is a recorded absence, not a doubt about the trail.

Named as a pet exception on the NPS pets page. Searched for an AllTrails listing under the exact name and found none — TrailLink and Gaia GPS have it, AllTrails does not.

other_links.note: Authority. Publishes the length, the paving, the elevation loss and the Riley Creek spur.

other_links.note: "Roadside Bike Trail spans 1.7 from AK 3 to Denali Visitor Center." Corroborates the NPS length.

other_links.label: Gaia GPS — Roadside Bike Trail
other_links.note: Records it as a bicycle trail through Denali National Park.

offroad.name: Denali Highway (Alaska Route 8), Cantwell to Paxson
offroad.distance: 135 miles Paxson to Cantwell, "mostly gravel"
offroad.difficulty: "max speed varies from 35-55 mph depending on surface conditions"; Alaska DOT designates it a No Winter Maintenance route
offroad.season: "winter conditions close the road every year from October through mid-May"
offroad.note: The big one of this leg, and the west end is at Cantwell, about 27 miles south of the park entrance - so it is a day trip out of this stop rather than a re-route. "You can drive the highway in a day, but we recommend at least one over night." BLM manages much of the corridor: Tangle Lakes Campground at MP 21.5 from the Paxson end, inside the Delta Wild and Scenic River corridor and the 226,660-acre Tangle Lakes Archaeological District between MP 15 and MP 32. Late July is dead centre of the open season. Alaska's own DOT site cannot be fetched from here - it fails TLS verification - so the closure wording is a travel guide's, not the department's.

offroad.name: Stampede Road, Healy
offroad.distance: paved to mile 4; most cars to about mile 5; high clearance and/or 4WD beyond
offroad.difficulty: NPS: "Stampede is paved to mile 4 and then it is drivable in most cars to about Mile 5. High clearance and/or four wheel drive is necessary to go farther."
offroad.season: NPS: "There is heavy ORV use along the portions of the roadbed outside the National Park, especially during moose hunting season (August to September). Wear bright colors during this time"
offroad.note: Leaves Highway 3 a few miles north of Healy - about 15 miles from Riley Creek - and is the major access route to the Stampede country on the park's north boundary. The roadbed is roughly 50 years old and "boggy or overgrown in many areas" with no bridges; on foot westward it crosses the Savage and then the Teklanika, and NPS says "The Teklanika crossing cannot be made dependably on foot. A pack raft is recommended for mid-summer." This is a drive-in-and-turn-round, not a through route. SEASON NOTE THAT LANDS INSIDE THIS STAY: the hunting-season ORV traffic NPS warns about starts in August and the stay runs to 5 Aug.

denali.dogs_source_quote: In general, pets are not permitted on park trails, nor off-trail in the wilderness.
denali.dogs_source_note: Confirms our card's naming note: this page calls it the "Roadside Hiking Trail", alongside "the Roadside Bike Trail". Leash rule reads "Pets must be leashed (6' or shorter leash) at all times."

trapper-creek.dogs: Alaska State Parks: "a person may not have a dog or other pet in a developed facility of a state park unless the dog or other pet is on a leash not exceeding nine feet in length, and is under control by a person at all times." In the backcountry unleashed dogs are permitted provided they remain within voice command. Owners must clean up after their animals.
trapper-creek.dogs_exception: Individual parks may post stricter rules than the statewide regulation, and the Denali State Park page publishes none — read the trailhead board. Note the Alaska leash limit is nine feet, not six.

offroad.name: Petersville Road
offroad.distance: 40 miles from George Parks Highway milepost 114.9; first 3 miles paved, remaining 37 unpaved
offroad.difficulty: no vehicle rating published; "The gravel surface requires regular maintenance in order to avoid deterioration of the traveled surface"
offroad.season: Alaska DNR: "There is no winter maintenance beyond mile 14."
offroad.note: The reason this stop exists for the truck. Alaska DNR's own corridor management plan: "Petersville Road connects the Trapper Creek and Petersville communities. It starts at milepost 114.9 of the George Parks Highway, and leads west and north 40 miles. The first three miles of the road are paved and the remaining 37 miles are unpaved." It is maintained by Alaska DOT&PF, carries about 200 vehicles a day, and runs through gold mining country, homesteads and the Peters Creek recreational mining corridor to the Forks Roadhouse - which is listed as eligible for the National Register. The Alaska Range, including Denali, is visible along it. In August the gravel is at its dustiest; DNR notes dry spells plus fishing traffic "quickly reduces the driving quality".

trapper-creek.dogs_source_quote: a person may not have a dog or other pet in a developed facility of a state park unless the dog or other pet is on a leash not exceeding nine feet in length, and is under control by a person at all times.
trapper-creek.dogs_source_note: The page attributes this to 11 AAC 12.130(a). Backcountry voice-command allowance and the clean-up duty are both on the page.

trails.name: Solomon Gulch Viewpoint
trails.was: Solomon Gulch Trail — no url

trails.name: Dock Point Trail
trails.was: Dock Point Trail — no url
trails.note_source: Short and easy, with the marsh, the small-boat dock and the ring of mountains around Valdez. AllTrails indexes it only as a point of interest, not a trail listing, so it carries no trail link — but the figures are real. alaska.org also documents it.

trails.name: Shoup Bay Trail, Section A (to Gold Creek)
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title for 'Shoup Bay Trail Section A' as displayed. No star rating was visible.
trails.needs: No published pet rule from the City of Valdez or the Valdez Adventure Alliance. Recorded as unknown.

alltrails.name: Shoup Bay Trail Section A
alltrails.note: AllTrails indexes the two sections separately, the same way the city does. 'Section A of the Shoup Bay Trail runs from the trail head to Gold Creek bridge.'

other_links.label: City of Valdez / Discover Valdez — Shoup Bay Trail
other_links.note: Source for every figure above, credited on the page to Valdez Parks & Recreation. Also the source for the Section B figures: Difficult, 10 hours round trip, 12.6 miles, 1,100 ft — that is the full run to Shoup Glacier and the kittiwake rookery, and it is a very long day, not a five-night-stop day.

trails.season: Open and at its best in August, with one real caveat the authority states plainly: 'The Gold Creek riverbed is prone to flooding and the stream channel changes often.' Mid-August is Valdez's wettest stretch. Expect mud on Section A, and treat a wet week as a reason to turn round at the meadow rather than push to Gold Creek.
trails.note: The walk this box was missing — the only trail on the card that gets out of town and onto the coast. It leaves from Shoup Bay Park at the very end of Egan Drive, crosses the Mineral Creek flats through alder and spruce and opens onto meadow and Port Valdez. Sea otters and harbour seals in the water, bears and mountain goats on the slopes above, and eagles, Arctic terns and peregrines along the shore. Section A to Gold Creek is the sane version at four hours; the camping area there has restrooms, food lockers and a firepit. Section B beyond it is graded Difficult, badly overgrown with Devil's Club and salmonberry, and is explicitly 'only recommended for experienced hikers' — it is recorded above but not proposed.

trails.name: The Goat Trail, Keystone Canyon
trails.distance: About 2.5 miles one way — the City of Valdez states the trail 'is passable for the first 2.5 miles'. AllTrails indexes the walked route as 4.3 mi (6.8 km) out and back.
trails.time: About 2 hours out and back (AllTrails average 2 h 2 min)
trails.difficulty: Moderately challenging (AllTrails). The City of Valdez publishes no grade for this trail; recorded as the trail database's figure, not the authority's.
trails.elevation_gain: Not published by the City of Valdez, and no figure was read that could be attributed to the authority. Recorded as unknown rather than guessed.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed; the en-gb mirror read 168 the same day. No star rating was visible.
trails.needs: No published pet rule. Recorded as unknown.

alltrails.name: Goat Trail
alltrails.note: Note the '--3' suffix — copied from a result, never derivable. There are other trails called Goat Trail in Alaska, including one in Wrangell-St. Elias; this is the Valdez one, and the AllTrails description confirms it as 'near Valdez, Alaska'.

other_links.label: City of Valdez / Discover Valdez — The Goat Trail & Wagon Road
other_links.note: Source for the trailhead and the passable distance: 'The trail begins at the wood sign just past Horsetail Falls in Keystone Canyon (Mile 13.5 Richardson Highway)... is passable for the first 2.5 miles.' Map credited to Valdez Parks & Recreation. Also records that the Goat Trail and the Wagon Road became two separate trails when the Snowslide Gulch bridge was destroyed in the 2006 floods — so do not expect a through route.

trails.season: Snow-free and open in August, and this is the right month for it: the two waterfalls at the trailhead, Horsetail and Bridal Veil, are still running on summer melt. Two plant hazards the authority names specifically — Devil's Club, which is covered in spines, and wild celery, which causes a burn-like skin reaction. Long sleeves, not shorts.
trails.note: The historic walk, and the reason to stop in Keystone Canyon rather than drive through it. This is the 1899 Abercrombie pack trail that became the Valdez-to-Fairbanks wagon road — the route the whole interior of Alaska was reached by before the Richardson Highway, cut into the canyon wall a few hundred feet above the Lowe River. It looks down on the new highway and across at the waterfalls. Two hours, 13.5 miles from camp, and it is a completely different kind of day from anything else on this card.

trails.name: Worthington Glacier Lookout Trail
trails.distance: Short — Alaska State Parks publishes no length, describing only accessible trails within the 113-acre site. AllTrails describes it as 'an easy, paved trail [that] leads to a viewing station and right down to the glacier waters.'
trails.time: Under an hour including time at the viewing station
trails.difficulty: Easy — Alaska State Parks flags the site as an ADA facility with accessible (♿) trails and toilets.
trails.elevation_gain: Not published by Alaska State Parks. Recorded as unknown.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible.
trails.needs: Alaska State Parks publishes no pet rule for this recreation site. The site is operated day-to-day by the Valdez Adventure Alliance, who would answer it. Recorded as unknown.

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Worthington Glacier State Recreation Site
other_links.note: 'Worthington Glacier State Recreation Site is located in spectacular Thompson Pass, 28 miles north of Valdez on the Richardson Highway.' 113 acres, ADA facility, accessible toilets and trails, pavilion with benches and interpretive panels. Milepost 28.7 Richardson Highway. 'This site is operated by Valdez Adventure Alliance.'

other_links.label: Valdez Adventure Alliance — Worthington Glacier
other_links.note: The site operator. Two things worth knowing before driving up: there is a $5 parking fee and the operator states it receives no state funding or maintenance assistance; and the operator warns that the Worthington Glacier Ridge Trail and Worthington Loop Trail are SOCIAL trails, not maintained routes. The entry above is the maintained, accessible lookout trail only — the ridge scramble is deliberately not proposed.

trails.season: Open and at its best in mid-August. Thompson Pass sits at about 2,700 ft and collects some of the heaviest snowfall in Alaska; this is one of the few months the site is straightforward. It is directly on the Richardson Highway at milepost 28.7, so it is on the road IN and the road OUT — no separate day required.
trails.note: One of the most accessible glaciers in Alaska and the obvious thing this card was missing, given the coach drives past its car park twice. A paved, wheelchair-accessible path from the pavilion out to a viewing station and down toward the ice, with interpretive panels and benches. It costs an hour on a travel day rather than a day out of the five, which is exactly why it belongs on a card that already has three short walks near the harbour and nothing at Thompson Pass.

Dock Point Trail.entity: Short loop on the Valdez waterfront. No article, and the full text of Valdez, Alaska never mentions Dock Point.

Drive Mineral Creek Road in the truck on.entity: The truck-only road up Mineral Creek out of Valdez. No article; Valdez, Alaska never mentions Mineral Creek.

Solomon Gulch Trail & fish hatchery.entity: Solomon Gulch Trail and the Valdez Fisheries Development Association hatchery. No article under Solomon Gulch, Solomon Gulch Hatchery or Solomon Gulch Dam, and Valdez, Alaska mentions neither the gulch nor a hatchery.

valdez.dogs: Dock Point is a City of Valdez park and the city requires animals to be restrained everywhere except four named off-leash areas, none of which is Dock Point; nothing is published for either Solomon trail.
valdez.dogs_source_quote: Owners must keep their animals restrained to prevent them from running loose.
valdez.dogs_exception: Dock Point Trail is listed by the city as one of its own facilities (https://www.valdezak.gov/facilities/facility/details/Dock-Point-Trail-23), so the city restraint rule reaches it — on lead, not off. The city's four designated off-leash areas are Dump Haul Road, the Old Town area, behind the Gold Fields and Mineral Creek (https://www.valdezak.gov/905/Off-Leash-Areas); Dock Point is not among them. Solomon Gulch and Solomon Lake are outside the city facility list and no land manager publishes a rule for them, so they are unknown, not open.

Dock Point Trail.quote: Dogs can run freely under control in designated off-leash areas

dogs_needs_check: Solomon Gulch Viewpoint and Solomon Lake Trail — land manager not established (city trail guide is a 10 MB+ PDF that would not load). Valdez Parks & Rec, 907-835-4526.

offroad.name: Mineral Creek Road
offroad.distance: 1.5 miles of rough gravel road to the Horsetail Creek washout, then about four more miles of gravel to a gate
offroad.difficulty: City of Valdez: "Four-wheel drive vehicles are recommend for those traveling over the washout at Horsetail Creek." Rated Moderate.
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: The classic Valdez 4x4 day and it starts in town. "The trail is a rough gravel road that begins on Mineral Creek Drive that crosses a bridge over the creek and continues for a 1.5 miles to a washout at Horsetail Creek Falls"; past the washout the gravel runs about four more miles up a steep-sided glacial valley of waterfalls to a gate, beyond which it is foot only to the W.L. Smith Stamp Mill, built 1913. The washout is the decision point - the truck crosses it, nothing else should. Landslides are a known recurring problem in the canyon.

offroad.name: Valdez Glacier Lake road (Airport Road)
offroad.distance: about 15 minutes from town; "About 3/4 miles before the lake the road turns to gravel"
offroad.season: icebergs on the lake "from roughly June through September"
offroad.note: "Turn off the Richardson Highway and onto the Valdez Airport Road, where you'll follow it all the way to the end." Short, and only the last three-quarters of a mile is gravel, ending at the open sandpits along the lake shore - but it is the one place on the road system where you can park beside floating icebergs, and mid-August is inside the season for them.

valdez.dates_checked: 10-15 Aug 2027, 5 nights. Mid-August in Valdez is the pink and silver salmon run, the wettest month of the year, and full brush growth on every unmaintained trail.
valdez.trails_note: The card had three walks, all of them short and all of them within a couple of miles of the harbour — Dock Point, Solomon Gulch Viewpoint and Solomon Lake. That is a good half day, not five nights. Nothing on the card touched the two things Valdez is actually famous for: Keystone Canyon, and the glacier at Thompson Pass that you drive past to get here. Three are added — the coastal trail west out of town, the historic wagon route through the canyon waterfalls, and Worthington Glacier — which takes the box to six for five nights and covers all three directions out of Valdez instead of one.
valdez.dogs_stop_level: No managing authority read for this stop publishes a pet rule for any Valdez trail. The City of Valdez trail guides carry safety, plants and bear guidance and say nothing about dogs; Alaska State Parks' Worthington Glacier page lists facilities and no pet policy. Every `dogs` value below is therefore null. That is the safe state, not an oversight — Valdez Parks & Recreation would settle all of them in one call, and it is worth adding to CALLS.md.

mccarthy.authority: National Park Service — Wrangell-St. Elias National Park & Preserve

trails.name: Root Glacier Trail
trails.was: Root Glacier Trail — no url
trails.note_source: Departs Kennecott Mill Town, which is 4.5 mi from McCarthy on foot — or a $10 shuttle to the trailhead. Crampons or ice spikes needed to step onto the ice.

trails.name: Bonanza Mine Trail
trails.was: Bonanza Mine Trail — no url

trails.name: Crystalline Hills Trail
trails.note: The only trail on the McCarthy Road for which the park publishes a measured length - a loop up into open hills off the road in, with the Wrangells across the valley. Dogs are legal: NPS says plainly that 'Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry', leashed to six feet.
trails.note_source: NPS Wrangell-St Elias 'McCarthy Road and Kennecott' trails page, fetched: 'Crystalline Hills - 2.5 mile loop, Easy to Moderate'. Pet rule from the park's own pets page, which also requires leashing inside the Kennecott Mines National Historic Landmark area.

other_links.label: NPS — McCarthy Road and Kennecott trails
other_links.note: Authority for the trail list and the 2.5-mile loop figure.

other_links.label: NPS — Pets at Wrangell-St Elias
other_links.note: 'Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry.' Leash 6 ft.

trails.name: Wagon Road and Toe of Kennicott Glacier
trails.note: NPS grades it an easy day hike from Kennecott down to the glacier's toe. This is the low-effort alternative to the Root Glacier trail already on the card - no crampons, no guide, and it works on a wet day. The park publishes no distance for it.
trails.note_source: NPS 'McCarthy Road and Kennecott' trails page, fetched: listed as an 'Easy day hike'; no distance published there, the figures are on downloadable PDF maps.

other_links.label: NPS — McCarthy Road and Kennecott trails
other_links.note: Authority; lists it as an easy day hike.

trails.name: Jumbo Mine Trail
trails.note: The second mine climb out of Kennecott alongside Bonanza, which is already on the card, and graded Strenuous by the park just as Bonanza is. Listed so the card shows both; on a six-night August stay one of the two is enough.
trails.note_source: NPS 'McCarthy Road and Kennecott' trails page, fetched: listed as a 'Strenuous day hike'; no distance published.

other_links.label: NPS — McCarthy Road and Kennecott trails
other_links.note: Authority for the difficulty grade.

trails.name: McCarthy Creek Trail
trails.distance: 13.1 mi (21.1 km) out and back to the far end (AllTrails). NPS publishes no distance and presents it as an out-and-back to be walked as far as suits — 'Take a day hike and explore a riverside trail.'
trails.time: A full day for the whole thing; an hour or two covers the good riverside section from town
trails.difficulty: Two answers, both recorded. NPS lists it plainly among its McCarthy-area day hikes with no grade attached. AllTrails grades the full 13.1 mi route 'challenging'. Walked from McCarthy as far as the creek stays pleasant it is an easy riverside stroll; walked to its end it is a long day on an old wagon road with creek crossings.
trails.elevation_gain: Not published by NPS, and no figure was read that could be attributed to the authority. Recorded as unknown.
trails.reviews_note: Two reviews. Read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. That number says nothing about the trail's quality — it says almost nobody logs a walk that starts at the end of McCarthy's main street. It is on the card because the MANAGING AUTHORITY lists it as one of six area day hikes, not because a trail database rates it.
trails.dogs_source: NPS Wrangell-St. Elias Pets page: 'Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry', on a leash not exceeding six feet.

other_links.label: NPS — McCarthy Road & Kennecott Trails
other_links.note: The authority's complete list of area day hikes, and the source for the claim that the card was missing only this one. NPS links a McCarthy Creek trail PDF from this page: 'Take a day hike and explore a riverside trail. Accessible from McCarthy.' The PDF itself could not be rendered in the browser pane, so no figures are taken from it.

other_links.label: NPS — Day Hiking in Wrangell-St. Elias
other_links.note: 'While the McCarthy Road has very few day hikes, Kennecott has several trails, including the best ones in the park for glacier viewing.'

trails.season: Snow-free and walkable in August. The one thing to check is water: this follows a glacier-fed creek drainage and the crossings rise and fall with the day's melt and rain — alaska.org's own note on it is 'Don't underestimate the swiftness of the [creek]'. Late August is past peak melt but a wet week still changes it. Ask at the Kennecott Visitor Center, which is open in summer.
trails.note: The only NPS-listed day hike in the McCarthy area that was not already on the card, and the only one that starts in the town itself rather than up at Kennecott — walk straight down McCarthy's main street past Ma Johnson's and the Wrangell Mountain Center and you are on it. It follows an old wagon road up the creek drainage into the interior of the park, so it is an easy out-and-back for as long as you feel like going and a serious day if you go to the end. On a six-night stop it is the low-effort day between Bonanza and Jumbo, and the dog is allowed on it.

Root Glacier Trail.entity: Root Glacier — no article of its own; the Kennecott article describes it and the glacial trail from Kennecott

Bonanza Mine Trail.entity: Bonanza Mine — no article of its own; documented in the Kennecott, Alaska article

mccarthy.dogs: NPS: "Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry." "Pets must be physically restrained at all times, on a leash which does not exceed six feet in length."

offroad.name: Nabesna Road
offroad.distance: 42 miles from Slana to Devil's Mountain Lodge, where the maintained road ends
offroad.difficulty: NPS: "High clearance and 4-wheel drive is recommended." Conditions deteriorate beyond Mile 28.1.
offroad.season: NPS on the fords: "Generally, these creek beds are dry, but during spring run off or following prolonged rain, high-clearance and/or four-wheel drive may be necessary."
offroad.note: The other road into Wrangell-St. Elias and the one the truck was brought for - but understand the distance: it starts at Slana on the north side of the park, a long way round from McCarthy, so it is a full day out of a six-night stay rather than an afternoon. Three creeks cross the roadbed and may be flowing over it: Trail Creek at Mile 29.8, Lost Creek at 31.2, Boyden Creek at 34.3. Stop at the Slana Ranger Station at Mile 0.2 for current road conditions, or call the park on 907-822-5234 first. One thing to know before hoping to go further: NPS's ORV rules for the Nabesna District PROHIBIT street-legal vehicles and custom 4x4s on the permitted ORV trails, so the pickup stops where the road does.

mccarthy.stats_note: Wrangell-St Elias publishes trail names and difficulty words for the Kennecott area but a distance for only one of them. The missing figures are recorded as needed rather than filled from a third party. `unlisted` here means no AllTrails search was run for these three, not that no listing exists.
mccarthy.dogs_source_quote: Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry.
mccarthy.verdict: THIS SET WAS ALREADY ALMOST COMPLETE, and it is the other card in this batch that was clearly chosen rather than assembled. NPS's own McCarthy Road & Kennecott trail page lists exactly SIX day hikes for the area: Crystalline Hills, McCarthy Creek, the Wagon Road & Toe of the Kennicott Glacier, the Root Glacier / Erie Mine Trail, the Jumbo Mine Trail and the Bonanza Mine Trail. Five of the six were already on the card. Only McCarthy Creek was missing, and it is the one added.
mccarthy.trails_note: Two corrections that apply to entries already on the card and are recorded here rather than re-added. (1) NPS titles the Root Glacier trail 'Root Glacier/Erie Mine Trail' and then states flatly: 'This is not a trail to the Erie Mine.' Anyone reading the AllTrails name and setting out for the Erie Mine on it will be wrong. (2) NPS's own grading of the two mine trails is STRENUOUS for both Jumbo and Bonanza, against Easy/Moderate for Root Glacier and the Wagon Road — worth carrying on the card, because on a six-night stop the difference decides which two days are the hard ones. Also: Bear Resistant Food Containers are REQUIRED for all backcountry camping in this park, and NPS notes the food storage box on the Erie Mine Trail 'was REMOVED'.
mccarthy.dogs_stop_level: This is the good news of the whole Alaska leg and it deserves to be on the card. NPS Wrangell-St. Elias, Pets page, verbatim: 'Dogs are allowed on trails and in the backcountry, but they must be properly controlled at all times on leash.' 36 CFR 2.15 as applied here: 'Dogs are allowed on trails within the park and in the backcountry.' Six-foot leash, no dogs inside buildings, and leashes specifically required within the Kennecott Mines National Historic Landmark area and on the grounds around contact stations. After Arches, Canyonlands, Zion, Bryce, Glacier and Rocky Mountain, this is a national park where the dog walks EVERYTHING on the card. NPS adds one Alaska-specific warning worth heeding: trapping is legal from autumn through spring and unleashed dogs get caught in snares.

austin-depart.activities_note: Reimer's Ranch has no Wikipedia article — the batch resolver fuzzy-matched it to 'The Alamo (2004 film)', which is exactly the near-miss that produced wrong links before. It gets no wiki link.

Visit the Saratoga Museum and make a hal.entity: Encampment, WY and the Grand Encampment Museum

not_a_route.entry: Loaded camper: maintained gravel only when dry.
not_a_route.problem: A standing rig constraint, not a route, and superseded by the settled decision that offroad is always the truck. Saratoga's offroad box is now empty — that is an honest empty, not a gap.

saratoga.authority: BLM Rawlins Field Office (Encampment River Canyon WSA); USFS Medicine Bow-Routt National Forests (Six Mile / Platte River Wilderness); Town of Saratoga / Carbon County (Veterans Island Park)
saratoga.trails_note: Saratoga is genuinely thin, and mid-April makes it thinner. AllTrails indexes 4 trails for the whole Saratoga area. Everything with real elevation — the Snowy Range off WY-130, Huston Park, the Sierra Madre — sits at 8,000-10,000 ft and the stop's own activity text already says to assume the high byway is closed. What is left is the North Platte valley floor in town and the Encampment River canyon 22 miles south-west. The Medicine Bow Rail Trail turns up under 'Saratoga' on TrailLink but its trailheads are Pelton Creek Rd and Dry Park Rd near the Colorado line in Albany County, roughly 75 road miles away and at rail-trail elevation in the Snowies — it is not a Saratoga trail and is deliberately not listed.

trails.name: Encampment River Trail (#470), Encampment River Canyon WSA
trails.distance: 15.8 mi point-to-point end to end; the canyon section from the BLM campground reads 6.3 mi out-and-back
trails.time: 6-7 h end to end; about 2 h 50 min for the canyon section
trails.elevation_gain: 1,984 ft end to end; 609 ft on the canyon section

alltrails.name: Encampment River Trail from Odd Fellows

other_links.label: BLM — Encampment River Canyon
other_links.note: Managing authority, Rawlins Field Office, 307-328-4200. 'The trail, which traverses the WSA and enters Colorado to the south, follows the scenic Encampment River. Located two miles south of Encampment and easily accessible from BLM's Encampment River Campground.' Listed activities include BIKING, HIKING and HORSEBACK RIDING — that is where `uses` comes from, not from inference. No fee. BLM publishes no length and no seasonal closure for this trail.

other_links.label: BLM — Encampment River Campground (trailhead)
other_links.note: The trailhead. BLM's directions: from Encampment follow WY-70, County Road 353 is a quarter mile west of town, one mile south to BLM Road 3407, campground about three quarters of a mile. Park at the back of the campground by the kiosk.

other_links.label: Komoot — Encampment River Trail
other_links.note: The short version out of the BLM campground: 6.3 mi (10.1 km), 2 h 48 min, 609 ft (186 m) gain, graded Moderate. This is the figure to plan a day around.

trails.stats_note: Two different things share one name. BLM's trail runs the length of the river into Colorado; AllTrails indexes the full 15.8 mi point-to-point as 'Encampment River Trail from Odd Fellows' (Odd Fellows is the Encampment River Campground area — AllTrails' own POI page for the campground carries the same 15.8 mi / 1,984 ft figures and the 4.5-from-90 rating). Komoot's 6.3 mi is the canyon section from the campground and back. The 4.5 (90) rating belongs to the full route.
trails.season: BLM publishes no seasonal closure and the trailhead sits at roughly 7,300 ft, which is why this is the one Saratoga-area trail worth planning on in mid-April. The access is unpaved BLM road; snow and mud on the road, not the trail, is the thing that would stop the day.
trails.needs: No published dog rule. BLM's page for the WSA says nothing about pets either way; recorded as unknown rather than guessed. Rawlins Field Office 307-328-4200 would settle it.

trails.name: Veterans Island Park Trail, Saratoga

other_links.label: Carbon County Visitors Council — Veterans Island Park
other_links.note: County tourism authority confirms the park: 'Located south of Pick Pike Road on the way to the Saratoga Inn.' A 6.9-acre island park on the North Platte in town.

trails.stats_note: AllTrails' listing carries 7 reviews and publishes no star average at that count. Distance, route type, time and the 2 m gain are all from the indexed snippet.
trails.needs: star rating — AllTrails publishes a count but no average for this listing. No published dog rule for the park.
trails.tag: The only flat, in-town, shoulder-season walk at this stop. Riverside, ten minutes, and it works on an arrival evening.

trails.name: Platte River Trail, Six Mile Gap (Platte River Wilderness)

other_links.label: USFS Medicine Bow-Routt — Six Mile Trailhead
other_links.note: Managing authority. 'The Six Mile Trailhead is located at the Six Mile Gap Campground, approximately 2 miles off Highway 230 and provides access to the North Platte River and Platte River Wilderness.' Recreation opportunities listed as Day Hikes and Backpacking. Trailhead at 41.0445, -106.3969. $5 per vehicle per day. Directions: from Encampment, 22 miles south on Hwy 230 to Forest Road 492, then 2 miles.

trails.season: USFS operational hours for the site are 'May - October weather permitting'.
trails.season_conflict: Stop arrives 16 Apr 2027 and leaves 20 Apr — the whole stay falls before the Forest Service opens this site. Listed so the card says what is being missed and why, not because it is walkable on these dates.
trails.needs: Length, time and difficulty are all unpublished by the Forest Service, which describes the trailhead rather than the trail. AllTrails has a 1.5 mi 'Platte River Trail' listing (26 reviews) but its nearest-town label is Centennial, on the far side of the Snowy Range, and it could not be confirmed as this trail — so it carries no link here rather than a plausible wrong one. Brush Creek/Hayden Ranger District would settle both the length and whether the FR 492 access is drivable in April.
trails.stats_note: It is roughly 44 road miles from Saratoga: down to Encampment, then 22 miles south on WY-230, then 2 miles of forest road.

trails.name: Treasure Island Bridge (North Platte River Public Access Area)
trails.dogs_note: NEEDS CHECK. The managing authority is the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission, through a cooperative agreement with private landowners, and its Public Access Area listing publishes no pet rule. Recorded as unknown, not assumed — and on a cooperative PAA the landowner's signage is the rule that counts.
trails.season: AllTrails gives best months as May through July, so a 16 Apr arrival is outside the published window. Nothing in the Game and Fish listing indicates a closure, and this is valley-floor river bottom rather than a mountain trail — but the early date is unverified and high spring flow on the North Platte is the thing to check before driving out.
trails.note: Six miles south of Saratoga on WY-230, with a parking area, an outhouse, a boat ramp and foot bridges giving nearly two miles of river frontage. The valley-floor walk the mid-April dates actually allow, and the only one of the area's four AllTrails listings that the earlier pass did not carry.
trails.note_source: AllTrails result title and stat line read in browser; Wyoming Game and Fish Department Public Access Area page for location, management and facilities

other_links.label: Wyoming Game & Fish — North Platte River Treasure Island PAA

offroad.name: WYO 130 — Snowy Range Scenic Byway seasonal gate section
offroad.distance: the closed section spans mile markers 36-48
offroad.difficulty: paved two-lane highway — listed only because it is the gate
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. WYDOT: "The closure spans mile markers 36-48, from the Green Rock trailhead in the east to just above Ryan Park in the west." In a recent year it closed 26 Nov and reopened 7 May the following spring (https://www.dot.state.wy.us/news/wyo-130-through-the-snowy-range-opens-for-the-season). The Saratoga chamber puts it more loosely at "usually opens by Memorial Day weekend". Either way 16-20 Apr 2027 is inside the closure.
offroad.note: Not an off-road route, and listed here only because it is the gate controlling access to the whole Snowy Range unpaved road network from Saratoga. Tops out at 10,800 ft. With WYO 130 and WYO 70 both shut, there is effectively no high-country backcountry driving available from this stop on these dates — which is the finding, and it is better on the card than a blank box.

offroad.name: Bennett Peak Road (BLM Road 3404) via County Road 660
offroad.distance: 7 mi on BLM Road 3404, after 12 mi of gravel County Road 660
offroad.difficulty: not published; BLM describes CR 660 only as a "graveled road"
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. BLM publishes: "Use season predominately from June 1st through November 15th depending on winter conditions." The stop is 16-20 Apr 2027, six weeks before the season opens.
offroad.note: BLM's directions verbatim: "From I-80, take Wyo 130 and Wyo 230 south aprox 38 miles to Riverside, take Wyo 230 east for 4 miles. Turn left onto County Rd 660 for 12 miles on graveled road to Bennett Peak Rd (BLM Road 3404) and follow it 7 miles to the campground." Ends at a BLM campground and boat ramp on the North Platte. This is the lowest-elevation unpaved route found near Saratoga and it still does not open until June.

offroad.name: Deep Creek Road (FR 801) to Aspen Alley
offroad.difficulty: not published by any authority
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP, indirectly. The road leaves WYO 70 about 25 miles west of Encampment, inside the Battle Pass seasonal closure (mile markers 27-50). WYDOT closed that stretch on 5 Dec in a recent year and crews only begin plowing the 23-mile section in mid-April to early May; one early year reopened 1 May and was described as almost three weeks ahead of normal (https://www.dot.state.wy.us/news/wyo-70-over-battle-pass-opens-for-the-season-4). The stop is 16-20 Apr 2027, so the access highway is very unlikely to be open.
offroad.note: From Encampment travel west about 25 miles on Highway 70 to Deep Creek Road (FR 801), then north 0.8 miles — "a half mile stretch of dirt road" overarched by tall aspens. Medicine Bow-Routt National Forest publishes no mileage, grade or surface rating for FR 801, so this entry is chamber-of-commerce sourced.

saratoga._review: 4 nights, arrive 16 Apr 2027. The existing three were re-checked against the area rather than topped up, and they hold: Encampment River #470, Veterans Island in town, and Six Mile Gap on the Platte are the right three for mid-April, because everything with elevation — the Snowy Range, Huston Park, the Sierra Madre — is at 8,000-10,000 ft and shut. AllTrails indexes only four trails for the whole Saratoga area and one addition was found that the earlier pass missed, so this is a nearly-right box with one gap closed.

Genuine rest / resupply day.entity: A logistics day, not a place — laundry, rig maintenance and pet downtime. Nothing named to link; the Klondike/Cassiar push referred to in the detail is linked from the driving entries, not from a rest day.

offroad.name: Dempster Highway to Tombstone Territorial Park
offroad.distance: the Dempster leaves the Klondike Highway 40 km east of Dawson City. Park southern boundary at km 50.5; Tombstone Interpretive Centre and the road-accessible campground at km 71.5 — about a 110 km drive from Dawson, gravel from km 0
offroad.difficulty: not graded. Gravel throughout, surface swinging between dusty-firm and slick mud with the weather
offroad.season: NO CONFLICT, and the timing is deliberate. The Tombstone Interpretive Centre runs daily 9am–5pm from mid-May to about 20 September (2026 season was 16 May – 20 Sep). The stop arrives 30 Aug 2027, inside that window and inside the 25 Aug – 5 Sep tundra colour peak this stop is anchored to. The centre closes roughly three weeks after arrival, so the whole stay is covered.
offroad.note: Only Canadian road that crosses the Arctic Circle, though the Circle is at km 406, far past Tombstone. For the Tombstone day trip you need no ferries and no Eagle Plains fuel stop — those matter only if the drive continues north. Still: carry at least one full-size spare, extra fuel and emergency kit, and expect no cell service, no food and no services past the highway junction. Yukon 511 carries current Dempster road conditions.

dawson-city.dogs: On leash (max 1 m) anywhere in the City of Dawson outside the north-end dog park, so the 9th Ave Trail and the dike are fine; the City names Crocus Bluff Park as a dog-free area but does not say whether the Crocus Bluff trails are inside it, so treat those two as unresolved until the trailhead signs say otherwise; Tombstone's trails on the Dempster are Yukon Parks and allow dogs under physical control.
dawson-city.dogs_source_quote: The soccer field, Minto Park, and Crocus Bluff Park are dog free areas.

watson-lake-2.dogs: Allowed on leash — YUKON PARKS, not Parks Canada or BC Parks, neither of which has jurisdiction here. The Parks General Regulation is stricter than the card used to say: pets must be leashed on trails AND within 50 m of trails, and in campgrounds, day-use areas and recreation parks. Elsewhere in a park they must be under active control.

trails.name: Wye Lake Loop
trails.was: Wye Lake Park — renamed to the listing's own title
trails.season: Best June-August; arrival 12 Sep is past it.
trails.note_source: Reviewers note missing interpretive signs and bugs.

trails.name: Liard Canyon Interpretive Trail
trails.distance: 2.2 km (1.4 mi) one way, so 4.4 km return — the Town of Watson Lake describes the same route as 3 km
trails.difficulty: Easy — Komoot grades the route easy and Trailforks calls it very clear and easy to follow
trails.reviews: no AllTrails listing — official source only. No trail database publishes a review count for it
trails.dogs_note: YUKON PARKS, not Parks Canada or BC Parks — the same jurisdiction and the same rule already recorded at this stop: pets must be leashed on trails AND within 50 m of trails, and in campgrounds, day-use areas and recreation parks; elsewhere in a park under active control. The 50 m rule matters on this one because the trail runs to a river bank where a dog off the path is still inside it. Note also that the car park is shared with the Town of Watson Lake's Lucky Lake day-use area, which is a municipal site and may carry its own bylaw.
trails.season: The trail itself is not gated, but the day-use area is closed 11 pm to 7 am and Yukon recreation-site services wind down in September — a 12-14 Sep arrival is the tail of the season, same as Wye Lake. Trailforks warns that the old trail at the far end is washed out, with a singletrack workaround about 50 m to the left, and that the Liard runs fast and dangerous in high water. Walk to the viewpoint, not down to the water.
trails.note: Forested one-way trail with interpretive panels, starting from the west end of Lucky Lake Park and ending at a view over the Liard River canyon — the Kaska name for the river is Nêt'i Tué', 'river flowing from mountains'. It follows historic routes of the explorer Robert Campbell, which ties it to the Robert Campbell Highway already in this stop's offroad box. Lucky Lake itself has a beach, a water slide and picnic tables at the trailhead.
trails.note_source: Government of Yukon Liard Canyon Recreation Site page (authority) for the 2.2 km length, the interpretive panels, the shared car park and the day-use hours; Town of Watson Lake parks and trails page for the 3 km figure and the Robert Campbell connection; Trailforks for the washout and river warning; Komoot for the easy grade

scenicDrives_patch.name: Alaska Highway (Yukon Highway 1) through Watson Lake
scenicDrives_patch.was_name: Alaska Highway through Watson Lake, past the Sign Post Forest into the Southern Lakes region.
scenicDrives_patch.note: Dawson Creek BC to Delta Junction AK, 2,232 km today. Watson Lake sits at Mile 635, at the Alaska Highway / Robert Campbell Highway junction; the Sign Post Forest is free and open year-round. Road conditions for the territory: 511yukon.ca.
scenicDrives_patch.season: Highway open year-round. The Watson Lake Visitor Information Centre — where you can make a sign — runs mid-May to mid-September, 8am–8pm. Arrive 12 Sep 2027: just inside that window, but only just.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: Travel Yukon (official Yukon tourism); Sign Post Forest listings

offroad.name: Robert Campbell Highway (Yukon Highway 4)
offroad.distance: 583 km / 362 mi Watson Lake to Carmacks, about 60% gravel
offroad.difficulty: "the road condition can vary dramatically according to recent weather and maintenance"
offroad.season: maintained year-round; no gate dates published
offroad.note: Two nights here on the way south, and the Campbell leaves the Alaska Highway right at Watson Lake - so an out-and-back up the first gravel is the natural day. "There are few services along the highway", fuel at Ross River and Faro only, and mid-September is when to carry more of it than the distance suggests. Yukon's own road pages return 403 from here; 511Yukon in the morning.

offroad.name: Nahanni Range Road (Yukon Highway 10)
offroad.difficulty: "The Nahanni Range Road proper is entirely gravel, and is not recommended for general public use"
offroad.season: unknown
offroad.note: Listed so it is recognised and left alone. It branches off the Campbell and serves the Cantung mine at Tungsten, NWT; the road "has been restored for the use of the mining company" but "general public travel is still not advised", and Yukon lists it among roads carrying weight restrictions. In mid-September, with no published maintenance calendar and no services, this is not the one.

watson-lake-2.dogs_source_quote: Pets must be on leash; on trails; within 50m of trails; and in all other areas where a sign says they must be leashed.
watson-lake-2.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — OUR CARD NAMES THE WRONG AUTHORITIES. It says "Parks Canada and BC Parks both permit dogs on trails"; neither has jurisdiction in Watson Lake, Yukon. The governing authority is Yukon Parks under the Parks General Regulation, and its rule is STRICTER than ours: leashed on trails AND within 50 m of trails, with "active control" elsewhere — "In all other areas of a park, pets must be under active control at all times." CAVEAT ON SCOPE: this regulation covers Yukon territorial parks, campgrounds and recreation sites. This stop's actual walks — the Sign Post Forest and the Wye Lake Park boardwalk — are Town of Watson Lake municipal facilities and are NOT covered by this citation; no municipal dog bylaw for them was found, so those remain unsourced. ACCESS NOTE: yukon.ca answers 403 to WebFetch but loads normally in the browser pane — the CLAUDE.md note calling it unreachable is too pessimistic.
watson-lake-2._review: 2 nights, arrive 12 Sep 2027. One trail on the card — Wye Lake Loop in town, already flagged as past its season. Two nights wants two walks, and Watson Lake has a second one that the earlier pass missed and that the Yukon government documents itself.

boya-lake.authority: BC Parks — Tā Ch'ilā Provincial Park
boya-lake.dogs: Allowed on leash — Parks Canada and BC Parks both permit dogs on trails, unlike the US national parks on this route. Note the park is now Tā Chʼilā Provincial Park — BC Parks renamed it, and signage and the reservation system use the new name. Jurisdiction is BC Parks alone; Parks Canada has none here.

trails.was: Beaver Lodge Trail (south end) — no url
trails.note_source: Ta Ch'ila's best-rated trail — from the campground along the lake edge into the forest. Recovered on an open search. Note there are Beaver Lodge trails in Oklahoma (marked CLOSED) and New York; this is the BC one.

Paddle only in calm weather with cold-wa.entity: The paddling water is Boya Lake, in what is now Ta Ch'ila Provincial Park (renamed from Boya Lake PP). The article documents the lake and park; it says nothing about rentals or conditions, which are the researched part of this note.

offroad.name: Cassiar townsite road (10 km west off Highway 37)
offroad.distance: "A 10-km drive west off the highway leads to the ghost town of Cassiar"
offroad.season: n/a - closed
offroad.note: CLOSED, and worth knowing before driving out there. The old asbestos-mining town of Cassiar is the obvious curiosity from this stop, a few km north at Jade City, and the road to it exists - but "there are no public facilities in the old Cassiar town-site, and it is closed to visitors." The same source notes "Old mining trails into the mountains can be travelled on foot or with 4x4 vehicles or ATVs" in the surrounding country, but names none of them and no managing authority publishes a route, a length or a condition. Ta Ch'ila (Boya Lake) itself is a paved-access park; this is a stop with essentially nothing driveable published.

boya-lake.finding: NOTHING TO ADD, and that is the answer rather than a failure. BC Parks' own page for Tā Ch'ilā Park (a.k.a. Boya Lake Park) says the park 'offers two short hiking trails, a mountain bike trail' and names exactly two: Lakeshore Trail, 1.5 km, and Beaver Lodge Trail, 1.5 km. Both are already on the card. AllTrails' park page likewise indexes 2 trails and no more. The mountain bike trail is neither named nor measured by the authority, so it cannot be listed as an entity. The nearest alternative walking of any size is 200+ km away down Highway 37. Three nights here is a canoe-and-sit stop, not a hiking stop, and the card should say so rather than be padded.
boya-lake.dogs_note: BC Parks, quoted: pets 'must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings', and 'Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to the potential for problems with bears and other wildlife.' Both listed trails are front-country and legal on a leash; the beach at the end of them is not.

other_links.label: BC Parks — Tā Ch'ilā Park (a.k.a. Boya Lake Park)
other_links.note: Authority. Source of the two trail names, the 1.5 km lengths and the pet rule.

boya-lake.trails_finding: Cannot be thickened, and this is the answer rather than a gap. BC Parks names exactly two trails at Tā Chʼilā (Boya Lake) — Lakeshore and Beaver Lodge, 1.5 km each — and both are on the card. AllTrails indexes the same two. The only other path is an unnamed mountain-bike trail, which cannot be listed as an entity without inventing a name for it.
boya-lake.dogs_source_quote: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings.
boya-lake.dogs_source_note: DRIFT, two things. (1) THE PARK HAS BEEN RENAMED: BC Parks now publishes it as "Tā Ch'ilā Park [a.k.a. Boya Lake Park]" — worth carrying on the card, since signage and reservations use the new name. (2) Our card's sentence ("Parks Canada and BC Parks both permit dogs on trails") is OUR generalisation, not a quotation from anyone, and Parks Canada has no jurisdiction here — this is a BC provincial park. The page also adds a restriction we omit: "Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to the potential for problems with bears and other wildlife."

dease-lake.note: The single trail entry here was 'Boya Lake trails (Tā Ch'ilā PP)' — those belong to the Boya Lake stop two days earlier, not to Dease Lake. Left in place pending a real Dease Lake trail; not linked to another stop's trails.

A product model designation: no Wikipedia article, and no parent article documents it. Recorded as unknown rather than linked to a generic 'truck camper' article, which would not be the same thing.

offroad.name: Telegraph Creek Road
offroad.distance: BC Ministry of Transportation: "115 kilometres (71 miles) southwest from Dease Lake", "2.5 to three hours each way"
offroad.difficulty: BC MoTI: "very steep grades, up to 20 per cent, and a gravel surface"; "RV trailers are not recommended for this trip"
offroad.season: no gate dates published; BC advises "Check in Dease Lake for the current road conditions to Telegraph Creek"
offroad.note: The single best offroad day of the whole Cassiar and it starts in this town. Sharp-angled switchbacks and narrow passages along the canyon walls with no guardrails, dropping into the Stikine to the most remote road-accessible town in BC. British Columbia's tourism authority adds the practical line: "The road is not suitable for trailers, which can be left in Dease Lake." Six hours of driving plus stops - it wants a whole day of a two-night stop, and mid-September is late enough that the morning conditions check is not a formality.

dease-lake.trails_note: Dease Lake has essentially no published trail, and that is a researched finding rather than a gap. Recreation Sites and Trails BC lists exactly three assets whose closest community is Dease Lake — French Creek (REC0564), Morchuea Lake (REC0598) and Sawmill Point (REC0886) — all of them recreation SITES, none of them a recreation trail, and none listing hiking among its activities. A search of the RSTBC register for Tanzilla, Stikine, Telegraph, Iskut, Gnat, Tuya and Edziza returns nothing in this district. AllTrails has no Dease Lake area page at all; the only thing it indexes nearby is a point-of-interest entry for Allan Lake. Mount Edziza Park is the real hiking ground here and it is float-plane and multi-day expedition country — BC Parks' own page is about bear caches, aircraft Letters of Authorization and not walking on the lava — so it is not listed, because the stop text does not name it and nothing in a two-night September stop reaches it.
dease-lake.trails_warning: A trail called the 'Dease Lake Alpine Trail' turns up all over the web and IS NOT AT DEASE LAKE. Ten near-identical listings (veronikasadventure, happytovisit, jtgtravel, powertraveller, evendo, peek, travelersuniverse and others) syndicate the same guided-tour copy, and the Tripadvisor version places it on 'Sea to Sky Highway, Highway 99' — Squamish, about 1,200 km south. It is a content-farm product with a misleading name. Do not book it, and do not let it back into this box.

trails.name: Tuya River Valley viewpoint trail, Stikine River Park
trails.dogs_note: BC Parks, Stikine River Park: 'Pets and domestic animals must always be on a leash and are not permitted on beach areas or in park buildings.' Leashed on the trail is fine.

other_links.label: BC Parks — Stikine River Park
other_links.note: Managing authority. Under Things to do → Hiking: 'As you enter the park (approximately 60 km west of Dease Lake), you will notice a pullout parking area on the right. From here, a short trail leads to a viewpoint overlooking the Tuya River Valley.' Safety: 'Sharp drop-offs border the entire Grand Canyon. These, combined with broken rock prevalent in the area, make it extremely dangerous to approach the canyon rim.' Off-road vehicles, including ATVs, are prohibited in the park.

trails.stats_note: BC Parks publishes no length, no time and no grade — only 'a short trail' from a signed pullout. Recorded as unknown rather than estimated. 60 km west of Dease Lake on Telegraph Creek Road, which this stop already plans to drive in the truck.
trails.needs: distance, time, difficulty. BC Parks Stikine Area 250-771-4591 is the number that would settle all three, and is worth the call anyway to ask whether Telegraph Creek Road is in shape in mid-September.

trails.name: Grand Canyon of the Stikine viewpoint hike
trails.distance: about 4 km (2.5 mi) to the canyon rim

other_links.label: Edziza Trails — Day Tours
other_links.note: The only published description of this walk, from a Tahltan-run guiding company in Dease Lake: 'After a one hour drive west of Dease Lake on the Telegraph Creek Road you'll enjoy a four kilometer hike to the Grand Canyon of the Stikine River. There you will have lunch on the hilltop taking in the spectacular view of the Stikine River Grand Canyon.' $100 per person plus fuel, maximum group of 5, roughly a 6-7 hour day.

trails.stats_note: This is on the card because it is the one real hike anybody publishes for this stop, and it is flagged because it is sold as a guided outing rather than signed as a public trail. BC Parks names no trailhead for it and Recreation Sites and Trails BC has no record of it, so the parking spot cannot be sourced from a map. Do not drive out looking for a trail sign.
trails.needs: Whether it can be walked unguided, and from where. Two numbers settle it: Edziza Trails direct, and BC Parks Stikine Area 250-771-4591. Recorded as unknown rather than treated as a public trailhead.

Fish Creek wildlife viewing may be past.entity: Fish Creek Wildlife Observation Site, Hyder

offroad.name: Salmon Glacier Road (Granduc Road)
offroad.distance: about 25 miles from Hyder at sea level to the Salmon Glacier summit viewpoint, climbing roughly 4,300 ft
offroad.difficulty: not published as a grade. Active mining road — sharp switchbacks, steep drop-offs, no guardrails, loose gravel; high clearance and durable tyres recommended
offroad.season: TIGHT AGAINST THE STOP DATES. The road is not open year-round; the usable window is roughly mid-June to September, and snowbanks can persist even mid-summer. The stop arrives 19 Sep 2027, at the very tail of that window — an early storm can shut the upper road with no notice. Verify locally in Stewart before driving up rather than assuming.
offroad.note: The route crosses back into British Columbia above Hyder, so carry passports for the return through the Canadian border post at Stewart. Fish Creek Wildlife Observation Site is six miles up the same road, with brown and black bears on the salmon from late July into September — that part of the drive is short, paved-adjacent and worth doing even if the upper road is closed. Land-manager coverage is thin: this is a private mining road, so state tourism is the best source found and there is no BLM/USFS/BC Parks page for it.

stewart-hyder.authority: BC Parks — Meziadin Lake Park; the Hyder-side trails are USDA Forest Service (Tongass NF) and the Town of Stewart
stewart-hyder.dogs: District of Stewart requires dogs on leash in public, so the Rainey Creek trail and municipal park are fine; BC Parks' Meziadin Lake Park: "Pets/domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement." The Ore Mountain trail starts at a Forest Service recreation site and no manager publishes a dog rule for it.
stewart-hyder.dogs_exception: No pets page was found for the Tongass NF around Hyder or for the Town of Stewart, so those two are unknown. Separately, the Fish Creek bear-viewing site is a place to leave the dog behind regardless of what the rule turns out to be.
stewart-hyder.dogs_source_quote: It is the law! Plain and simple.

prince-george.authority: BC Parks — Ancient Forest / Chun T'oh Whudujut
prince-george.dogs: Allowed on leash — BC PARKS, not Parks Canada, which has no jurisdiction here. At Ancient Forest / Chun T’oh Whudujut the rule is boardwalk-specific; check the park page before assuming the universal-access boardwalk takes the dog.

trails.name: Big Tree and Treebeard Loop
trails.was: Ancient Forest Boardwalk Trail — renamed to the listing's own title
trails.note_source: Ancient Forest / Chun T'oh Whudujut, 120 km east of Prince George — 2.3 km of boardwalk to the Big Tree, Tree Beard and a cascading waterfall, through thousand-year-old western red cedars. BC Parks: bcparks.ca/ancient-forest-chun-toh-whudujut-park

trails.name: Cottonwood Island Loop Trail (Cottonwood Island Nature Park)
trails.distance: 1.7 mi loop (the city gives the park's trails as 2.2 km)
trails.elevation_gain: less than 10 m of change across the park
trails.reviews: 4.3 (355) — title count 355; the star line shows 256 ratings
trails.cruise_reason: Paved, granular and dirt, flat, and part of the Heritage River and Centennial Trail network — the surface is right. But the City of Prince George's park page does not state whether bikes are permitted on the park trails and AllTrails lists it for hiking, running and walking only, so cruise is left unset rather than claimed.
trails.dogs_note: The City of Prince George, the managing authority, states on its own park page: 'Cottonwood Island Nature Park is an on-leash area. Keep your pet on a leash at all times.' It also warns the park holds wildlife and to keep dogs close. This is a published authority rule, not an AllTrails inference — and it is a cleaner source than the stop's existing BC Parks boardwalk rule, which is specific to the Ancient Forest.
trails.season: No seasonal window published; the park is a riverside city park open year-round. Reviewers note it can be muddy when the river is high. A 24-26 Sep arrival is the good half of the shoulder — cottonwoods turning.
trails.note: 32 hectares on the Nechako shoreline just north of downtown, next to the Prince George Railway and Forestry Museum, with heritage bridges, wetlands, washrooms, a picnic shelter and a canoe launch. The tree-bark carvings by Elmer Gunderson are the thing people remember. Flat, paved, forty minutes, five minutes from camp — exactly the walk a two-night stop with a 230 km day trip in it needs on the other day.
trails.note_source: AllTrails result title and stat line read in browser; City of Prince George park and trail pages (authority) for the leash rule, the trail network, the surface, the amenities and the carvings; hiking.princegeorge.tech for the 32-hectare area, 2.2 km length and sub-10 m elevation change

offroad.name: Hungary Creek Forest Road (Sugarbowl-Grizzly Den)
offroad.distance: about 13 km south on the Hungary Creek Forest Road to the Grizzly Den trailhead, 2.6 km further to Raven Lake
offroad.difficulty: no 2WD/4WD statement published
offroad.season: BC Parks notes "the Hungary Creek Road was no longer plowed in the winter" after harvesting ended
offroad.note: The closest alpine country to Prince George, about 80-95 km southeast on Highway 16 - "turn right on to the Hungary Creek Forest Road and drive south keeping on the main road". Sugarbowl trailhead at 80 km from Prince George, Viking Ridge at 85 km, the Hungary Creek access at about 88 km from the east end of the Yellowhead Bridge. Late September is inside the drivable season but the road is not maintained for snow, so an early storm is the thing that ends it.

offroad.name: Tabor Mountain trail system
offroad.distance: "extensive 407km multi-use trail system interlinking 27 staging areas"
offroad.difficulty: not published per route
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: Recreation Sites and Trails BC manages this as a motorized and non-motorized network about 20 minutes east of the city, reached off Highway 16 via Stewart Road / Tabor Lake East Road and Giscome Road. 27 staging areas means the truck can be parked in and the day chosen on the spot. The RST BC pages are a JavaScript app that returns an empty document to a plain fetch, so the figures here are the indexed record of the authority's own listing; individual route difficulty and surface are not published.

prince-george.dogs_source_quote: Pets must be on leash on the Ancient Forest boardwalk trails.
prince-george.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — our card's sentence is a generalisation naming Parks Canada, which has no jurisdiction at this stop. The relevant authority is BC Parks at Ancient Forest / Chun T'oh Whudujut, and its rule is boardwalk-specific. It also states "Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears." The stop's other walks — Cottonwood Island Nature Park and Lheidli T'enneh Memorial Park — are CITY of Prince George parks and are NOT covered by this citation; they remain unsourced.
prince-george._review: 2 nights, arrive 24 Sep 2027, and the single trail on the card is at the Ancient Forest — 115 km east on Highway 16, a 230 km round trip. That is a whole day of a two-day stop and there is nothing in Prince George itself. Added the in-town walk, which also happens to be the one place here with an explicit, published, on-leash dog rule.
prince-george._also_considered: L.C. Gunn Trail is the highest-count trail in the Prince George index at 389 reviews — 6.9 km out-and-back, moderately challenging, 2 hr 3 min, on the cutbanks above the Fraser. It is the better walk of the two and the right choice if the Ancient Forest day is dropped. Left off only because two nights does not stretch to three walks; if this stop ever gains a night, this is the trail to add. Moore's Meadow Loop (2.2 mi, easy, 54 min, 4.4 from 182) is the third.

clearwater.authority: BC Parks — Wells Gray Provincial Park
clearwater.dogs: BC PARKS, not Parks Canada — Wells Gray is a provincial park. The rule is ZONED and the card was wrong in both directions: leashed in the frontcountry, within 1 km of a road, and BC Parks explicitly permits dogs OFF leash in the backcountry. Banned from beaches and buildings.

trails.name: Trophy Meadows Trail
trails.was: Trophy Meadows Trailhead — a trailhead, not a trail
trails.note_source: Wildflowers peak late July; arrival is 26 Sep, so expect the meadows gone over.

trails.name: Moul Falls Trail
trails.was: Moul Falls Trailhead — a trailhead, not a trail
trails.season: AllTrails lists this trail as CLOSED. Check BC Parks before counting on it — it is the stop's marquee walk.

trails.name: Helmcken Falls Rim Trail
trails.note: The stop's obvious missing walk. Wells Gray's icon is a 141 m (463 ft) plunge on the Murtle River, and the card carried no route to it at all - only Moul Falls, which AllTrails flags CLOSED, and Trophy Meadows, which is over by late September. The rim trail follows the canyon edge above the falls from the viewpoint car park. AllTrails: the road to Helmcken Falls is plowed in winter, so late-September access is not in question; parking is limited.
trails.note_source: AllTrails trail page snippet read in the browser (rating, count, length, gain, estimated time, difficulty on one line). BC Parks Wells Gray page for the pet rule.
trails.dogs_source_quote: In the backcountry (anywhere more than 1 km from a highway or park road), dogs may be off leash.
trails.dogs_note: Wells Gray is ZONED, not blanket: leashed within 1 km of a highway or park road, off leash permitted beyond that. This trail leaves a road-side car park, so treat it as leash-required for its first kilometre. Murtle Lake is a total pet ban and is not part of this stop.
trails.stats_note: Review count drifts across indexed snapshots - 769, 816 and 840 were all read this pass. 4.6 (816) is the star-and-count pair read together in a single AllTrails snippet; good enough to order the box, not to quote.

trails.name: West Lake Loop via Bailey's Chute
trails.note: The substantial easy loop the card was missing - three waterfalls on one walk. Bailey's Chute is under 1 km in; the loop continues past Marcus Falls and Myanth Falls and comes back around West Lake. Late September is the tail of the chinook run that makes Bailey's Chute worth standing at: salmon hurl themselves at the chute and fail. The out-and-back stub to the chute alone is 0.8 mi / 82 ft / 0.5-1 hr if the loop is more than the day needs.
trails.note_source: AllTrails: 'West Lake Loop via Bailey's Chute is considered an easy hike that covers 3.3 mi, with an elevation gain of 547 ft'; the 4.6 (160) pair from the Bailey's Chute point-of-interest page. Stub figures from the separate Bailey's Chute listing (126 reviews, 0.8 mi, 82 ft, 0.5-1 hr, out and back).
trails.dogs_source_quote: In the backcountry (anywhere more than 1 km from a highway or park road), dogs may be off leash.

other_links.label: AllTrails - Bailey's Chute (short version)
other_links.note: The 0.8 mi out-and-back to the chute only, 126 reviews. Same trailhead.

trails.name: Dawson Falls South
trails.note: The second of Wells Gray's three signature falls and the one the card skipped. Dawson spreads wide across the Murtle rather than plunging - a 90 m curtain rather than a drop - and it is on the same road as Helmcken, a few minutes short of it. Short, flat and easy with the dog. AllTrails reviewers describe a well-maintained main path plus a rougher side path down to the water's edge; the side path is the one that needs care.
trails.note_source: AllTrails Dawson Falls point-of-interest page: 'the best place to hike near Dawson Falls is Dawson Falls South, which has a 4.6 star rating from 422 reviews. This trail is 1.4 km long with an elevation gain of 25 m.' A second POI page read the same trail as 4.7 from 489 reviews; the trail page title showed 502.
trails.dogs_source_quote: In the backcountry (anywhere more than 1 km from a highway or park road), dogs may be off leash.
trails.stats_note: Counts read this pass: 422, 489, 502. Star read as 4.6 on one POI page and 4.7 on another. Ordering signal only.
