offroad.name: Mush Lake Road
offroad.distance: 52 km, 30 m elevation change
offroad.difficulty: Parks Canada: "A four wheel drive road. Two-wheel drive vehicles with good clearance can drive the first 5 km to Alder Creek when conditions are good." Graded Moderate.
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: The only road INSIDE Kluane that Parks Canada states is drivable - most of the park is reached on foot, by raft or by ski, and the only other vehicle access is Kathleen Lake and Thechal Dhal. Parks Canada also calls it a "Good mountain biking trail", so the far end is rideable if the road turns. Trailhead is off the Kathleen Lake area south of Haines Junction.

offroad.name: Alsek Valley (old mining road)
offroad.distance: 52.8 km total; "The first 15 km may be drivable with 4-wheel drive/high clearance vehicles"
offroad.difficulty: Parks Canada grades the route Easy; "Trail is in the valley bottom with some variable creeks to cross (no bridges)"
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: "Follows an old mining road." The creeks are the variable - Parks Canada says no bridges, and how far the 15 km actually goes depends on what they are running. Late June is high-water season off the icefields, so this is a turn-back-early day rather than a distance target. The Haines Junction visitor centre will have the current state.

offroad.name: Aishihik Road
offroad.distance: about 120 km to Aishihik village; Aishihik Lake Campground at km 43
offroad.difficulty: "gravel/dirt", "mostly a clay-dirt that's very slippery when it's wet"; "mudholes are common, some surprisingly deep"
offroad.season: Yukon Parks services Aishihik Lake Campground 22 May - 1 Oct; the road beyond km 43 "is not maintained" at normal levels
offroad.note: Runs north from Historic Mile 995 on the Alaska Highway - the Otter Falls Cutoff, about 34 km east of Haines Junction - past Otter Falls (the falls on the 1954 five dollar bill) and Canyon Lake to the campground at km 43, then on to Aishihik village. The clay is the whole story: dry it is an easy gravel run, wet it is the reason to turn round. Several bridges have had major rebuilds after flood damage.

kluane-1.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be on a leash of 3 metres or less, and under control at all times – it is the law.
kluane-1.dogs_source_note: Same national Parks Canada page; Kluane's own pages state a leash requirement without the 3 m length. Our card's "local bulletins can close individual trails to dogs" is not stated on any Kluane page — treat it as prudent advice rather than a published Kluane rule.

kluane-2.dogs: Allowed on trails, leash 3 m or less — Parks Canada. Local bulletins can close individual trails to dogs; check the trailhead boards.

Revisit Kathleen Lake, Rock Glacier, and.entity: Kathleen Lake; Kluane National Park and Reserve

offroad.name: Mush Lake Road
offroad.distance: 52 km, 30 m elevation change
offroad.difficulty: Parks Canada: "A four wheel drive road. Two-wheel drive vehicles with good clearance can drive the first 5 km to Alder Creek when conditions are good."
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: One night here, so this is the one to pick: the first 5 km to Alder Creek is a short evening out and the only road access into Kluane other than Kathleen Lake and Thechal Dhal. Late August is past the meltwater peak, which is when the road is at its best.

offroad.name: Alsek Valley (old mining road)
offroad.distance: "The first 15 km may be drivable with 4-wheel drive/high clearance vehicles"
offroad.difficulty: "some variable creeks to cross (no bridges)"
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: Late August is the better half of the year for the unbridged creeks than the June visit was, but it is still a road whose usable length is decided on the day by the water. Ask at Haines Junction before setting out.

kluane-2.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be on a leash of 3 metres or less, and under control at all times – it is the law.
kluane-2.dogs_source_note: As kluane-1 — national page carries the 3 m rule; the trail-bulletin clause is not published by Kluane itself.

Walk West Yellowstone and visit the Griz.entity: West Yellowstone, Montana; Grizzly & Wolf Discovery Center

offroad.name: Two Top Loop Snowmobile Trail
offroad.distance: about 30 miles groomed, ~2,000 ft of climb, straddling the Continental Divide
offroad.difficulty: not published as a wheeled-vehicle grade — it is graded as a groomed snowmobile route
offroad.season: CONFLICTS WITH THE STOP DATES. Two Top is a groomed winter route: open 1 Dec to 31 Mar per the Custer Gallatin NF, with some listings running the season to 15 Apr. The stop arrives 12 May 2027 — the grooming season has been over for a month at minimum. No summer wheeled-vehicle opening date could be sourced for the Two Top road at ~8,700 ft, and mid-May at that elevation near the Divide is normally still snow.
offroad.note: This is the famous 'snow ghosts' ride out of West Yellowstone, and it is a genuinely good reason to be here — in February, not in May. Filed as a route rather than deleted so the card says what is being missed. If a May 4x4 day out of West Yellowstone is wanted, it needs a different, lower road picked by name.

not_a_route.entry: Loaded camper: paved and good maintained gravel only.
not_a_route.problem: Standing rig constraint, not a route. Superseded — offroad is always the truck.

west-yellowstone.authority: National Park Service — Yellowstone National Park
west-yellowstone.dogs: NPS: "Pets are not allowed on boardwalks, hiking trails, in the backcountry, or in thermal areas." Pets are allowed only "in developed areas and must stay within 100 feet (30.5 meters) of roads, parking areas, and campgrounds", in a car, crate, or on a leash no longer than six feet.
west-yellowstone.dogs_exception: Every trail on this card is a geyser-basin boardwalk or a hiking trail — none of them is walkable with the dog. The 100 ft strip beside the roads and parking areas is all that is open.
west-yellowstone.dogs_source_quote: Pets are not allowed on boardwalks, hiking trails, in the backcountry, or in thermal areas.

bozeman.dogs: Gallatin Valley Land Trust publishes a dog rule on each Main Street to the Mountains trail page: off-leash on Drinking Horse Mountain and the College M, on-leash on Triple Tree and the Gallagator — only Grotto Falls, which is Custer Gallatin NF in Hyalite, has no published rule.

offroad.name: Hyalite Canyon Road (FSR 62)
offroad.difficulty: not published; the Forest Service notes only that during the spring closure the saturated roadbed "cannot support the weight of motorized traffic"
offroad.season: OPEN ON THESE DATES, BUT ONLY JUST — THE TIGHTEST MARGIN ON THIS LEG. The Custer Gallatin publishes an annual spring closure of the Hyalite Canyon Recreation Corridor to all motorized vehicles "from April 1 through May 15, with a scheduled reopening May 16." The stop is 20-22 May 2027, so the gate lifts four days before arrival. A late spring that pushes the reopening back takes the whole canyon out of this stop.
offroad.note: The main recreation corridor south of Bozeman, in the Bozeman Ranger District. The closure protects the roadbed during spring break-up: "As temperatures rise and snow melts, the ground beneath Hyalite Road becomes saturated." Non-motorized use is allowed throughout. No mileage or surface breakdown is published.

offroad.name: Storm Castle Road (FSR 132)
offroad.season: PARTIAL CONFLICT. The lower gate opens 16 May, the upper 16 June, with a further upper section opening 16 July — so on 20-22 May 2027 the lower road should be open and both upper sections shut. Not a Forest Service source, so treat the dates as indicative; the 16 May lower-gate pattern is corroborated by the official Hyalite reopening date.
offroad.note: Off the Gallatin Canyon south of Bozeman, giving access to the Storm Castle and Rat Lake area. The three-stage gate structure means the driveable portion in late May is the lowest section only. No mileage, surface or difficulty published.
offroad.source: Outside Bozeman 'Gates & Dates' (road managed by USFS Custer Gallatin NF)

offroad.name: Portal Creek Road (FSR 984)
offroad.difficulty: not published by the Forest Service
offroad.season: PARTIAL CONFLICT, AND THE TWO AVAILABLE FIGURES DISAGREE. Outside Bozeman's gate-date list records a lower gate opening 16 May and an upper gate opening 16 June, which would put the lower section open and the upper shut on 20-22 May 2027. A separate community source states the road "is gated near Highway 191 from December 2 through June 15th" (https://www.bozemannet.com/forest_service_cabins/windy.php), which would make the whole road shut during the stay. Neither is a Forest Service page. Worth a call to the Bozeman Ranger District rather than a guess.
offroad.note: Runs east off US-191 in the Gallatin Canyon into the southern Gallatin Range toward Windy Pass. The Outside Bozeman list is a 2017 compilation, so its dates are indicative rather than current.
offroad.source: Outside Bozeman 'Gates & Dates' (road managed by USFS Custer Gallatin NF)

offroad.name: Fairy Lake Road (FSR 74)
offroad.season: CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. The lower gate opens 1 June — "Fairy Lake Rd. #74 and South Fork Bracket Rd. #631 - lower gates, June 1". The stop is 20-22 May 2027, ten days early. Not a Forest Service source, so treat the exact date as indicative; the direction of the answer is not in doubt given the elevation.
offroad.note: The rough road up the west side of the Bridger Range to Fairy Lake, north of Bozeman. Recorded because it is the obvious Bridger objective and it is the one nearby road that is definitely still gated during this stay — useful to know before driving out to find a locked gate.
offroad.source: Outside Bozeman 'Gates & Dates' (road managed by USFS Custer Gallatin NF)

Fort Nelson Heritage Museum.entity: Fort Nelson Heritage Museum, Fort Nelson BC — the museum itself has no article; the town article does

Parker Lake.entity: The lake west of Fort Nelson, BC. No article. Fort Nelson, British Columbia names Parker Lake once, but only as the origin of the May 2024 wildfire that evacuated the town -- it documents the fire, not the lake, so it is not a parent for a things-to-do highlight.

fort-nelson.authority: BC Parks — Stone Mountain Park (Flower Springs, Summit Lake); the town trails are Northern Rockies Regional Municipality
fort-nelson.dogs: Northern Rockies Regional Municipality requires dogs leashed in public, which covers the Community Trail, the Demonstration Forest and Tetsa River Regional Park; BC Parks' Stone Mountain Park: "Pets must be leashed and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or any pets due to the potential for problems with bears and other wildlife." Parker Lake Ecological Reserve publishes no pet rule at all.
fort-nelson.dogs_exception: Parker Lake is an ecological reserve, a different designation from a provincial park with its own access rules — treat the silence there as a real unknown and check before taking the dog.
fort-nelson.dogs_source_quote: Dogs must be leashed when in public

offroad.name: Andy Bailey Lake access road
offroad.distance: 12 km of gravel off the Alaska Highway
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: Tourism Northern Rockies: "Access the lake and campground by following 12 kms of road located just off the Alaska Highway", at Mile 265 / km 427. The shortest real gravel outing from Fort Nelson - campground, day-use area and a long gravel boat launch (non-motorized boats only) in boreal forest. No vehicle restriction is published.

offroad.name: Sikanni Chief Falls access road
offroad.distance: 15 km west of the Alaska Highway
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks: "Access is via a 4x4 gravel/dirt petroleum road. Watch for industrial traffic."
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: The one genuine 4x4 route on this stretch of the Alcan, and BC Parks says so in as many words. A 1.5 km hiking trail leads from the parking area to a viewpoint beside the 30 m falls; "No ATVs are allowed on the trail" and "ORVs are prohibited in this park", so the 4x4 gets you to the trailhead and no further. Distance is the catch: BC Parks places it "approximately 200 km northwest of Fort St. John", which is roughly 140 km south of Fort Nelson - a half-day each way out of a two-night stop.

offroad.name: Liard Highway (BC 77 / NWT 7, the Liard Trail)
offroad.distance: 254 km of gravel on the NWT side
offroad.season: no seasonal closure published; NWT Infrastructure maintains it year-round
offroad.note: NWT Infrastructure: "Highway 7, also known as the Liard Trail, is a gravel highway that begins at the BC border and continues north for 254 kilometres", following the Liard River to the Highway 1 junction. Fort Liard is 5 km off the highway, 38 km north of the BC border. The junction with the Alaska Highway is 28 km north of Fort Nelson (DriveBC camera 485), so the BC 77 approach plus the first gravel out of the border is a full day. NWT adds "Travellers are very likely to encounter wood bison along this route. Drive with caution."

liard.authority: BC Parks — Liard River Hot Springs Park
liard.dogs: BC Parks: "Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings." "Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears."
liard.dogs_exception: BC Parks does not say whether pets may go onto the boardwalk or the pool deck at the springs — the published rule names beach areas and buildings only. Worth asking at the gate rather than assuming; and the dog cannot be left in the coach here in summer heat.

official_links.label: Liard River Hot Springs Park (BC Parks)

offroad.name: Smith River Falls access road
offroad.distance: about 2.4-2.6 km of gravel off the Alaska Highway
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks: "The road is very narrow and may not be suitable for larger vehicles" and "Passing oncoming traffic can be extremely difficult"
offroad.season: BC Parks: the viewpoint is "reachable by vehicle, except in winter"
offroad.note: Smith River Falls - Fort Halkett Park sits at the confluence of the Smith and Liard rivers, "near kilometre 820 of the Alaska Highway, and 30 km west of Liard River Hot Springs Park" - the closest real side road to this stop. From the parking lot a short trail drops to the base of the 35 m falls; BC Parks warns "Sections of the trail are very steep and can be treacherous." Exactly the outing the truck exists for, and exactly the road the coach must not follow.

offroad.name: Whirlpool Canyon access road
offroad.distance: short unpaved spur off the Alaska Highway
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: Tourism Northern Rockies: "This area is accessed by a short unpaved road off the Alaska Highway; please note that the parking area has limited space for turning around." Overlooks the Liard River where rock and timber debris is thrown up by the water; a short walking trail leads downriver from the left of the parking area to more canyon features. Coordinates given as 59.6348, -126.9833, which puts it a short run east of the hot springs.

liard.dogs_source_quote: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings.
liard.dogs_source_note: Both sentences on the card are verbatim from this page. Note the URL slug is "liard-river-hot-springs-park" (hot springs, two words), not "hotsprings".

Simulated aurora show, Northern Lights S.entity: Aurora (the phenomenon the show simulates). The Northern Lights Space & Science Centre in Watson Lake has no article.

Northern Lights Centre if the schedule f.entity: The aurora science centre in Watson Lake. It has no article of its own, but the town article documents it by name as one of the town's two tourist attractions: 'Tourist attractions in Watson Lake include the Northern Lights Centre and the much-imitated original Sign Post Forest.'

Wye Lake Park boardwalk loop.entity: Town boardwalk park in Watson Lake. No article, and the Watson Lake, Yukon full text never mentions Wye Lake.

not_a_trail.problem: Superseded by the researched entry for this stop, or belongs to another stop / is not a trail.

offroad.name: Robert Campbell Highway (Yukon Highway 4)
offroad.distance: 583 km / 362 mi Watson Lake to Carmacks, about 60% gravel
offroad.difficulty: no published rating; "the road condition can vary dramatically according to recent weather and maintenance"
offroad.season: maintained year-round; no gate dates published
offroad.note: Leaves the Alaska Highway at Watson Lake, so the first hours of it are a day trip straight out of camp rather than a commitment to the whole 583 km. "There are few services along the highway" - fuel only at Ross River and Faro. Yukon's own road pages (yukon.ca and 511Yukon) refuse every fetch from here with a 403, so this is a travel-guide description rather than the territory's; 511Yukon is the number to check on the morning.

offroad.name: Nahanni Range Road (Yukon Highway 10)
offroad.difficulty: "The Nahanni Range Road proper is entirely gravel, and is not recommended for general public use"
offroad.season: unknown
offroad.note: Recorded as a route to KNOW ABOUT AND NOT TAKE. It branches off the Campbell Highway and runs to the Cantung mine at Tungsten, NWT; since the mine reopened the road "has been restored for the use of the mining company" but "general public travel is still not advised". Yukon's 511 page lists it among roads carrying weight restrictions. If it is ever wanted, 511Yukon is the authority - and yukon.ca is unreachable from here, so it is a phone call, not a fetch.

offroad.name: Nabesna Road
offroad.distance: 42 miles one way, gravel the whole length, from mile 60 of the Tok Cutoff at Slana
offroad.difficulty: not graded by NPS. Most 2WD vehicles manage the first 29 miles; beyond mile 29 the unbridged stream crossings need high clearance and sometimes 4WD
offroad.season: No gate and no published closure, but the crossings are the season. NPS warns that spring run-off and heavy rain can make the streams beyond mile 29 impassable. The stop arrives 25 Jun 2027, which is still late run-off in that valley — the first 29 miles should be fine, the last stretch is a day-of decision.
offroad.note: One of only two roads into Wrangell-St. Elias. Flat tires and washouts are common along the whole length; carry a full-size spare and the means to fit it. The maintained road ends at a private hunting lodge at mile 42, and NPS does not recommend driving the last four miles — deeply rutted and wet. Stop at the Slana Ranger Station at mile 0.5 for current crossing conditions and the free Nabesna Road Guide before committing.

tok-1.dogs: Leashed dogs are fine — the overlook trail is in Eagle Trail State Recreation Site, and Alaska State Parks allow pets throughout on a leash of nine feet or less in developed areas, voice control in the backcountry.
tok-1.dogs_source_quote: Yes, Pets are welcome at state parks and campgrounds if leashed and accompanied by the owner at all times; unleashed dogs are allowed in the backcountry but must be within voice command.
tok-1.dogs_note: Eagle Trail State Recreation Site, Mile 109.5 Tok Cut-Off, is an Alaska State Parks unit; its own page describes 'the 2.5-mile hiking trail with an overview of the Tok River Valley' (https://dnr.alaska.gov/parks/aspunits/northern/eagletrailsrs.htm) but publishes no pet rule of its own, so the statewide rule is what applies.

Chena Hot Springs Road and Angel Rocks a.entity: Chena Hot Springs; Dalton Highway ('the Dalton'). Angel Rocks has no article.

scenicDrives_patch.name: Steese Highway National Scenic Byway
scenicDrives_patch.note: Fairbanks to Circle, 161 mi. First 81 mi paved, the rest gravel. Eagle Summit at 3,685 ft is one of the highest road passes in Alaska and is the midnight-sun viewpoint. BLM's Cripple Creek campground at mile 60. Truck only — this is a day out, not a coach transfer.
scenicDrives_patch.season: Open year-round; the gravel section is the constraint, not a gate. Arrive 26 Jun 2027 — solstice window, which is the whole point of Eagle Summit.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: Alaska DOT&PF scenic byways; BLM Steese/Elliott brochure

fairbanks-1.dogs: Leashed on Birch Hill, which is a Fairbanks North Star Borough facility; the borough's other four trails on this card have no published dog rule at all, so treat them as unknown rather than open.
fairbanks-1.dogs_source_quote: Except in designated off-leash areas, all pets must be on-leash and under the owner's control at all times. Pet waste must be picked up and disposed of in provided trash receptacles.
fairbanks-1.dogs_exception: The borough rules apply to 'any Parks and Recreation controlled and borough-owned or leased amenity including facilities, parks, trails and landscaped areas', which covers Birch Hill Recreation Area. Ester Dome sits on Tanana Valley State Forest land administered by DNR, which publishes no dog rule for it. Wander Lake is inside the privately owned Fountainhead Wedgewood Wildlife Sanctuary and the owner publishes nothing. Creamer's Field is Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game; three ADF&G refuge pages were read and none mentions pets. No managing authority could be established for the Chena River Nature Trail — it is not on the borough's trail-map list and not on the Chena River SRA page.

Birch Hill White Bear Loop.quote: Except in designated off-leash areas, all pets must be on-leash and under the owner's control at all times.

dogs_needs_check: Ester Dome Inner Loop — DNR Fairbanks / Division of Forestry, Tanana Valley State Forest. Phone the Fairbanks DNR office.

Chena River Nature Trail — authority not established; it is neither on the FNSB trail-map list nor on the Chena River SRA page. Identify the landowner before assuming either the borough or state-park leash rule applies.
Wander Lake Trail — private, Fountainhead Wedgewood Wildlife Sanctuary. Ask the resort.
Boreal Forest and Seasonal Wetland Trail — ADF&G Creamer's Field, (907) 459-7307. The ADF&G access page also lists the Boreal Forest Trail as closed; worth confirming before the visit.
fairbanks-1.authority: Alaska State Parks — Chena River State Recreation Area, Northern Region (907-451-2695)
fairbanks-1.dates_checked: 26 Jun - 3 Jul 2027, 7 nights. Days either side of the solstice at 64.75°N: effectively no darkness, which changes what a seven-night stop can hold.
fairbanks-1.trails_note: Five trails for seven nights, and every one of them was a flat urban or near-urban loop — Ester Dome Inner Loop, the Chena River Nature Trail, Wander Lake, Birch Hill White Bear Loop and the Boreal Forest & Seasonal Wetland Trail. Nothing on the card left the Fairbanks bowl, and nothing on it had a view. The Chena River State Recreation Area starts twenty-odd miles up Chena Hot Springs Road and is 397 square miles of forest, river and alpine tundra with the best hiking anywhere near Fairbanks; the card did not touch it. One addition, and it is the obvious one. Granite Tors Trail, in the same recreation area from the campground at milepost 39, was the runner-up and is the harder, longer version of the same idea — worth knowing about, not needed on a card that is now at six.
fairbanks-1.dogs_stop_level: Alaska State Parks publishes no pet rule for the Chena River State Recreation Area on the pages read, and none per trail. Recorded null. Northern Region office, 907-451-2695.

trails.name: Angel Rocks Trail
trails.distance: 3.7 mile loop. The same trailhead is also the start of the Angel Rocks to Chena Hot Springs traverse, an 8 mile one-way route ending at Chena Hot Springs at milepost 56.5.
trails.time: 2-3 hours for the loop; a full day for the 8 mile traverse
trails.difficulty: Moderate/strenuous (Alaska State Parks). Steep in its middle section — the climb to the tors is the work; the loop back down is easy.
trails.elevation_gain: 1,900 feet is the figure Alaska State Parks publishes, and it belongs to the 8 MILE TRAVERSE, not to the 3.7 mile loop. No separate gain figure for the loop alone was found in an authority source, so none is recorded for it.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible. It is by a wide margin the most-reviewed trail in the Fairbanks area, which is the other half of the argument for adding it.
trails.uses_source: Alaska State Parks lists the allowable uses for this trail as Hiking and Horseback Riding. Biking is NOT among them and is not claimed.
trails.needs: No published pet rule from Alaska State Parks for this trail or for the Chena River SRA as a whole. Recorded as unknown. Alaska State Parks Northern Region, 907-451-2695.

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Angel Rocks Loop (trail record, Chena River SRA)
other_links.note: Alaska State Parks' own trail record, carrying the agency's Northern Region contact number 907-451-2695. 'This 3.7 mile loop route provides access to alpine tundra, views of surrounding mountains, and unique rock outcroppings called tors... Trail Access: The trail begins at the Angel Rocks Trailhead at mi. 48.9 and ends at Chena Hot Springs at mi. 56.5 Chena Hot Springs Road. Allowable Uses: Hiking, Horseback Riding. Distance: 8 mile traverse (one-way). Total Elevation Gain: 1900 feet. Difficulty: Moderate/strenuous.'

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Chena River State Recreation Area
other_links.note: 'Chena River State Recreation Area is a park for all seasons, with 397 square miles of forests, rivers, and alpine tundra.' 254,080 acres. The state's own Angel Rocks trail guide is a PDF at dnr.alaska.gov/parks/maps/angelrockchena.pdf which would not render in the browser pane, so no figures were taken from it.

trails.season: Fully in season on these dates, and it is one of the better weeks of the year for it — the tors are above tree line with a view over the Chena valley, and in the last days of June at this latitude the light does not go. There is a small parking fee at the Angel Rocks trailhead; a picnic area and restrooms are there too. Blueberries on the slopes come later, in August, so that is one thing these dates miss.
trails.note: The trail this stop was missing, and the answer to a card of five flat town loops. Granite tors — pinnacles of intruded rock left standing as the ground eroded around them — reached by a steep climb out of birch and spruce onto open alpine tundra, about fifty road miles from Fairbanks up Chena Hot Springs Road. Do the 3.7 mile loop. The alternative is to walk the 8 mile traverse right through to Chena Hot Springs and get in the pool at the far end, which needs two vehicles or a lift back and is a proper day; with seven nights and a towed truck, that is genuinely on the table and it is the best day available out of Fairbanks.

Flattop Mountain Trail.entity: Flattop Mountain, Chugach State Park, Anchorage

offroad.name: Arctic Valley Road
offroad.distance: about 7 miles from the Glenn Highway to the Alpenglow ski area; the pavement ends as the road starts climbing and the rest is wide gravel
offroad.difficulty: not published. Wide graded gravel with switchbacks — no low range needed, but it is exposed
offroad.season: Open in summer; the ski area itself runs mid-November to late March. The stop arrives 7 Jul 2027, which is the good season — alpine tundra, and late-summer berry picking a little later.
offroad.note: Split out of a combined entry. The other half, Eklutna Lake Road, is fully paved for all ten miles from the Glenn Highway to the lake — narrow and winding for the last seven, with no shoulders, but tarmac throughout. It is a scenic drive, not an offroad route, and should move to the scenic-drives box rather than stay here. Arctic Valley Road is the one that actually leaves the pavement.

anchorage.authority: Alaska State Parks — Chugach State Park (Rabbit Lake); the other three trails are Municipality of Anchorage
anchorage.dogs: Chugach State Park: "Pets must be under control whether on or off leash. 11 AAC 12.130 (e)." Statewide, Alaska State Parks require a leash "not exceeding nine feet in length" in developed facilities — 11 AAC 12.130(a). Neither page enumerates what counts as a developed facility, so the card no longer pretends to.
anchorage.dogs_exception: The three city-trail entries are Municipality of Anchorage, not state park — no municipal rule was sourced, so they are unknown. Chugach State Park also warns that trapping is legal in parts of the park, which is a separate reason to keep the dog close.

Tony Knowles Coastal Path.quote: A person who owns a domestic animal, shall control it at all times. In a public place, with some exceptions, the municipal ordinance requires that an owner shall have his/her animal under control and shall not allow it to roam neighborhoods or have access to other people's property.

In a public place, with some exceptions, the municipal ordinance requires that an owner shall have his/her animal under control and shall not allow it to roam neighborhoods or have access to other people's property.

anchorage.dogs_exception_add: The three city-trail entries are resolved: the Municipality of Anchorage permits dogs in public places on a leash, so all three are walkable with the dog on lead. Off-leash is only lawful in sanctioned off-leash areas, and the Muni states plainly that off-leash walking, skiing and biking are not among the exceptions. Rabbit Lake remains Chugach State Park and keeps its existing rule.
anchorage.dogs_source_quote: Pets must be under control whether on or off leash. 11 AAC 12.130 (e)
anchorage.dogs_source_note: DRIFT — the statewide half of our card is our own gloss. The nine-foot leash rule is real and sourced (https://dnr.alaska.gov/parks/faq.htm, 11 AAC 12.130(a)), but neither that page nor the Chugach page enumerates "developed facility" as "campgrounds, picnic areas, trailheads, swim beaches and boat ramps". That list needs the 11 AAC 12 definitions section behind it or it should be cut. Access note: dnr.alaska.gov returns Access Denied on some paths (/parks/units/chugach/) while serving others fine — a 403 there does not mean the page is gone.

Visit Holy Transfiguration of Our Lord R.entity: Holy Transfiguration of Our Lord Chapel, Ninilchik, Alaska (1901) — article confirms Ninilchik

links.label: Wikipedia — Holy Transfiguration of Our Lord Chapel

trails.name: Ninilchik Beach Trail

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Ninilchik State Recreation Area
other_links.note: Managing authority. Lists Hiking among the unit's activities and covers Ninilchik Beach Campground, Ninilchik River Campground, Ninilchik Scenic Overlook and Ninilchik View Campground. 'While you are in Ninilchik, be sure to see the historical Ninilchik Village and the Russian Orthodox Church.'

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Ninilchik View Campground
other_links.note: 'This campground is located on a bluff above Ninilchik Beach. A stairway leads down the bluff.' Milepost 135.7 Sterling Highway. The bluff stairway is the beach access this walk uses.

trails.stats_note: AllTrails' slug reads `ninilchik-river-overlook-and-beach-trail` while the page title is 'Ninilchik Beach Trail' — a good example of why these are copied and never built. The route starts at the Ninilchik Overlook campground near the river and runs down to the beach, then along the sand toward Deep Creek. The 4.1 star average was published against 17 reviews on AllTrails' Deep Creek POI page; the trail-page title now reads 22 reviews.
trails.tag: This is the walk the stop is actually for: the old village, the Russian Orthodox church on the hill, and the beach below it in one loop out of camp. Minimal shade.

trails.name: Ninilchik River Campground river trail

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Ninilchik River Campground
other_links.note: Managing authority. 'Ninilchik River Campground is in a beautiful spruce and birch forest with developed campsites, one group picnic shelter and a hiking trail to the river.' Facilities list wheelchair-accessible Trails; activities list Camping, Day Use, Fishing and Hiking. Milepost 134.5 Sterling Highway, 93 acres, first come first served.

trails.stats_note: Alaska State Parks confirms a maintained, wheelchair-accessible hiking trail here and gives it no name and no length. Recorded as it is published rather than measured off a map.
trails.needs: name, distance, difficulty. Alaska State Parks Kenai Region is the source; the campground is managed on the ground and the length would come off a sign at the trailhead.

trails.name: Ninilchik Scenic Overlook trails
trails.difficulty: Wheelchair accessible per Alaska State Parks

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Ninilchik Scenic Overlook
other_links.note: Managing authority. 'Ninilchik Scenic Overlook is a great place to view the Ninilchik River and watch the eagles soar. Trails provide access to fishing along the Ninilchik River.' Facilities list wheelchair-accessible Trails, toilets, picnic sites and shelter. 93 acres, 9 campsites, milepost 135 Sterling Highway, 35 ft RV size limit.

trails.stats_note: A separate state park unit from the river campground above, with its own trails, and the trailhead for the Ninilchik Beach Trail. Short river-access paths rather than a hike.
trails.needs: name and distance — Alaska State Parks publishes neither.

not_a_trail.problem: Superseded by the researched entry for this stop, or belongs to another stop / is not a trail.

offroad.name: Skilak Lake Road
offroad.distance: 19 miles, entrances at Sterling Highway mileposts 58 and 75.2
offroad.season: no seasonal closure published
offroad.note: About an hour north up the Sterling and the best gravel drive within reach of this stop. ADF&G: "Drive the road slowly at 10 to 15 mph early in the day (before boaters start driving) or late in the evening." Campgrounds and boat launches at Quartz/Crescent and Lower and Upper Skilak Lake.

offroad.name: Oilwell Road into the Caribou Hills
offroad.difficulty: not published
offroad.season: not published for summer
offroad.note: NOT SOURCED, and that is the finding. Oilwell Road leaves Ninilchik east into the Caribou Hills, the big off-road area of the southern Kenai, but the only thing Alaska State Parks publishes for it is a pair of GROOMED SNOWMACHINE trail maps - Caribou Hills North and Caribou Hills South. No summer road description, no length, no surface, no statement of where a full-size truck can get to in July. The network beyond the road end is ATV and snowmachine country, not necessarily truck country. Kenai Peninsula Borough road maintenance would settle how far the maintained gravel runs; until then this is recorded as unknown rather than driven at.

ninilchik.authority: Alaska State Parks, Kenai Region — Ninilchik State Recreation Area (Ninilchik River Campground, Ninilchik View Campground, Ninilchik Scenic Overlook) and Deep Creek State Recreation Area
ninilchik.dogs: Alaska State Parks: 'Pets are welcome at state parks and campgrounds if leashed and accompanied by the owner at all times.' The regulation is a leash not exceeding nine feet in developed facilities. That covers every trail below, all of which are inside state park units.
ninilchik.trails_note: Ninilchik is a fishing, clamming and Russian-village stop, not a hiking stop, and the trails box should say so rather than pretend otherwise. Alaska State Parks lists Hiking as an activity at Ninilchik SRA and Anchor River SRA but names no trail at either; Deep Creek SRA lists ATV riding, camping, clam digging, fishing and picnicking and no hiking at all. AllTrails' own Ninilchik State Recreation Area park page is useless as a heading link — its top result is 'Sterling Highway: Homer to Tern Lake', a 132.6-mile drive — so no area browse is set for this stop. The real Kenai hiking is 40 miles south at Homer, which is the next stop and gets six nights; Diamond Creek, the Homestead Trail and Bishop's Beach are deliberately filed there, not here.

Musk Ox Farm.entity: Muskox — the Musk Ox Farm in Palmer has no article

Large Animal Research Station tours and.entity: Robert G. White Large Animal Research Station — no article of its own; documented in the UAF article

offroad.name: Dalton Highway — Arctic Circle and Coldfoot
offroad.was_name: Dalton Highway detour to the Arctic Circle / Coldfoot
offroad.distance: the Dalton runs 414 miles from Livengood (84 miles north of Fairbanks) to Deadhorse. Arctic Circle BLM Wayside is at Dalton mile 115.5; Coldfoot at mile 174.8 — call it a 500-mile round trip from Fairbanks to Coldfoot and back
offroad.difficulty: not graded. Mostly gravel, open to ordinary vehicles, but with heavy truck traffic, no shoulders, and long stretches with no fuel or cell coverage
offroad.season: Open year-round — this is a working pipeline haul road, not a seasonal one. The stop arrives 23 Aug 2027, which is fine: the tundra is turning and the worst of the dust season is past, though early snow on Atigun is possible by then (Atigun is well north of Coldfoot and not on this detour).
offroad.note: BLM publishes a free 24-page Dalton Highway Visitor Guide and runs the Arctic Interagency Visitor Center at Coldfoot — pick both up. Carry two full-size spares; windshield damage from passing trucks is routine. This is a two-day out-and-back at minimum if Coldfoot is the turnaround, and a long single day if the Arctic Circle sign is enough.

fairbanks-2.authority: Alaska State Parks, Northern Area Office, Chena River SRA (907-451-2695); BLM Eastern Interior Field Office, White Mountains NRA (907-474-2200); ADF&G Creamer's Field Migratory Waterfowl Refuge (Farmhouse Visitor Center 907-459-7307)
fairbanks-2.dogs: Alaska State Parks: 'Pets are welcome at state parks and campgrounds if leashed and accompanied by the owner at all times; unleashed dogs are allowed in the backcountry but must be within voice command.' The regulation is a leash not exceeding nine feet in developed facilities. That covers the Chena River SRA trails below.
fairbanks-2.trails_note: Four nights, 23-27 Aug, and the stop's real job is the Dalton Highway run and Chena Hot Springs. These are chosen to fit around that: one short evening loop, one half-day, one that ends in the hot spring pool, one that is the best fall-colour ridge within an hour of town, and one flat in-town dog walk. Late August is the good half of the season here — tundra colour is turning, the mosquitoes are past, and Alaska State Parks warns that trapping runs fall through spring, so the dog is fine now and would not be in October.

trails.name: Angel Rocks Trail, Chena River SRA

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Angel Rocks trail handout (PDF)
other_links.note: Managing authority. 'Difficulty: Moderate / Strenuous. Total Elevation Gain: Approx. 900 ft. A 3.5 mile loop trail leads to large granite outcroppings near the north boundary of the recreation area. It is an easy day hike for most people, as the top of the rocks is less than two miles from the trailhead.' Access mile 48.9 Chena Hot Springs Road; trailhead 1,000 ft, high point 1,750 ft; hiking time 2-3 hours. Rules: 'Vehicles including mountain bikes are prohibited' — that is where uses = hike only comes from.

other_links.label: AllTrails — Chena River State Recreation Area
other_links.note: Park browse page and the source of the 4.7 star figure: 'the best place to hike in Chena River State Recreation Area is Angel Rocks Trail, which has a 4.7 star rating from 1,306 reviews.' Note the `--2` on the slug; it is not the slug you would have guessed.

trails.stats_note: The star average of 4.7 was published against 1,306 reviews on the park browse page; AllTrails' own trail-page title now reads '1,343 Reviews'. The count moved, the average has not been republished against it.
trails.tag: The best half-day at this stop and the one everybody does. Steep and rocky in places — Alaska State Parks says to wear suitable footgear.

trails.name: Granite Tors Two Mile Loop, Chena River SRA
trails.url_check: Tap this one before relying on it. Two search passes rendered the slug as `granite-toors-two-mile-loop` (a character-by-character read-back confirmed t-o-o-r-s) and a third rendered it `granite-dtoors-...`. The typo is AllTrails' own, which is exactly why it cannot be reconstructed from the name. The trail itself is not in doubt — Alaska State Parks documents it — only the link.

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Guide to Granite Tors Trail (PDF)
other_links.note: Managing authority. 'Trail Access: the trail begins at the Granite Tors Campground Day-Use Area at milepost 39.5 Chena Hot Springs Road. Allowable Uses: Hiking. Distance: 15 mile loop or optional 2 mile loop. Elevation Gain: 2900 feet. Difficulty: Moderate/strenuous.' The two-mile option: 'In less than a mile, you'll encounter a boardwalk heading to your right. This connects with the West Trail, giving the option of a two mile loop hike.' Park rules: 'Vehicles including mountain bikes are prohibited.'

trails.stats_note: The full Granite Tors Loop is a different day entirely — AllTrails records it as a 14.7 mi loop, challenging, average 7 h 47 min, 4.6 from 250 reviews (https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/alaska/granite-tors-loop-trail), and Alaska State Parks calls it 15 miles with 2,900 ft of gain and a first-come shelter cabin at about mile 7. It does not fit a four-night stop built around the Dalton. The two-mile boardwalk loop off the same trailhead does, and reaches the bog and river section rather than the tors.
trails.needs: star rating for the two-mile loop — AllTrails publishes the 81-review count but no average alongside it. The 2,900 ft gain figure belongs to the 15-mile loop, not this one; no gain is published for the short loop.

trails.name: Angel Rocks to Chena Hot Springs Trail

alltrails.name: Chena Hot Springs via Angel Rocks Trail

other_links.label: Alaska State Parks — Chena River SRA brochure (PDF)
other_links.note: Managing authority, trail descriptions section. 'Angel Rocks to Chena Hot Springs Trail. Access: milepost 48.9 (shares with Angel Rocks Trail). Travel means: foot. Distance: 8.3 miles one way. From the Angel Rocks loop, this trail travels through mixed spruce and birch forests, and along a ridge above tree line to reach Chena Hot Springs. Eye-catching views include the Chena River, Alaska Range, granite tors, Chena Dome, and Far Mountain.'

trails.stats_note: Point to point, ending at the hot springs resort — which this stop is already driving to. It needs two vehicles or a lift back the 4.5 miles of road, and that is the thing to arrange, not the walking.
trails.needs: time, difficulty and reviews. Alaska State Parks publishes the distance and the travel means and nothing else; AllTrails' indexed snippet for this listing carries no stats either. Northern Area Office 907-451-2695.

trails.name: Summit Trail to Wickersham Dome, White Mountains NRA

other_links.label: BLM — Summit Trail, Alaska
other_links.note: Managing authority, Eastern Interior Field Office, 907-474-2200. 'After leaving the trailhead, the trail climbs over a small dome then drops into the trees before the junction with the Ski Loop Trail. The trail continues to climb past Wickersham Dome then to the Summit Trail Shelter at mile 8 and to its highest point at 3,100 feet near mile 10. The trail then descends through the spruce forest to Beaver Creek Wild and Scenic River and Borealis-LeFevre Cabin.' Listed activities: BIKING, HIKING, WINTER SPORTS. No fee. Trailhead at 65.27236874, -147.9685796 — the Wickersham Dome parking lot, milepost 28 Elliott Highway, north of Fairbanks.

trails.stats_note: Two different lengths for one trail and both are right. BLM describes the whole Summit Trail, which runs about 20 miles to Beaver Creek with a shelter at mile 8; AllTrails' 6.9 mi is the out-and-back to the dome, which is the day hike people actually do. The 4.4 star average was published alongside 280 reviews on AllTrails' Wickersham Dome POI page while the trail-page title reads 294.
trails.season: BLM publishes no seasonal closure — it is open ground, not a gated site. Late August is when the White Mountains tundra turns.
trails.needs: No published dog rule. BLM's page says nothing about pets on this trail, and it is not covered by the Alaska State Parks rule above; recorded as unknown. 907-474-2200 would settle it. BLM also warns 'crossing Beaver Creek Wild and Scenic River in the summer can be very dangerous at high water' — that is well past the dome and not on the 6.9 mi version.
trails.cruise_reason: BLM lists BIKING as a permitted activity, so it is bike-legal, but 1,568 ft of climbing in 3.5 miles on an alpine tundra trail is not rail-grade and no surface description is published. Not a dog-in-the-carrier gravel cruise.

trails.name: Boreal Forest and Seasonal Wetland Trail, Creamer's Field

alltrails.name: Boreal Forest and Seasonal Wetland Trail

other_links.label: ADF&G — Creamer's Field Visitor Information
other_links.note: Managing authority. Names three nature trails: 'Boreal Forest Trail — Wander through forest typical of Interior Alaska. Highlights include wildlife viewing from the observation tower and a self-guiding brochure', 'Seasonal Wetland Trail — This trail borders a wetland where water level and wildlife vary seasonally. Interpretive signs and observation platforms are along the path. It is wheelchair accessible during snow-free months', and 'Farm Road Trail — Stroll past open fields and patches of woods.' ADF&G's separate wildlife-viewing page describes 'a three-mile-long network of nature trails' across the 2,000-acre refuge.

other_links.label: Komoot — Boreal Forest and Seasonal Wetland Trail
other_links.note: Source of the 1.9 mi / 10 ft figures: 'an exceptionally easy 1.9-mile (3.0 km) hike with only 10 feet of elevation.'

trails.season_conflict: ADF&G currently marks the Boreal Forest Trail '[Currently Closed]'. The Seasonal Wetland Trail and Farm Road Trail carry no closure. The AllTrails route above combines the closed trail with an open one, so half of it may not be walkable. No reopening date is published.
trails.needs: Whether the Boreal Forest Trail is open by 23 Aug 2027 — Farmhouse Visitor Center 907-459-7307. Also the dog rule: ADF&G's own trail page says only 'Pets - Keep them under strict control', which is guidance rather than a stated permission, so this is recorded as unknown rather than as a yes. Review count for the 4.2 average is not published alongside it (the figure comes from AllTrails' Creamers Field State Game Refuge browse page: 'the most popular is Boreal Forest and Seasonal Wetland Trail with an average 4.2 star rating').
trails.tag: Flat, in town on College Road, two miles, and the only one of these that works as an evening walk between a Dalton day and an aurora night.

Tok is a logistics stop; do not consume.entity: Tok, Alaska — the town itself, which the headline names. Matches the two sibling entries on this stop that already use the Tok article.

offroad.name: Nabesna Road
offroad.distance: 42 miles one way, gravel the whole length, from mile 60 of the Tok Cutoff at Slana
offroad.difficulty: not graded by NPS. Most 2WD vehicles manage the first 29 miles; beyond mile 29 the unbridged stream crossings need high clearance and sometimes 4WD
offroad.season: No gate and no published closure. The stop arrives 27 Aug 2027 — the best time of the three Alaska windows for this road: run-off is long past, so the stream crossings beyond mile 29 are at their lowest and the far end is most likely to go. No conflict.
offroad.note: Second bite at Nabesna, and the better one — if the crossings were up in late June on the tok-1 stop, this is the visit to push past mile 29. Flat tires and washouts are still common the whole length. The maintained road ends at a private lodge at mile 42; NPS does not recommend the last four miles, which are deeply rutted and wet. Slana Ranger Station at mile 0.5 has current conditions.

tok-2.dogs: Leashed dogs are fine — the overlook trail is in Eagle Trail State Recreation Site, and Alaska State Parks allow pets throughout on a leash of nine feet or less in developed areas, voice control in the backcountry.
tok-2.dogs_source_quote: Yes, Pets are welcome at state parks and campgrounds if leashed and accompanied by the owner at all times; unleashed dogs are allowed in the backcountry but must be within voice command.
tok-2.dogs_note: Same trail as tok-1. Eagle Trail State Recreation Site, Mile 109.5 Tok Cut-Off, is an Alaska State Parks unit.

Favor a rest day, river walk, museum, or.entity: Generic pacing advice with no single referent — 'a museum' and 'a river walk' are unnamed (the Whitehorse article has no 'museum' mention at all). The city article is already linked from 'Revisit only the Whitehorse attractions missed in June.' on this same stop, so nothing is lost.

whitehorse-2.dogs: On leash everywhere inside Whitehorse city boundaries (Animal Control Bylaw s.53), which covers the Miles Canyon and Yukon River riverfront trails; Fish Lake is outside city limits on Kwanlin Dun settlement and Yukon Crown land, and no authority publishes a dog rule for that trail.
whitehorse-2.dogs_source_quote: Under Section 53 of the Animal Control Bylaw, except in a designated off-leash area, no owner of a dog shall permit such dog to run at large, and where such animal is found running at large, it shall be deemed to be doing so with the consent of the owner.

offroad.name: Grey Mountain Road
offroad.distance: 6.3 km to the viewpoint parking area, 4 km more to the communication towers
offroad.difficulty: "easily driveable in a vehicle with good clearance" to the viewpoint; the upper 4 km "becomes unmaintained and rougher with narrow sections towards the top"
offroad.season: "the unmaintained part of the road after the Grey Mountain Viewpoint parking area is not always passable in the winter and late into the spring"
offroad.note: The one that fits a single overnight - it starts inside the city (Lewes Boulevard, Alsek Road, Grey Mountain Road) and the viewpoint is 6.3 km up. Late August is dry season on the upper 4 km.

whitehorse-3.dogs: On leash everywhere inside Whitehorse city boundaries (Animal Control Bylaw s.53), which covers the Miles Canyon and Yukon River riverfront trails; Fish Lake is outside city limits on Kwanlin Dun settlement and Yukon Crown land, and no authority publishes a dog rule for that trail.
whitehorse-3.dogs_source_quote: Under Section 53 of the Animal Control Bylaw, except in a designated off-leash area, no owner of a dog shall permit such dog to run at large, and where such animal is found running at large, it shall be deemed to be doing so with the consent of the owner.

offroad.name: Grey Mountain Road
offroad.distance: 6.3 km to the viewpoint parking area, 4 km more to the communication towers
offroad.difficulty: "easily driveable in a vehicle with good clearance" to the viewpoint; the upper 4 km "becomes unmaintained and rougher with narrow sections towards the top"
offroad.season: "the unmaintained part of the road after the Grey Mountain Viewpoint parking area is not always passable in the winter and late into the spring"
offroad.note: Mid-September is the last comfortable window for the unmaintained top section - the source's warning is about winter and late spring, but the first snow on that ridge is a September event most years and there is no gate and no published date. Judge it at the viewpoint lot.

offroad.name: Fish Lake Road (Lu Zil Man)
offroad.distance: about 15 km to Fish Lake, then 600 m more on a narrower road to the trailhead
offroad.season: no seasonal dates published
offroad.note: "From the intersection of the Alaska Highway and Hamilton Boulevard/Two-Mile Hill in Whitehorse, drive 3 km north on the Alaska Highway and turn left on to Fish Lake Road. Follow this road until you reach Fish Lake (about 15 km)." Reports describe the last stretch as rutted after rain; on a September visit that is the thing to look at before committing the truck to the berm road.

whitehorse-3.authority: City of Whitehorse (Grey Mountain Road and the Grey Mountain area). No City of Whitehorse or Government of Yukon page with trail figures was found for this trail in the searches read; the figures below come from yukonhiking.ca, the Yukon's established hiking guide, and are tiered `community`, not `official`. That is recorded plainly rather than dressed up.
whitehorse-3.dates_checked: 8-12 Sep 2027, 4 nights, third visit to Whitehorse.
whitehorse-3.trails_note: Three trails for four nights and all three are at river level in or beside the town — Miles Canyon, the Yukon River trail, and Fish Lake. Fish Lake Lookout is the only one with any height in it. On 8-12 September the Yukon is in full autumn: the subalpine is turning and the alpine is already gold, and the card had nothing above the trees to see it from. One addition, chosen for exactly that.
whitehorse-3.dogs_stop_level: No managing authority read for this stop publishes a pet rule for the Grey Mountain trails. Recorded null.

trails.name: Grey Mountain (The May)
trails.distance: 5 km (3.1 mi) return to the first summit — 2.5 km each way. AllTrails reads it as a 3.1-mile out-and-back, which matches.
trails.time: 2 hours return (yukonhiking.ca); AllTrails averages 1 h 42 min
trails.difficulty: The two sources disagree and both are recorded: yukonhiking.ca rates it EASY, on the grounds that 'the trailhead starts only 200 m lower than the summit, which means more alpine walking'; AllTrails calls it 'moderately challenging'. There are switchbacks that climb steadily near the top. Easy-to-moderate is the fair reading.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed. No star rating was visible. A separate, thinner AllTrails listing exists for 'Grey Mountain Summit' at 21 reviews and another for 'Grey Mountain via Dream Trail' — the 142-review page is the one for the walk described here.
trails.uses_source: Trailforks describes the Grey Mountain Summit Trail as multiuse and 'mostly bikeable but will require some pushing' — that is a community description of bike use, not an authority permission, so no bike use is claimed above.
trails.cruise_reason: Even the community source that calls it bikeable says it needs pushing and that the route braids and requires wayfinding. That fails the walk-your-bike test in §4 outright.
trails.needs: No published pet rule found from the City of Whitehorse or the Government of Yukon. Recorded as unknown.

other_links.label: yukonhiking.ca — Grey Mountain (The May)
other_links.note: Source for distance, time, gain and the driving directions. 'Total Distance: 5 km. Return Time: 2 hours. Elevation Gain: 200 m. Difficulty: Easy.' Traditional Territory: Kwanlin Dün First Nation and Ta'an Kwäch'än Council. The Southern Tutchone name, The May, refers to the grey-white colour of the rocks.

trails.season: Early September is the best week of the year for this and the reason it is the one addition. The trail starts in the alpine, so the ground cover — dwarf birch, bearberry, blueberry — is already turning red and gold on these dates, and the view runs from Marsh Lake in the south to Lake Laberge in the north. Snow can arrive on the ridge any time from late September, so 8-12 Sep is ahead of it but not by much. Bears: the guide warns there is 'evidence of bear activity such as bear droppings and digging marks' despite how close it is to town, and to make noise on the crests.
trails.note: The one thing this box lacked — height, and a view of where you actually are. Grey Mountain is the landmark above Whitehorse and the trail starts at the communication towers, only 200 m below the first summit, so almost the whole walk is above the trees. Two hours return for a view over the town, the Yukon River and both lakes. THE ACCESS IS THE PLANNING POINT: Grey Mountain Road runs 6.3 km to the Grey Mountain Viewpoint car park, and the last 4 km up to the towers is unmaintained, rougher and narrow in places. That is a TRUCK errand, not a coach one, and on the third visit to Whitehorse the truck is already unhitched. Turning round at the first summit is the sensible plan; the ridge continues over two more peaks, the third of which has the best view of the city, and the connection between them involves faint trail and some bushwhacking.

smithers.dogs: Town of Smithers Animal Control and Licencing Bylaw No. 1780 requires leashing in public, which covers the Perimeter Trail and Riverside Park; BC Parks allows leashed pets at Call Lake and in Babine Mountains Park, where dogs are also discouraged from the alpine because of mountain goats; nobody publishes a rule for Crater Lake or Seymour Ridge.
smithers.dogs_source_quote: Leashing when in public and maintaining control of the dog at all times;

offroad.name: Hudson Bay Mountain Road
offroad.distance: about 19 km from downtown Smithers to the ski area parking lot
offroad.difficulty: "The road to the trailhead is steep and gravel; a reliable vehicle with good brakes is recommended for the descent."
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: "From downtown Smithers, drive west on Main Street toward Hudson Bay Mountain. Main Street turns into Hudson Bay Mountain Road - follow it all the way up toward the ski hill." Nineteen km of steep gravel straight out of town to sub-alpine, and the Crater Lake trail (2.81 km, moderate, roughly 11 km return to the lake itself) leaves the parking area. The warning here is the brakes on the way down, not the climb.

offroad.name: Babine Lake Road and Upper Fulton (3000) Forest Service Road
offroad.distance: BC Parks: 38.4 km on Babine Lake Road, 12 km on the Upper Fulton (3000) FSR, then 800 m up the 312 road to the Cronin Creek trailhead
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks: the Upper Fulton (3000) is "narrow with poor sight lines in certain corners"
offroad.season: no gate dates published
offroad.note: The full directions from BC Parks: "From Smithers, head South-East on Highway BC-16E for 6.3 km. Turn left onto Babine Lake Road and continue North for 38.4 km. Take a slight left onto Upper Fulton (3000) Forest Service Road, continuing 12 km before turning left onto the 312 road, marked by blue BC Parks directional signage." The Little Joe Creek and Cronin Creek trailheads sit at 30.5 km and 32.5 km. The hazard is industrial, not technical: "Expect active log hauling Monday to Saturday, and large industrial vehicles at any time" - so a Sunday is the quiet day for it. The west end of the park is reached off Old Babine Lake Road past Driftwood Canyon, and the road there ends at a summer parking area beyond which "the road is not passable to vehicle traffic".

Mount Baldy hiking / scenic drive.entity: Mount Baldy / Baldy Mountain Resort, BC

trails.name: Frosty Mountain Trail
trails.was: Frosty Mountain Trail (Manning Park) — no url
trails.note_source: No direct listing url surfaced in search. Name and stop kept; no constructed slug — the fabricated-URL episode is why.

trails.name: Canal Walkway
trails.season: Open year-round.
trails.note: Flat loop along the Okanagan River channel - the best-reviewed easy walk in town and, being level and rideable, the gravel-cruise candidate here. Frosty Mountain, the only trail previously on this card, is a long subalpine day two hours' drive away; this is the one you can do on an arrival evening.

trails.name: Osoyoos and Haynes Point
trails.season: Open year-round.
trails.note: Lakeshore route out to the s̓wi̓ws (Haynes Point) spit, the sand bar that runs most of the way across Osoyoos Lake. Five flat miles at the hottest, driest place in Canada, walked at the start of October when that is finally pleasant.
trails.stats_note: Title gives 96 Reviews; the star line reads 3.7/5 (75).

trails.name: Nk'Mip Desert Loop
trails.season: AllTrails gives March through July; the 30 Sep - 3 Oct stay falls outside that window. Kept on the card because the reason for the window is wildflowers and interpretation season, not closure - but check the Nk'Mip Desert Cultural Centre's autumn hours before driving over, since the boardwalk is reached through it.
trails.note: Boardwalk through the antelope-brush desert on Osoyoos Indian Band land - the short walk that explains what this landscape actually is.

trails.name: Gyro Beach and Desert Sunrise Marina from Downtown Osoyoos
trails.season: April through October per AllTrails - the stay is at the very end of the window.
trails.note: Lakefront walk from downtown out to the marina. Short, flat and paved for most of its length; the town stroll rather than a hike.

alltrails.name: Gyro Beach and Desert Sunrise Marina from Downtown Osoyoos

not_a_route.problem: Two things, neither of them an offroad route. Mount Baldy Road (Baldy Ski Hill Road) is the all-weather public access road to Baldy Mountain Resort — partly paved, partly hard-packed dirt, ordinary two-wheel-drive in summer, reached via McKinney Road from Oliver or Canyon Road off Hwy 3 from Osoyoos. That is a scenic drive. The hiking at the resort is trails. Nothing here needs 4x4 and nothing here is a named 4x4 route.

osoyoos.dogs: E.C. Manning Park: "Dogs and other domestic animals must be leashed and are not allowed in most beach areas or park buildings." There is a designated pet area east of the restaurant at Manning Park Resort.
osoyoos.dogs_exception: Frosty Mountain is a long subalpine day out in bear country — legal with the dog on a leash, but BC Parks' general advice against taking pets into the backcountry applies to the upper half of it.
osoyoos.stats_note: BC Parks' page for s̓wi̓ws Park was fetched and names no trails and no lengths - it mentions only 'the marsh area and self-guided interpretive trail'. The Haynes Point figures above are therefore AllTrails', not the authority's. South Okanagan Grasslands Lookout (8.5 km, challenging, 3 h 19 min, 3.9/5 from 85) also surfaced but no direct URL did, so it is recorded here rather than as an entry.

offroad.name: Kobau Lookout Forest Service Road (Mount Kobau summit road)
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks: "Both Kruger Mt. Rd. and the road to Mt. Kobau are gravel roads and maintained infrequently"
offroad.season: NO PUBLISHED SEASONAL CLOSURE FOUND. BC Parks publishes no gate or opening dates for this road and none could be sourced elsewhere. The summit is high enough that early-season snow is a real possibility around 30 Sep - 3 Oct 2027, but that is inference, not a published date, and it is recorded here as unknown rather than as open.
offroad.note: Turn off Highway 3 10.75 km west of the Highway 97/3 junction in Osoyoos. BC Parks is explicit about what may be driven: "The main road to the summit of Mt. Kobau is open to motor vehicles, all other roads are closed", with a further motor vehicle restriction above 1,700 m elevation in the Mount Kobau section. Destination Osoyoos describes a 17 km forest service road; BC Parks publishes no length and a separate community account says roughly 20 km, so the length is not settled. A 5 km trail runs from the top.
offroad.source: BC Parks — South Okanagan Grasslands Protected Area

offroad.name: Kruger Mountain Road
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks: gravel road, "maintained infrequently"
offroad.season: NO PUBLISHED SEASONAL CLOSURE FOUND. Lower and drier than Mount Kobau, so more likely to be usable in early October, but no authority publishes dates either way.
offroad.note: Turn off Highway 3 6.75 km west of the Highway 97/3 junction in Osoyoos. This is the exception road in the Kilpoola area: BC Parks states "Kilpoola is closed to motor vehicles with the exception of Kruger Mountain Road." The Chopaka East and Chopaka West sites of the protected area are closed to motor vehicles entirely. No length published. Note that Anarchist Mountain Lookout, often suggested here, is a paved Highway 3 viewpoint and not an off-road route at all.
offroad.source: BC Parks — South Okanagan Grasslands Protected Area

offroad.name: Strawberry Creek Access Road
offroad.difficulty: BC Parks, verbatim: "a very rough, unmaintained dirt road. Some sections may be difficult to pass even with a 4 x 4 vehicle"
offroad.season: NO PUBLISHED SEASONAL CLOSURE FOUND. Given BC Parks' own warning that sections may defeat a 4x4 in normal conditions, wet early-October weather would make it worse. No dates published either way.
offroad.note: The hardest of the three roads BC Parks names in this protected area and the only one for which the managing authority publishes an explicit difficulty warning. Treat as a turn-back-when-it-gets-bad outing rather than a through route. No length published.
offroad.source: BC Parks — South Okanagan Grasslands Protected Area

osoyoos.dogs_source_quote: Dogs and other domestic animals must be leashed and are not allowed in most beach areas or park buildings.
osoyoos.dogs_source_note: The pet-area sentence is on the same page and reads "There is a designated pet area to the east side of the restaurant at Manning Park Resort." — our card drops the "to", which is paraphrase, not drift.

Blue Lake Trail.entity: The Blue Lake trail off SR 20 below Liberty Bell. No article, and no parent documents it: the Washington Pass, Liberty Bell Mountain and Lexington Tower articles contain no 'Blue Lake' text (Lexington Tower's only hit is a compass-neighbour nav box, not documentation).

Goat Peak Lookout.entity: Goat Peak, 7,001 ft, in the North Cascades — the article documents the working USFS fire lookout on the summit, the Methow River valley views and the Forest Road 52 trailhead 1 mile southeast of Mazama, matching this entry exactly. (One of three Washington summits named Goat Peak; this is the Mazama one.)

Grasshopper Pass from Harts Pass.entity: The PCT segment south from Harts Pass. Neither pass has an article — 'Harts Pass', 'Hart's Pass' and 'Harts Pass (Washington)' are all redlinks. The only article containing 'Grasshopper Pass' is Mount Ballard, and only in a photo caption ('seen from PCT at Grasshopper Pass'); Slate Peak mentions Harts Pass Road only as a closure note. Neither documents the pass.

trails.name: Maple Pass Trail
trails.was: Maple Pass Loop — no url
trails.note_source: The larch stop exists for this. Most popular and hardest trail in Winthrop, and the fall colour is why 3 Oct is a frozen date.

trails.name: Blue Lake Trail
trails.was: Blue Lake Trail — no url

trails.name: Goat Peak Lookout Trail
trails.was: Goat Peak Lookout — no url

trails.name: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass
trails.was: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass via PCT — two entries for one route

trails.name: Grasshopper Pass from Harts Pass
trails.was: Grasshopper Pass from Harts Pass — no url
trails.note_source: Harts Pass road is the highest drivable road in Washington and is not coach ground — truck only, and it closes early with snow. No direct listing url surfaced.

trails.name: Rainy Lake Trail #310
trails.distance: 1 mile (1.6 km) one way — 2 mi round trip
trails.time: 20 minutes each way (USFS); AllTrails estimates about 30 minutes for the round trip
trails.difficulty: Easy — USFS: 'The popular Rainy Lake Trail #310 is fully accessible. This is an easy, one-mile paved trail with no elevation gain.' Universally accessible, suitable for wheelchairs and strollers.
trails.elevation_gain: USFS states NO elevation gain. AllTrails reads 131 ft, which is the usual database noise on a contouring path; the authority figure is the one to plan on.
trails.reviews_note: Count read from the AllTrails result title as displayed on duckduckgo.com. Three mirrors of the same page read 1,726, 1,758 and 1,769 within days of each other — good enough to order the trail, not good enough to quote.
trails.uses_source: USFS lists the recreation opportunities for this trail as Hiking, Fishing, Outdoor Science and Learning, and Picnicking. Biking is not among them, so no bike use is claimed.
trails.needs: The USFS trail page publishes NO pet rule — its Restrictions section is empty of one. NPS states pets are 'allowed on most surrounding national forest lands', which is a description of someone else's land, not a rule for this trail. Recorded as unknown rather than assumed. Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Road, Winthrop, (509) 996-4000, would settle it in one call, and it is worth making because this is the trail most likely to be walked with the dog on the whole stop.

alltrails.name: Rainy Lake Trail
alltrails.note: One AllTrails locale mirror titles this page 'Rainy Lake Trail [CLOSED]'. The managing authority does not corroborate that: the USFS page was last updated 29 June 2026 and describes the trail as open, popular, fully accessible and heavily used, with no closure notice anywhere on it. An AllTrails closure tag against an authority page that says otherwise is not evidence of a closure — but it is worth one look at the Methow Valley Ranger District page before driving 35 miles for it.

other_links.label: USFS — Rainy Lake Trail, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF
other_links.note: Source for length, surface, accessibility and time. 'From Winthrop, take Highway 20 west for about 35 miles, to Rainy Pass. Park in the south parking lot on the left side of the highway.' Same trailhead complex as Heather-Maple Pass, which is already on the card.

other_links.label: USFS — Heather Maple Pass / Rainy Pass Picnic Site (the trailhead)

trails.season: In season on these exact dates, and the authority says so in its own words: 'In the fall, the golds and reds of the changing shrubs and trees are spectacular.' The trailhead is at Rainy Pass, milepost 158 on WA-20, the same lot the Heather-Maple Pass loop leaves from — so a Maple Pass day and a Rainy Lake half-hour are the same drive. The one dependency is WA-20 itself, which WSDOT closes over Washington and Rainy Passes each winter; early October is normally weeks ahead of that, but an early storm closes the highway with no notice and takes four of the six trails on this card with it.
trails.note: Added as the only easy, short, paved and accessible walk in a box of six alpine climbs. One flat mile through the trees to a lake ringed by high cliffs with waterfalls coming straight down into it — twenty minutes each way, benches and a paved picnic spot at the end. It is the walk for the afternoon after Maple Pass, the walk in the rain, and the walk when the knees have had enough of larch season, and it shares a car park with a trail already on the card so it costs no extra driving.

not_a_trail.problem: Superseded — folded into the Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass entry, the single listed route.
The same route as the entry above, under a second name.

offroad.name: Harts Pass Road (FR 5400)
offroad.distance: climbs from Mazama in the Methow Valley to Harts Pass at 6,198 ft — the highest maintained road in Washington
offroad.difficulty: not published as an offroad grade. The Forest Service describes it as narrow and steep with only intermittent turnouts; the exposure, not the surface, is the difficulty
offroad.season: NO CONFLICT, BUT NARROW. The standing Forest Order closes FR 5400 to all motorized wheeled vehicles 1 December to 31 March every year, and snow in practice takes it from late October through to June or early July most years. The stop arrives 3 Oct 2027 — inside the open window, but within weeks of the usual first closing snow. A second, current problem: as of March 2026 Harts Pass Road is closed indefinitely from the Monument Creek Trailhead to the pass after December 2025 flood damage, with the Forest Service aiming to reopen after contractor repairs 'in early summer'. That is 2026 news, not a 2027 forecast, but it needs re-verifying before the trip.
offroad.note: Trailers of any type are prohibited on FR 5400 year-round under a Forest Order in effect since April 2014, with a narrow exemption for snowmobile trailers of 20 ft or less in two spring/autumn windows. Irrelevant here — the truck goes up alone — but it tells you what the road is like. The 3 Oct arrival is set by the larch anchor, and larch and Harts Pass are the same week, so this is the right stop for it if the road is open.

offroad.name: Slate Peak spur
offroad.distance: about 3 miles beyond Harts Pass, ending at the Slate Peak lookout — the highest point a vehicle reaches in Washington
offroad.difficulty: not published
offroad.season: Governed entirely by FR 5400 below it — closed 1 Dec to 31 Mar by the same Forest Order, and snow-blocked well outside those dates most years. The stop arrives 3 Oct 2027; if Harts Pass is open the spur normally is too, but it goes higher and holds snow longer.
offroad.note: No listing found. No separate land-manager page exists for the spur — the Forest Service documents it only as part of the FR 5400 order, and the detailed write-ups are on hiking blogs. Recorded with no URL rather than pointing at something that is not about this road. Ask the Methow Valley Ranger District at 509-996-4003 for the gate position; the final stretch to the lookout is walk-only in some years.

winthrop.authority: USDA Forest Service — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
winthrop.dogs: Okanogan-Wenatchee NF: dogs are allowed on most wilderness trails under control at all times, and the forest is firmer than a recommendation — "Certain trails require them to be leashed." Two outright bans on this forest: the Enchantment Permit Area and Ingalls Lake. The Blue Lake leash sentence this card used to quote could not be found on any current Forest page and has been removed rather than left attributed.
winthrop.dogs_exception: One hard closure on this forest, well away from Winthrop: "Dogs and all pets are prohibited within the Enchantments Permit Area", service animals excepted.

scenicDrives_patch.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) over Washington Pass
scenicDrives_patch.note: The through-drive west from Winthrop over Washington Pass and Rainy Pass, with the paved fully-accessible Washington Pass Observation Site looking at Liberty Bell and the Early Winters Spires. WSDOT's own pass page is the live status.
scenicDrives_patch.season: OPEN ON THE DATE, closes soon after. WSDOT shuts SR-20 for the winter between Ross Dam and Early Winters every year — 4 Dec in 2025, typically Nov–Dec, reopening April/May. Arrive 3 Oct 2027: open, and this is the larch-gold week at Washington Pass. Note SR-20 opened LATER than usual in 2026 while repairs continued, so the spring date is not a fixed thing.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: WSDOT pass page; WSDOT 2025 closure release; WSDOT blog Apr 2026

scenicDrives_patch.name: Goat Creek Road (FR 52) to the Goat Peak trailhead
scenicDrives_patch.note: From Winthrop, 9 mi west on SR-20, right before Weeman Bridge onto Goat Creek Road (CR 1163), 3.3 mi, right onto FR 52 for 2.7 mi, then left onto FR 5225. Goat Peak carries a 1923 fire lookout at 7,000 ft, the most visible landmark in the Methow. The walk from the trailhead is 3.6 mi / 1,446 ft, rated hard.
scenicDrives_patch.season: Okanogan-Wenatchee forest roads are seasonally gated and snow-closed in winter. Arrive 3 Oct 2027 — normally still open, but this is the tail of the season at that elevation. Check the forest's current conditions page before driving up.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: USFS Goat Peak Trailhead and Trail #457 pages; WTA

scenicDrives_patch.name: Harts Pass and Slate Peak
scenicDrives_patch.was_name: Harts Pass and Slate Peak (truck only)
scenicDrives_patch.note: Highest road you can drive in Washington. Narrow shelf road with no guardrail; trailers prohibited and it is a truck-only day in any year. Removed '(truck only)' from the name because every drive on this trip is the truck — that belongs in the note, not the title.
scenicDrives_patch.season: THE BIG ONE ON THIS LEG. Two separate problems. (1) Annual: FR 5400 closes for winter, usually 1 Dec. (2) Standing: as of 26 Mar 2026 the road was closed INDEFINITELY from FR 5400-015 (Monument Creek TH) to Harts Pass, from December 2025 rain-and-flood damage plus saturated soils. That closure takes out six trailheads — Robinson, Rattlesnake, Harts Pass, Brown Bear, Slate Pass and Slate Peak — and four campgrounds (Ballard, Riverbend, Harts Pass, Meadows). The Forest Service intended to contract repairs and reopen 'in early summer' 2026, with no date given. Arrive 3 Oct 2027: date is fine, ACCESS IS NOT CONFIRMED. Methow Valley District, 509-996-4000.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: USFS Okanogan-Wenatchee alerts; Methow Valley News, 26 Mar 2026, 'Harts Pass, other Forest Service roads closed indefinitely'

scenicDrives_patch.name: Methow Valley to Twisp and Sun Mountain
scenicDrives_patch.note: Not a designated byway and there is no official route page — it is the valley run south from Winthrop to Twisp plus the climb up to Sun Mountain Lodge, which sits about 1,000 ft above the valley floor and holds the best Cascade view in the Methow. Linked to the state tourism site because nothing more official exists for it; the designated routes in this valley are SR-20 and the wider Cascade Loop, both listed separately.
scenicDrives_patch.season: Valley roads, open year-round. Arrive 3 Oct 2027 — larch and cottonwood colour.
scenicDrives_patch.note_source: scenicwa.com (State of Washington Tourism); Sun Mountain Lodge

winthrop.dogs_source_quote: Dogs are allowed on most other wilderness trails, providing that they are under control at all times.
winthrop.dogs_source_note: DRIFT, and one quote could not be found at all. (1) NOT FOUND: our card attributes to the Blue Lake trailhead page the sentence "Please keep pets on leash to protect wildlife and pets." No current Okanogan-Wenatchee page carrying that sentence could be located. Treat it as unsourced. (2) Our card says "the forest recommends leashing"; the page is firmer — "Certain trails require them to be leashed." (3) The page carries a prohibition our card omits entirely: "Dogs and all pets are prohibited in the Enchantment Permit Area and Ingalls Lake area of Alpine Lakes Wilderness except for Service Dogs."
winthrop.dates_checked: 3-9 Oct 2027, 6 nights. Arrival 3 Oct is a FROZEN anchor — alpine larch prime is 29 Sep to 8 Oct.
winthrop.verdict: THIS SET WAS ALREADY LARGELY RIGHT and it is the best-chosen of the thirteen. Blue Lake, Heather-Maple Pass, Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass, and Grasshopper Pass from Harts Pass are the four canonical alpine larch hikes on the WA-20 / Harts Pass corridor, and Goat Peak Lookout is the right Methow-side addition. Whoever picked those picked for the anchor date, not from a list. Only one thing is added.
winthrop.trails_note: The gap is not a missing famous trail — it is that every single trail on the card is a moderate-to-hard climb of 4 to 11 miles with 1,000-2,000 ft of gain. Six days of that is not what a 53-year-old driver with a dog and a cat aboard will actually do, and there is no wet-day option, no short-evening option and no accessible option in the box at all. Rainy Lake fills all three at once and it is a larch-and-fall-colour walk in its own right. Two things to flag rather than change: (1) DOGS. Pets are permitted on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land but the Heather-Maple Pass Loop, already on the card, runs along the boundary of NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK, where NPS states 'Pets are not allowed within the national park except leashed on the Pacific Crest Trail.' Whether the loop's high traverse crosses that boundary is exactly the sort of thing AllTrails gets wrong, and no authority page read here settles it.
